title: LLM conceptual questions
question:
Conceptual Questions on Transformers and Language Models

These questions and answers cover foundational concepts relevant to understanding Transformer-based language models.

1. What is the time complexity of a Transformer self-attention layer?
2. What is the time complexity of an LSTM layer?
3. Why does the Transformer divide the attention score by √dₕ?
4. Why do Transformers use multi-head attention?
5. Why do Transformers need positional encoding?
6. What are the limitations of the original sinusoidal positional encodings?
7. Why do modern models use RoPE (Rotary Positional Embeddings)?
8. What is the purpose of the attention mask?
9. What is the difference between Pre-LayerNorm and Post-LayerNorm?
10. Why does self-attention enable parallelism, unlike RNNs?
11. What problem does self-attention solve compared to RNNs?
12. Why is dot-product attention preferred over additive attention?
13. Why is softmax used in the attention mechanism?
14. Why are Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) separate projections?
15. What is the role of residual connections in Transformers?
16. Why does the Transformer include an FFN (Feed-Forward Network) after attention?
17. Why is masking required in autoregressive models like GPT?
18. Why did the original Transformer use sinusoidal positional encodings?
19. Why does self-attention model long-range dependencies better than RNNs?
20. What is the mathematical definition of scaled dot-product attention?

steps: Why are Q, K and V separate projections? Attention is a learned lookup: a query says what to find, a key says what can be matched, and a value carries what to copy.
Write Q=XWq, K=XWk and V=XWv, with X shaped (B,T,d_model).
Compute scores QKᵀ, normalize each query's row over keys, then mix the value vectors.
Separate Q and K allow asymmetric relevance. Separate V lets the features used for matching differ from the features transmitted; the output projection mixes heads.
Why divide attention logits by the square root of the head dimension? It controls the initial scale of the dot products so softmax is less likely to become nearly one-hot before learning.
Assume independent, zero-mean, unit-variance query and key coordinates. Each product has variance one.
A sum of d_k such products has variance d_k and standard deviation sqrt(d_k).
Divide by sqrt(d_k), then subtract the row maximum before exponentiation. The divisor controls scale; max subtraction prevents overflow. These are different mechanisms.
Trace every shape in multi-head self-attention. Heads are parallel attention computations over smaller feature spaces; they do not each attend to a disjoint piece of the sequence.
Project X:(B,T,d) into Q,K,V:(B,T,H*d_h). Reshape and transpose to (B,H,T,d_h).
Multiply Q by K transposed on its last two axes to obtain (B,H,T,T). Softmax over the final key axis.
Multiply by V to obtain (B,H,T,d_h), transpose to (B,T,H,d_h), concatenate to (B,T,H*d_h), and apply Wo to return to (B,T,d).
Where does the causal mask go, and why? A decoder must predict using only tokens already available at that position. The mask prevents future-token information from entering the weighted sum.
For query position i, allow key positions j<=i, including the current input token.
Set forbidden scores to negative infinity before softmax; their exponentials become zero and the allowed probabilities are renormalized.
Combine causality with padding and any segment restrictions. Ensure each valid query has at least one allowed key or explicitly define zero output for an empty row.

Why do Transformers need positional information, and what does RoPE do? Without position information, ordinary self-attention cannot reliably distinguish token order. RoPE puts position-dependent rotations into queries and keys.
Split each head vector into coordinate pairs and rotate each pair by its position times a frequency.
Use rotated Q and K in the attention dot product. The relative rotation depends on the difference between their positions.
At cached decoding time, continue the absolute position offset from the prefix. Long-context extension still needs validation; relative structure alone does not guarantee extrapolation.
Compare pre-norm, post-norm, LayerNorm and RMSNorm. Normalization controls activation scale; its placement also changes how gradients travel through a deep residual stack.
Post-norm computes LN(x+F(x)); pre-norm computes x+F(LN(x)). Pre-norm leaves an explicit identity route through the residual addition.
LayerNorm subtracts each token's feature mean and divides by sqrt(feature variance+epsilon), then applies learned scale and usually bias.
RMSNorm divides by sqrt(mean(x²)+epsilon), usually with scale but no centering. Compare stability and quality empirically; neither architecture removes the need to tune training.

Why are residual connections and the feed-forward network both needed? Attention moves information between positions; the feed-forward network transforms the features at each position. Residual additions preserve an easy path for useful existing information.
An attention sublayer creates context-dependent mixtures of token values.
A position-wise nonlinear MLP expands the feature dimension, applies an activation or gate, and projects back. Its weights are shared across positions, not across all layers by default.
Add each sublayer's result to its input. Without nonlinearities, stacked affine feed-forward layers collapse into one affine map; attention's own input-dependent mixing remains nonlinear.

What makes attention quadratic, and what does FlashAttention change? Dense attention compares every query with every key. FlashAttention computes the same attention operation with a different memory-access schedule.
At sequence length T, the logical score matrix has T² entries per head; forming QKᵀ and multiplying by V cost O(T²*d_h).
A naive implementation materializes scores and probabilities in high-bandwidth memory, creating heavy memory traffic.

Tiled exact attention maintains rowwise normalization statistics and avoids storing the full matrix in that memory. Arithmetic remains quadratic for full attention; practical memory use and throughput improve.
solution.contract_notes: Remaining oral points: self-attention pairwise work is O(T²d), with projection/FFN work O(Td²) depending on widths; an LSTM is O(T*(d*h+h²)) and sequential over T. Multi-head attention gives distinct routing/content subspaces, not disjoint token ranges. Sinusoidal positions avoid a finite learned lookup table but do not guarantee useful extrapolation; RoPE rotates Q/K to expose relative phase. Dot-product attention maps efficiently to matrix multiplication; additive attention scores through a learned nonlinear network and is not universally inferior. Softmax gives nonnegative row-normalized mixing weights, with a saturation tradeoff. Scaled attention is softmax(QKᵀ/sqrt(d_k)+M)V. The mask and residual/FFN explanations above cover the remaining repeated why-questions.
solution.example: In “The dog chased the ball because it moved,” a pronoun's query may match an object's key while its value carries object attributes. The three vectors serve different jobs even though they start from the same token state.
solution.trap: Calling Q, K and V three different input sequences: self-attention projects the same input; cross-attention uses a different source for K and V.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### 1. Self-attention time complexity

Separate the projections from pairwise mixing. For length $T$ and width $d$, ordinary projections cost $O(Td^2)$; dense query–key and probability–value products cost $O(T^2d)$ across heads. The logical score tensor contains $H T^2$ entries per example. “Quadratic” names the all-pairs sequence interaction, not every operation in a Transformer. Tiled attention can avoid storing all scores without making full attention's arithmetic linear.

### 2. LSTM time complexity

For input width $d$ and hidden width $h$, the four gate/state projections cost $O(T(dh+h^2))$, up to constant factors. Unlike training-time full-sequence self-attention, the hidden-state recurrence introduces a dependency from step $t-1$ to $t$, limiting parallelism across positions. The comparison depends on both sequence length and width; do not compare only the letter $T$.

### 3. Why scale by the square root?

Assuming independent zero-mean unit-variance coordinates, each $q_jk_j$ has variance one, so

$$\operatorname{Var}(q^\top k)=d_k,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(q^\top k/\sqrt{d_k})=1.$$

This controls the initial softmax scale and reduces saturation. It is distinct from subtracting a maximum to prevent exponential overflow, and the assumptions need not remain exact after training.

### 4. Why multiple heads?

Different projections permit distinct matching and value-transfer patterns in parallel. They all can inspect the permitted sequence; heads do not receive disjoint chunks of tokens by definition. Concatenation and the output projection mix their contributions. More heads change per-head width and parameter/compute tradeoffs, so the benefit is an architectural choice to validate, not an automatic accuracy increase.

### 5. Why positions?

Without an order signal, ordinary attention does not know whether a token precedes or follows another except through supplied structure such as a mask. Add position information or encode position-dependent interactions so reversed/rearranged sentences can be distinguished. Vocabulary embeddings alone identify token content, not its particular occurrence's position.

### 6. Sinusoidal-position limitations

Sinusoids provide deterministic features beyond a finite lookup table, but accepting a larger index does not prove useful long-context behavior. Training length, learned attention patterns and frequency resolution affect extrapolation. Test evidence at different positions and distances; one exact-match “needle” task does not establish general long-range reasoning.

### 7. What RoPE changes

Rotate coordinate pairs of $Q$ and $K$ by position-dependent angles. Its key relation is

$$\langle R_mq,R_nk\rangle=\langle q,R_{n-m}k\rangle.$$

The dot product therefore exposes a relative phase. Ordinary RoPE does not add an embedding to $V$. Cache already-positioned keys consistently and advance decode positions; restarting them at zero changes the computation.

### 8. Attention masks

Apply a boolean allowed relation or an additive $0/-\infty$ mask **before** softmax. A forbidden key receives zero probability after exponentiation. Combine causality, valid keys and any segment isolation with an explicit polarity convention. At least one key must remain valid per queried row, or a separate empty-row policy is needed.

### 9. Pre-LayerNorm versus post-LayerNorm

The arrangements are

$$x'=x+F(\operatorname{LN}(x)),\qquad
x'=\operatorname{LN}(x+F(x)).$$

Pre-norm preserves a direct identity route through the residual addition; post-norm places normalization on that combined route. This changes deep-stack gradient behavior, but neither arrangement makes initialization, precision or learning-rate tuning irrelevant. LayerNorm uses feature statistics per token, not BatchNorm-style running batch statistics.

### 10. Training-time parallelism

Given the full teacher-forced input and mask, all positions' projections and attention products can be computed together. A recurrent model must propagate its hidden state along the sequence. Autoregressive **generation** remains sequential across newly sampled tokens unless an additional decoding scheme changes the execution; parallel training does not mean a basic decoder emits an entire unknown answer at once.

### 11. What long-range problem is addressed?

Self-attention can directly connect distant permitted positions instead of compressing all past information through one recurrent hidden-state update per step. That shorter interaction path helps access but does not guarantee the model selects the right evidence. Memory, context truncation and learned positional behavior still constrain practical use.

### 12. Dot-product versus additive attention

Dot-product scores map efficiently onto matrix multiplication. Additive attention uses a learned compatibility function, often with a nonlinear hidden layer. They express somewhat different scoring mechanisms; hardware efficiency and scale control help explain dot-product popularity without asserting additive attention is mathematically invalid or universally worse.

### 13. Why softmax?

For each query, softmax creates nonnegative weights summing to one, so the head outputs a convex combination of values:

$$p_j=\frac{e^{s_j}}{\sum_k e^{s_k}},\qquad o=\sum_jp_jv_j.$$

Its derivative is $\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top$, which becomes small near a one-hot distribution. This links score scale, saturation and learning. Other normalization/mixing rules are possible, but change the operator.

### 14. Separate Q, K and V

Queries express what to look for; keys express matching features; values express transmitted content. Separate query/key projections allow asymmetric compatibility. If the same projection were used for both on the same unmasked inputs, raw pairwise dot-product scores would be symmetric. A separate value projection avoids forcing “how to find me” and “what to return” into the same representation.

### 15. Residual connections

A residual update preserves existing features while learning a correction. Its derivative includes an identity contribution, which can support gradient propagation through depth. Repeated residual additions can still grow activation scales; residual design does not eliminate the need for normalization, initialization and monitoring.

### 16. The feed-forward network

Attention mixes information between positions; a positionwise nonlinear FFN transforms features within each resulting token state. A typical FFN expands width, applies an activation/gate and projects back. Two affine layers without a nonlinearity collapse into one affine map; that is why the nonlinear transformation matters. Gated and ordinary FFNs have different parameter counts.

### 17. Autoregressive masking

The logit predicting the next token must not use that token's future occurrence in the training input. Teacher forcing provides a complete training sequence, so the causal mask enforces the intended information boundary. Shift targets exactly once and test by changing future tokens: earlier logits must stay the same.

### 18. Why deterministic sinusoids originally?

They offered a parameter-free way to encode positions and express relationships using structured frequencies, without learning a fixed-size position table. That design motivation should not be confused with a guarantee of perfect length extrapolation. Learned absolute embeddings and relative/rotary schemes make different tradeoffs.

### 19. Long-range access versus recurrent compression

A head can retrieve a distant value in one attention interaction, whereas a recurrent representation passes information through successive hidden-state updates. But “can attend” is not “will reason correctly.” Validate distraction resistance, multi-evidence tasks and middle-context retrieval at the actual deployment lengths.

### 20. The complete scaled-attention equation

$$\boxed{\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=
\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm keys}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\right)V.}$$

For $Q:(T_q,d_k)$, $K:(T_k,d_k)$ and $V:(T_k,d_v)$, scores have shape $(T_q,T_k)$ and output $(T_q,d_v)$. State mask meaning and the normalization axis alongside the equation. A diagonal-only allowed mask returns the corresponding values exactly, making a useful minimal correctness test.

title: Implement Scaled Dot-Product Attention
question:
Implement the forward pass of one scaled dot-product self-attention head with NumPy. Each token looks at every token that is allowed, takes a weighted average of their value vectors, and the weights come from how well its query matches their keys.

What to implement
def attention(X: np.ndarray, Wq: np.ndarray, Wk: np.ndarray, Wv: np.ndarray,
mask: np.ndarray | None = None) -> np.ndarray:
...
X has shape (n, d_model): one row per token.
Wq and Wk have shape (d_model, d_k), and Wv has shape (d_model, d_v).
mask is None or a boolean array of shape (n, n). mask[i, j] = True means token i may attend to token j.
Return an array of shape (n, d_v).
Rules
1.
Compute Q = X @ Wq, K = X @ Wk, V = X @ Wv.
2.
The scores are Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k), shape (n, n).
3.
Where mask is False, the pair gets attention weight 0. Every row of mask has at least one True.
4.
Each row of weights is the softmax of that row of scores over the allowed positions, so the weights of a row sum to 1.
5.
The result is weights @ V. Do not round it.
6.
The softmax must not overflow for large scores.
Examples

Example 1

X  = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]    Wq = Wk = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]    Wv = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
Output: [[1.6604769, 2.6604769], [2.3395231, 3.3395231]]

Here V = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. The scores are [[1, 0], [0, 1]] / sqrt(2), so row 0 puts weight 0.6698 on token 0 and 0.3302 on token 1.

Example 2: a mask

Same inputs, mask = [[True, False], [True, True]]
Output: [[1, 2], [2.3395231, 3.3395231]]

Token 0 may only look at itself, so its output is V[0]. Token 1 may look at both tokens, so its row is unchanged.

Constraints
1 <= n <= 512, 1 <= d_model, d_k, d_v <= 256.
Inputs are finite float64 arrays.

steps: Implement stable scaled dot-product attention. Compute a normalized weighted average of values, with one probability distribution per query.
Project X into Q,K,V, then form QKᵀ/sqrt(d_k).
Replace forbidden scores with negative infinity. Subtract each row's maximum, exponentiate, and divide by the row sum.
Return probabilities @ V. Check mask shape and reject rows with no valid keys. See the executable attention implementation in the coding lab.
solution.example: With only the diagonal allowed, output row i must equal value row i, regardless of the other scores.
solution.trap: Softmax over the query axis instead of the key axis, or allowing masked keys to retain probability.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Derivation and a complete small example

For one token matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_{\rm model}}$, learn projections

$$
Q=XW_Q,\qquad K=XW_K,\qquad V=XW_V,
$$

with $W_Q,W_K\in\mathbb R^{d_{\rm model}\times d_k}$ and $W_V\in\mathbb R^{d_{\rm model}\times d_v}$. The output has shape $n\times d_v$. Row $i$ asks which keys help query $i$; therefore softmax normalizes **across columns**, not across queries.

Let $X=W_Q=W_K=I_2$ and $V=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$. The score matrix is $I_2/\sqrt2$. The first row's probabilities are

$$
p_{11}=\frac{e^{1/\sqrt2}}{e^{1/\sqrt2}+1}\approx0.669762,
\qquad p_{12}\approx0.330238.
$$

Its output is $0.669762[1,2]+0.330238[3,4]\approx[1.660477,2.660477]$. This explicitly shows that the output is a weighted value mixture, not the selected key or a vocabulary probability.

For a boolean allowed-mask, set forbidden scores to $-\infty$ **before** softmax. Subtract each valid row maximum before exponentiation; this prevents overflow without changing the distribution. An all-forbidden row needs a declared policy because subtracting $-\infty$ from $-\infty$ creates NaN. This exercise guarantees at least one allowed key, and the reference rejects a violated contract.

**Cost.** Pairwise attention uses $O(n^2(d_k+d_v))$ arithmetic and $O(n^2)$ score storage in this straightforward implementation, in addition to the linear projections. **Checks.** Identity-only masking returns $V$ exactly; changing a forbidden future input must not change an earlier causal output.

title: Multi-Head Attention from Scratch
question:
Implement multi-head scaled dot-product attention from scratch, using only array operations (NumPy or tensor math). Library attention modules such as nn.MultiheadAttention or F.scaled_dot_product_attention are not allowed. The function splits the model dimension into several heads, lets each head attend over the sequence independently, and joins the heads back together.

What to implement

multi_head_attention(Q, K, V, num_heads, mask=None)

Q, K, V: arrays (or nested lists) of shape (batch, seq, d_model). The three share one shape.
num_heads: a positive integer that divides d_model. Each head works on d_k = d_model / num_heads consecutive features.
mask: optional boolean array that can be broadcast to (batch, num_heads, seq, seq). True means the query position may attend to that key position; False means it must not.
Returns a float array of shape (batch, seq, d_model).
Rules
1.
There are no learned projection matrices. Head j uses features j * d_k to (j + 1) * d_k - 1 of Q, K and V directly.
2.
For each head, the scores are Q_h @ K_h^T / sqrt(d_k), with shape (seq, seq) per batch item.
3.
Scores at masked positions (mask is False) are excluded from the softmax, so they get weight exactly 0. Every query row keeps at least one allowed position.
4.
The softmax runs over the key axis and must be numerically stable: huge scores must not overflow.
5.
Each head's output is the attention weights times V_h. The heads are concatenated in head order back to d_model features.
Examples
1.
Q = K = zeros((1, 2, 2)), V = [[[1, 2], [3, 4]]], num_heads = 1, no mask. All scores are 0, so every weight is 0.5 and both rows of the output are [2, 3].
2.
Same inputs with the causal mask [[True, False], [True, True]]. Position 0 sees only itself and position 1 sees both, so the output is [[1, 2], [2, 3]].
Constraints
1 <= batch, seq <= 64, 1 <= d_model <= 512.
num_heads divides d_model.

steps: Trace every shape in multi-head self-attention. Heads are parallel attention computations over smaller feature spaces; they do not each attend to a disjoint piece of the sequence.
Project X:(B,T,d) into Q,K,V:(B,T,H*d_h). Reshape and transpose to (B,H,T,d_h).
Multiply Q by K transposed on its last two axes to obtain (B,H,T,T). Softmax over the final key axis.
Multiply by V to obtain (B,H,T,d_h), transpose to (B,T,H,d_h), concatenate to (B,T,H*d_h), and apply Wo to return to (B,T,d).
Implement stable scaled dot-product attention. Compute a normalized weighted average of values, with one probability distribution per query.
Project X into Q,K,V, then form QKᵀ/sqrt(d_k).
Replace forbidden scores with negative infinity. Subtract each row's maximum, exponentiate, and divide by the row sum.
Return probabilities @ V. Check mask shape and reject rows with no valid keys. See the executable attention implementation in the coding lab.
solution.example: For B=2, T=3, H=4, d_h=8, each score tensor has shape (2,4,3,3); concatenating produces (2,3,32).
solution.trap: Reshaping without the transpose, which silently mixes token and head dimensions while preserving the total element count.
