title: Build an LLM Evaluation Harness with Ollama Integration
question:
Task: Build a Small LLM Evaluation Harness with Ollama Integration

Implement a small evaluation harness within 4 hours, including integration with Ollama (local model serving).

Goal

Build a runnable CLI tool that:

Loads a set of evaluation samples (prompts plus expected output / reference).
Calls a specified model served by local Ollama to generate responses.
Automatically scores generations and outputs a summary report.
Requirements

Ollama integration

Allow specifying the model name via configuration (e.g., llama3, mistral).
Send requests to a local Ollama server and obtain generations.
Handle common failures: service unavailable, timeouts, invalid response formats.

Eval harness

Define a sample schema: id, prompt, optional reference.
Implement at least two automatic metrics (pick any two):
Exact match
Keyword/substring match
Simple similarity (token overlap / Jaccard)
Rule-based checks (e.g., must output yes/no, must contain a JSON field)
For each sample, output: model output, score, and pass/fail.
Output aggregate metrics: average score, pass rate, and a list of failed samples.

Engineering

Clear modular structure (data loading, model calling, scoring, reporting).
Minimal usage instructions (CLI args or README).
Preferably add unit tests or a minimal reproducible test dataset.
Suggested input format

JSONL with one sample per line:

{"id":"1","prompt":"2+2=?","reference":"4"}
Output

Print to stdout or write a JSON report containing:

per-sample outputs and scores
*(remainder of the Output section was cut off in the source page)*

steps: Build an LLM evaluation harness. An evaluation harness is a reproducible experiment, not just a loop over prompts.
Version examples, prompts, model settings, scoring rules and code; keep development and final evaluation sets separate.
Store outputs and failure types; use deterministic checks where possible and validated human or model judgments where necessary.
Report per-task results, cost, latency and uncertainty. Make retries and missing outputs visible rather than silently dropping failures.
Evaluate an agent whose outputs vary between runs. Score whether it achieved the task safely and efficiently, not whether it followed one memorized trajectory.
Create tasks with explicit success checks and resettable environments. Run multiple seeds or repeated trials under fixed budgets.
Track outcome success, invalid actions, unnecessary tool calls, cost, latency and recovery behavior.
Audit trajectories to diagnose failures, while reporting uncertainty across tasks and runs rather than hiding nondeterminism.
solution.contract_notes: Implement the model caller as an injectable adapter and run tests with a deterministic stub rather than requiring a live server. Record prompt/model/configuration, validate returned JSON and retain timeouts as failed examples. Repeated calls and cache keys must use the same explicit version contract.
solution.example: A model that answers 90 of 100 requests correctly and times out on 10 has 90% end-to-end success, not 100% accuracy over completed requests.
solution.trap: Using an LLM judge's score as ground truth without measuring agreement, bias or stability.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Establish what the number actually estimates

Write the population, unit of analysis, outcome window and denominator next to the metric. A per-user mean and a per-impression mean answer different questions. A global mean over unequal batches is

$$
\bar\ell=\frac{\sum_b\sum_{i\in b}\ell_i}{\sum_b n_b},
$$

not generally the unweighted mean of batch means. Workers should reduce numerators and denominators separately when reporting that metric.

Use a comparison with matched examples, mature labels and unchanged definitions. For uncertainty, resample independent units; repeated events within a user or prompt are not automatically independent. A confidence interval measures sampling uncertainty under assumptions, not protection against leaked data or an inappropriate target.

Calibration asks whether predictions around probability $p$ are correct about fraction $p$ of the time. It is not the same as accuracy. A reliability plot should show bin populations, and a calibration-error formula must say whether bins or examples receive equal weight.

When quality regresses, trace data availability, feature freshness, label delays and cohort mix before automatically retraining. For example, a fraud model may look worse on immature labels even when its true behavior has not changed. Report missing/time-out outputs explicitly: dropping them from the denominator can turn an unreliable system into an apparently perfect one.

title: LLM API Practical and Output Validation
question:
LLM API Practical and Output Validation

Build a small backend or notebook function that calls an LLM API, writes a prompt for a given scenario, parses the output, and validates whether the model response satisfies the task. The API key may be provided during the interview.

Low · New	2026-05-01	onsite-coding
Requirements
Call an LLM API from code; one loop explicitly provides the API key.
Write a prompt for the given scenario.
Implement the first function that sends the prompt and handles the model's response.
Normalize or parse the output into the requested format.
Implement a second function that validates whether the previous output is correct.
Follow-up discussion covers:
Output-format validation.
What can go wrong in production.
How to make the feature reliable beyond a demo.
Senior FDE variant: fill in chunks of Python / notebook code to perform LLM evaluations.
Notes
The coding signal is API integration plus defensive engineering, not just prompt wording.
Treat the model output as untrusted. Validate schema, required fields, allowed values, and failure modes before returning it to the caller.
Mention retries and timeouts, but avoid blindly retrying non-idempotent calls. Keep request ids or trace ids if the prompt produces side effects.
For production discussion, cover logging, prompt/version management, cost controls, response validation, fallback behavior, and test fixtures with deterministic mocked responses.

steps: Design tool schemas and validate LLM outputs. A tool response becomes useful only when its structure and meaning are checked by ordinary code.
Specify names, field types, required fields, bounds and enumerations; validate syntax before execution.
Perform semantic checks such as date ordering, inventory availability, authorization and allowed resource identifiers.
Return structured errors that allow a bounded repair attempt. Keep untrusted tool output separate from higher-priority instructions.
solution.example: A JSON object with quantity=-3 can be syntactically valid but invalid for an order request.
solution.trap: Assuming successful JSON parsing proves that a tool call is safe or correct.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Keep evidence, decisions and side effects separate

For grounded generation, preserve a trace from authorized document versions to retrieved chunks to claims in the answer. Diagnose retrieval failures separately from unsupported generation: improving the prompt cannot recover evidence that never entered the context.

For an agent, maintain explicit state, typed tools, execution budgets and a completion predicate. A useful durable step record includes task id, step id, input/configuration version, status, output reference and idempotency key. Persist completion before releasing downstream work. A transcript alone does not encode enough to safely resume external effects.

A read-only model call and a payment or publication call have different recovery semantics. A timeout after a side effect means the outcome may be unknown; retrying with a new operation id can duplicate it. Query status or reconcile under the same id rather than assuming failure.

Enforce resource access and action authorization outside the language model. Retrieved text can contain imperative language; that does not make it a trusted instruction. Validate schemas **and meanings**: valid JSON with an unauthorized resource id is still an invalid request.

Measure end-to-end task success, evidence support, failure categories, latency and cost under fixed budgets. Evaluate with independent checks where possible. A successful tool call is not proof of a successful user outcome, and a fluent answer is not proof its citations support its claims.

title: Async Comparator for Answer Ranking
question:
Description

Ranking model outputs often relies on a judge that looks at two answers and says which is better. Each judge call is slow (0.1 s here), so calls that do not depend on each other should run at the same time with Python's asyncio. Using only the judge, write three functions: compare many pairs at once, find the best answer among N, and find the top k answers in order.

The provided judge

You may call async_compare but not read the scores behind it.

import asyncio

def _hidden_score(answer: str) -> float:
"""The judge's private quality score for an answer (do not call it)."""
...

async def async_compare(a: str, b: str) -> str:
"""Return the better of two answers; on a tie, return a. Takes 0.1 s."""
await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
return a if _hidden_score(a) >= _hidden_score(b) else b

The judge is consistent: equal strings always get equal scores, and a higher score always wins.

What to implement
async def batch_async_compare(pairs: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> list[str]: judge every pair; pairs is a list of (a, b) tuples.
async def find_best_answer(answers: list[str]) -> str: return the best answer; answers is the candidate list.
async def find_top_k_answers(answers: list[str], k: int) -> list[str]: return the k best answers, best first; k is how many to return.
Rules
1.
Ranking. Answer x ranks above answer y if its score is higher, or if the scores are equal and x comes earlier in answers. "Best" means ranked first.
2.
Duplicates. answers may contain the same string more than once. Each occurrence is a separate candidate, so a top-k list may repeat a string.
3.
batch_async_compare returns one winner per pair, in the same order as pairs, and async_compare(a, b) decides each pair. An empty list returns [].
4.
find_best_answer raises ValueError on an empty list and returns the only answer of a one-element list without calling the judge.
5.
find_top_k_answers returns min(k, len(answers)) answers ordered by rule 1. k = 0 returns []; a negative k raises ValueError.
6.
Time. A round is 0.1 s of waiting for the judge; calls started together finish in one round.
batch_async_compare finishes in one round, however many pairs there are.
find_best_answer on n answers uses at most n − 1 judge calls and at most ⌈log2 n⌉ rounds.
find_top_k_answers uses at most k·(n − 1) judge calls and at most k·⌈log2 n⌉ rounds.
Examples

All examples use the hidden scores A = 3, B = 9, C = 5, D = 1, E = 9.

Example 1

await batch_async_compare([("A", "B"), ("C", "D"), ("E", "B")])   # ["B", "C", "E"]

B beats A and C beats D. E and B tie, so the judge returns its first argument, E. All three calls run together, so this takes 0.1 s.

Example 2

await find_best_answer(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"])   # "B"

B and E share the top score, and B comes first in the list, so B ranks first. A knockout needs 4 calls and 3 rounds here: (A, B) and (C, D) in round 1, then (B, C), then (B, E).

Example 3

await find_top_k_answers(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"], 3)    # ["B", "E", "C"]
await find_top_k_answers(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"], 10)   # ["B", "E", "C", "A", "D"]
await find_top_k_answers(["C", "C", "A"], 2)              # ["C", "C"]

B outranks E because it comes first; C is next with score 5. A k larger than the list returns every answer in rank order. Duplicates count separately.

Constraints
0 <= len(pairs) <= 1000 and 0 <= len(answers) <= 1000.
0 <= k <= len(answers) in normal use; larger k is clamped as in rule 5.
Answers are non-empty strings.

steps: Rank answers with an expensive asynchronous pairwise judge. Concurrency can reduce elapsed time, but it does not make inconsistent pairwise preferences a valid total order.
Define the ranking procedure, tie behavior and what to do when the judge produces cycles or noise.
Limit concurrent calls with a semaphore, cache pair results and deduplicate in-flight comparisons. Retry only under a bounded policy.
Use a tournament or scored comparison graph appropriate to the budget; evaluate rank stability with repeated judgments.
solution.example: If A beats B, B beats C and C beats A, a standard deterministic sort comparator's transitivity assumption is violated.
solution.trap: Launching every pair at once and exhausting rate limits, or interpreting one noisy comparison as certainty.

title: RAG Notebook (ML Coding)
question:
RAG Notebook (ML Coding)

ML-coding round in a Colab notebook: fill in a simple RAG pipeline — generate text embeddings from a pandas DataFrame, retrieve the top-10 by cosine similarity to the query embedding, and run a short evaluation. Some utility functions are pre-provided.

Requirements
Conducted in a Colab notebook (the recruiter flags this in advance); some utility functions are pre-provided and you fill in / modify the implementation.
Build a simple retrieval-augmented pipeline:
Generate embeddings for text stored in a pandas DataFrame.
Embed the query and compute cosine similarity against the document embeddings; take the top-10.
Run an evaluation step over the retrieved results.
Notes
This is an ML-coding round, not a from-scratch algorithm — comfort with the numpy/pandas + embedding/cosine-similarity idioms is what's tested. Candidates without ML-coding reps report struggling here.
Pairs with a RAG-flavored system-design round in ML-leaning loops, since RAG over legal documents is Harvey's core product.

steps: Design a minimal retrieval-augmented question-answering system. Retrieve relevant evidence first, then generate an answer grounded in that evidence.
Ingest documents with stable ids, versions and access metadata; chunk them and build lexical and/or embedding indexes.
At query time apply authorization filters, retrieve candidates and rerank if needed. Supply bounded context with document identifiers to the generator.
Return evidence-linked answers or abstain when support is missing. Evaluate retrieval coverage separately from answer faithfulness and correctness.
Choose chunk size and overlap for retrieval. A chunk must be specific enough to retrieve accurately and large enough to preserve the context needed for interpretation.
Start with document structure: headings, paragraphs, tables and code boundaries rather than arbitrary character cuts.
Compare chunk sizes on realistic questions using retrieval coverage, context utilization and final answer quality.
Use overlap to preserve boundary context, then deduplicate retrieved evidence so repeated text does not waste the generation budget.
When should you combine lexical retrieval, embeddings and reranking? Different retrieval signals capture different kinds of matching and fail in different ways.
Use lexical retrieval for exact terms, identifiers and uncommon names; use embeddings for semantic similarity and paraphrases.
Fuse candidate rankings using a defined rule such as reciprocal-rank fusion rather than adding incomparable raw scores blindly.
Rerank a manageable candidate set with a stronger scorer, and measure the gain against latency and cost.
Diagnose a RAG system's wrong answer. Locate the first failed stage before changing the entire pipeline.
Check whether a correct, authorized answer exists in the indexed corpus and whether ingestion preserved it.
Inspect retrieved and reranked evidence, context truncation, query rewriting and access filters.
If adequate evidence reached the model, inspect prompt instructions, unsupported synthesis and answer evaluation. Maintain a stage-specific failure taxonomy.
Reduce RAG latency without sacrificing correctness blindly. Optimize the measured critical path while protecting retrieval and answer quality.
Trace query processing, retrieval, reranking, prompt assembly, prefill and generation separately, including p95 and p99.
Try bounded candidate counts, batching, parallel independent retrieval and version-aware caches. Shorten redundant context before discarding necessary evidence.
Compare quality, latency and cost on the same query set; canary changes and preserve timeouts and fallbacks.
solution.example: If the correct paragraph is never retrieved, changing the answer prompt alone cannot solve that query.
solution.trap: Treating a fluent answer with citations as proof that the cited text supports the claim.

title: Design a Grounded AI Chatbot App
question:

Support multi-turn chat with streamed answers and citations to source passages.
2.

Ingest document creates, updates, and deletes; changed content must become searchable within five minutes.

A document changed 30 seconds ago, but the assistant cites its old version. Trace and fix the failure.
2.
Two retrieved passages contradict each other. Define the answer and citation behavior.

Add authenticated tool calls while treating retrieved text as untrusted input.

title: Layered Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks
question:
This problem asks you to design and quantify layered safeguards that keep a tool-using language-model assistant from being manipulated into breaking its rules.

Task
Part 1 — Definitions
1.
Define a jailbreak and a prompt injection, and give one example of each.
2.
Explain why a more capable model does not remove either risk.
Part 2 — Defence in depth

An assistant can read a user's email and call tools that send and delete messages. Design a layered defence. For each layer, state what it inspects, what kinds of attack it catches, what it misses, and what it costs in latency and in wrongly refused requests.

Part 3 — Combining layers (quantitative)

Four layers miss 20%, 30%, 15% and 50% of attacks respectively.

1.
Compute the fraction of attacks that pass all four layers if the layers fail independently.
2.
Explain why real layers do not fail independently, in which direction this moves the true pass-through rate, and how you would measure the real rate.
3.
Explain how to choose layers so that their failures overlap as little as possible.
Part 4 — The cost to legitimate users (quantitative)

Three of the layers wrongly block 2%, 1% and 3% of benign requests, independently. Compute the fraction of benign requests that are refused end to end, and explain how you would set each layer's threshold.

Part 5 — Priorities

State which layer you would build first for this assistant, and justify the choice.

steps: Defend an LLM application against prompt injection. Treat retrieved pages, messages and tool results as untrusted data, and enforce permissions outside the language model.

Authorize actions and resource access in code. Validate arguments, isolate execution and avoid exposing secrets through prompts or broad tools.
Test indirect instructions embedded in retrieved content, exfiltration attempts and ambiguous action requests. Monitor and review failures.

title: LLM SQL Chatbot Access Control and Query Safety
question:
LLM SQL Chatbot Access Control and Query Safety

Design an LLM chatbot for SQL query generation over internal data. The discussion focuses on ensuring users can only query data they are allowed to access and preventing hallucinated or expensive queries such as accidental cross joins from crashing a Trino cluster.

DS Infra Eng · Tags: llm · sql · access-control · query-optimization · security · medium

Requirements

Design an internal LLM chatbot that generates SQL queries.

Functional requirements:

Accept natural-language analytical questions from users.
Generate SQL against governed internal datasets.
Enforce data access so each user can only query authorized tables, columns, and rows.
Prevent unsafe, nonsensical, or extremely expensive SQL from reaching the warehouse unchecked.
Return useful errors or clarifying questions when the request cannot be answered safely.

Constraints and design points:

Trino-cluster stability is a first-class constraint.
Cross joins and hallucinated table / column names are explicit failure modes.
Access control must be enforced outside the model, not only through prompting.
Notes

A strong design puts the LLM behind deterministic policy and validation layers:

Retrieve the user's authorized schema subset before generation and expose only that subset to the model.
Validate generated SQL against a parser and catalog before execution.
Apply a policy engine for table, column, and row-level permissions.
Add query guards: join limits, required predicates for large tables, cost estimation, timeout, row limit, and read-only execution.
Use dry-run / explain-plan checks before submitting to Trino.
Log prompts, generated SQL, policy decisions, and execution metadata for audit and improvement.

Audit query and policy versions with sensitive values redacted. Test indirect instructions, cross-tenant joins, data exfiltration through functions and unexpectedly expensive queries.

title: Design Prompt Playground
question:
Prompt Engineering Playground — Interview Question
Background

• Prompt engineering is the process of trying to alter the input prompt for a model in order to make it better at performing a certain task.

• Prompt playgrounds do not operate around conversations.

The goal is to find the best one-off request to the model by trying variants of a message repeatedly and looking at the response. Each run happens separately, and the model has no memory between runs.

• Developing prompts is a process of trial and error.

You might try something that makes the output worse and then want to revert back to an old version to try something else.

• This system is focused on text prompts only, and will never expand to multimodal.

• Example use case from the text:

A user trying to generate a recipe might begin with a simple prompt like “Write me a recipe,” then iteratively refine it with additions like “You are a great chef who has written many cookbooks,” or by including multiple examples of good and bad recipes.

Goal

We want to build a prompt playground service where:

• Users can build and iterate on prompts.

Interview Question

Design a backend system for this prompt playground.

Your design must address the following, directly based on the provided text:

One-off, stateless model calls

Each prompt run must be isolated.
The model should have no memory between runs.

Prompt iteration and versioning

Users must be able to try many variations of a prompt.
Users must be able to revert to previous versions after a bad iteration.

Text-only scope

The system must support *only text prompts*.
The design should explicitly ignore any multimodal considerations.

Usage scenario from the text

Users iteratively refine prompts such as recipe-generation prompts.
The system should support trying improved versions, adding context, or adding examples.

Your task:

• Propose the data model to support iterative prompt development and version tracking.

• Describe the API endpoints needed to run a single prompt (statelessly), save a new iteration, list past versions, and revert to a previous version.

• Explain the architecture needed to ensure each run is independent and the model has no memory.

• Ensure the design matches *only what is explicitly stated in the text*.

Do not add new features beyond what is given above.

Support side-by-side evaluation on a fixed test set, parameter sweeps with bounded concurrency and exportable reproducible configurations.
Keep provider credentials out of client code, authorize sharing and distinguish exploratory runs from locked benchmark results.

title: Live Coding: Replace a Heuristic Terminal Game with an LLM-Driven Agent
question:
Coding Task: Replace a Heuristic Python Implementation of a Terminal Text-Based Game with an LLM-Driven Agent

You are given a terminal text-based game and a large Python reference implementation (hundreds of lines) that relies on heuristic/rule-based logic.

Within the time limit, implement a new agent that:

Does not rely on the existing heuristics for decision making;
Instead calls an LLM API (or a local mock) to generate an action each step;
Can reliably win/reach the goal, and includes basic debugging/recovery when things go wrong.
Requirements
You may keep the environment/game engine interaction, but must replace the "decision logic".
Create a clear prompt including state representation, available actions, history/trajectory, and strict output formatting.
Implement at least one robustness strategy (retry, format validation, action legality checks, self-correction, etc.).
Add observability: logs for key steps, per-turn state/action, saving failed traces, etc.
Abstract I/O
Input: the game's per-turn textual state (stdout), optionally the set of available commands/actions.
Output: the chosen action/command for that turn (written to stdin or returned from a function).
Constraints
Needs to be runnable repeatedly during the interview.
LLM calls are limited; manage latency/cost and avoid unnecessary calls.
Example test cases (to be adapted to the actual game)
Basic success: run 10 episodes with a fixed seed; win at least 8.
Format robustness: handle malformed LLM outputs via validation + retry.
Action legality: detect illegal actions and recover to a legal action.
Observability: logs include state, action, raw LLM output, and validation result.
Degradation: after repeated LLM failures, fall back to a simple baseline and continue.

Note: AI coding tools are allowed; evaluation focuses on implementation, debugging, reliability, and verifiability.

Example Input:

seed=0
episodes=10
llm_mode=normal

Example Output:

wins>=8

Design tool schemas and validate LLM outputs. A tool response becomes useful only when its structure and meaning are checked by ordinary code.

title: Agents / Coding with LLMs
question:
Research-track 1-of-N option: write code in Colab that uses an LLM, via the Anthropic API, as a building block — designing prompts and a tool-use loop to solve a multi-step problem. Open-book on documentation; starter API code is supplied so you do not need to memorize syntax.

Requirements

The recruiter blurb is explicit:

"This interview will test writing code with LLMs as a building block, and prompting to create an agent. You should be conceptually familiar with Tool Use and Agents and how they are handled in our API. The interview is open-book and we provide starter code for using the API, so there's no need to memorize exact API syntax."

Reported shape
Colab notebook.
55 minutes on Google Meet.
Share-screen.
Starter cell wraps the Messages API and the tool-use schema.
The task itself is open-ended: design prompts for an agent that plans a small workflow, defines its own tools, and demonstrates progress on a concrete input.
Specific tasks have not been described in detail publicly.
Reported task — stock-price agent

One concrete instance: the starter code answers stock-price questions that need only a single tool call, and you extend it into an agent loop that handles questions requiring multi-step reasoning and multiple tool calls.

A second part asks you to reduce the number of turns the agent needs to reach an answer — partly a prompt-engineering exercise, partly a test of how you structure the loop.

Candidate task

You are given starter code for using the Anthropic Messages API with tool use. The starter code can already answer stock-price questions that require only one tool call, for example:

"What is the latest price of AAPL?"

Your task is to extend this starter code into an agent loop that can answer questions requiring multi-step reasoning and multiple tool calls, for example:

"Which performed better since 2024-01-02: Apple or Nvidia?"

or:

"If I bought USD 10,000 of Microsoft stock one year ago, approximately how much would it be worth today?"

The exact stock-data source is abstracted away. You may assume the starter notebook gives you simple Python functions such as:

def get_ticker(company_name: str) -> dict:
"""
Given a company name, return its stock ticker.
Example:
get_ticker("Apple") -> {"company_name": "Apple", "ticker": "AAPL"}
"""

def get_stock_price(ticker: str, date: str) -> dict:
"""
Given a ticker and date, return the closing stock price.
date may be an ISO date like "2024-01-02" or "latest".
Example:
get_stock_price("AAPL", "latest") -> {"ticker": "AAPL", "date": "latest", "price": 212.4}
"""

You may define additional tools if they make the agent more robust or reduce the number of turns.

Starter code

Assume the starter notebook gives you a wrapper around the Messages API, similar to:

from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()

def call_model(messages, tools, system_prompt):
return client.messages.create(
model="claude-3-5-sonnet-latest",
max_tokens=1024,
system=system_prompt,
messages=messages,
tools=tools,
)

You do not need to memorize exact API syntax. Focus on designing the prompt, defining tools, and implementing the agent loop.

What to implement

Implement an agent that:

1.
Defines a system prompt for a stock-question-solving agent.
2.
Defines tool-use schemas for the available stock tools.
3.
Sends the user question to the model.
4.
Parses the model response.
5.
Detects tool_use blocks.
6.
Dispatches each tool call to the corresponding Python function.
7.
Returns tool_result blocks back to the model.
8.
Iterates until the model reaches a final answer.
9.
Adds a max-turn limit to avoid infinite loops.
10.
Handles basic tool errors gracefully.
11.
Demonstrates progress on a concrete input.

You should show the agent working on:

"What is the latest price of Apple?"

and on at least one multi-step question such as:

"Which performed better since 2024-01-02: Apple or Nvidia?"
Part 2 — reduce the number of turns

After your first working solution, improve the agent so it needs fewer turns to reach an answer.

This is partly a prompt-engineering exercise and partly a test of how you structure the loop.

Possible approaches:

Encourage the model to call all independent tools in the same turn.
Add a batch tool, such as get_stock_prices.
Make the tool descriptions more explicit.
Add an output contract.
Make the exit condition clearer.
Refactor the loop so it handles multiple tool calls per assistant message.
Notes

Open-book on docs, no AI assistants beyond the supplied API. Screen-share lets the interviewer watch how you iterate on prompts.

AI-assisted coding variant — Claude Code CLI

A distinct rotation reframes this round from building an agent to coding with one. The recruiter blurb:

"This interview will evaluate your ability to write and review code using AI tools. You'll have access to the Claude Code CLI, and are allowed [to] search things up on Google, Stack Overflow, etc. You'll work on some practical engineering tasks in a browser-based environment that is similar to Visual Studio Code + GitHub. No account setup is required in advance."

Here AI assistance is the point, not a banned tool — you drive the Claude Code CLI to complete and review practical engineering tasks in a hosted VS Code-like environment, and you are graded on how effectively you delegate, verify, and review AI-written code.

This contrasts sharply with the standard live-coding rounds where assistants are forbidden. Task specifics are not public yet; treat it as a code-review plus agentic-workflow exercise rather than a from-scratch algorithm round, and practice reading and correcting AI-generated diffs quickly.

title: Evaluating an LLM Agent with Subjective, Nondeterministic Outputs
question:
Design an evaluation framework for an LLM-based agent that is deployed to users and whose outputs are subjective and nondeterministic. There is no single correct answer to compare against, and the same request can produce a different response each time. The framework must tell the team whether a new version of the agent is better or worse than the current one, both before release and after it ships.

Requirements
1.
Quality definition and metrics: turn "a good response" into measurable criteria. Separate objective checks (task completed, valid tool calls, right format, nothing unsafe) from judgment-based quality (helpfulness, tone, usefulness). Say which metrics block a release.
2.
Nondeterminism: a score must be a property of the agent version, not of one lucky or unlucky sample. Say how many samples you draw per request, how you compare them, and how you report the result.
3.
Offline evaluation: a repeatable evaluation that runs before release on a fixed set of requests. Say where the requests and labels come from, who produces the labels, how the automated graders work, and how you measure the graders' quality.
4.
Online evaluation: how you measure quality on live traffic after release, and how you compare two versions in production.
5.
Decision rule: how the offline and online results combine into a ship or no-ship decision, with the sample sizes needed for the result to be trusted.
6.
Walkthrough: the path of one new agent version from first build to full rollout.
Scope

Keep the agent generic: any LLM agent that takes a user request, may call tools, and returns a response. Training the agent itself is out of scope; state any traffic or labeling assumptions you make.

Follow-ups
Follow-up 1: the LLM judge is over-confident

An LLM used as a judge often reports high confidence and still disagrees with careful human raters. How do you measure how far it can be trusted, and how do you use it anyway?

Follow-up 2: users rarely give explicit feedback

Only a small share of sessions end with a rating, and those that do are skewed toward very happy or very unhappy users. What do you measure instead, and how do you know it reflects quality?

Follow-up 3: the developers' own judgment is biased

The people building the agent tend to rate their own changes favourably and to tune the agent to the examples they look at. How do you keep the evaluation honest?

steps: Evaluate an agent whose outputs vary between runs. Score whether it achieved the task safely and efficiently, not whether it followed one memorized trajectory.
Create tasks with explicit success checks and resettable environments. Run multiple seeds or repeated trials under fixed budgets.
Track outcome success, invalid actions, unnecessary tool calls, cost, latency and recovery behavior.
Audit trajectories to diagnose failures, while reporting uncertainty across tasks and runs rather than hiding nondeterminism.
Build an LLM evaluation harness. An evaluation harness is a reproducible experiment, not just a loop over prompts.
Version examples, prompts, model settings, scoring rules and code; keep development and final evaluation sets separate.
Store outputs and failure types; use deterministic checks where possible and validated human or model judgments where necessary.
Report per-task results, cost, latency and uncertainty. Make retries and missing outputs visible rather than silently dropping failures.

solution.trap: Rewarding matching tool-call sequences even when an alternative sequence is valid and more efficient.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Establish what the number actually estimates

Write the population, unit of analysis, outcome window and denominator next to the metric. A per-user mean and a per-impression mean answer different questions. A global mean over unequal batches is

$$
\bar\ell=\frac{\sum_b\sum_{i\in b}\ell_i}{\sum_b n_b},
$$

not generally the unweighted mean of batch means. Workers should reduce numerators and denominators separately when reporting that metric.

Use a comparison with matched examples, mature labels and unchanged definitions. For uncertainty, resample independent units; repeated events within a user or prompt are not automatically independent. A confidence interval measures sampling uncertainty under assumptions, not protection against leaked data or an inappropriate target.

Calibration asks whether predictions around probability $p$ are correct about fraction $p$ of the time. It is not the same as accuracy. A reliability plot should show bin populations, and a calibration-error formula must say whether bins or examples receive equal weight.

When quality regresses, trace data availability, feature freshness, label delays and cohort mix before automatically retraining. For example, a fraud model may look worse on immature labels even when its true behavior has not changed. Report missing/time-out outputs explicitly: dropping them from the denominator can turn an unreliable system into an apparently perfect one.

title: Design Durable Execution for Long-Running Agent Queries
question:
Design the backend for an AI assistant that answers research questions by running an agent. The agent is a loop that calls a language model and a web search API many times before it writes the final answer. Some questions finish in seconds, others keep working for hours.

Today a single request handler runs the whole loop in memory, so a crashed process, a deploy, a closed browser tab or a dropped connection loses the work. Redesign it so a question, once accepted, is answered even if the user disappears.

In this statement a step is one model or search call together with the checkpoint saved after it.

Current system
1.
A client calls an ask endpoint.
2.
The endpoint calls an ask service, which loops over the model and the search API (both are black boxes you do not change) and streams tokens back on the same connection.
3.
All state lives in the memory of that one process. There is no record that the question ever existed.
Requirements
1.
Durability: once the system has accepted a question, it must run to completion even if the browser tab is closed, the phone loses connectivity, or a worker process dies in the middle of a step.
2.
Long runs: a question may run for hours. A deploy or a node replacement must not cancel it.
3.
Progress streaming: the client sees progress (the plan, sources found, partial answer text) as it happens. After a disconnect it reconnects, possibly on another device, and continues from where it left off without missing or repeating events.
4.
Result access: a user who comes back later, with no connection open, can fetch the finished answer.
5.
Control: the user can cancel a question. The system enforces a step budget and a token budget per question.
6.
Cost safety: model and search calls cost money. A crash must not make the system pay for the whole question again.
Scale assumptions (assumptions for this exercise, not given facts)
5 million questions per day, 20 minutes on average, peak traffic 3 times the average.
About 40 model or search calls per question, and about 200 progress events of 300 bytes each.
A checkpoint after each step is a delta of about 20 KB; a final answer with its sources is about 200 KB.
About 60% of running questions have a client attached at any moment.
Finished answers are kept for 30 days.
Non-goals
Improving answer quality, ranking, or the model itself.
Authentication and billing design (assume a user id and a quota check exist).
Making the model or search calls themselves faster.
Deliverables
1.
The API: how a question is submitted, how progress is streamed and resumed, how the result is fetched, how it is cancelled.
2.
The architecture and the data model: where state lives and what is stored per question and per step.
3.
How execution survives a crash, and what exactly is repeated after one.
4.
Back-of-envelope sizing for running queries, workers, checkpoint write rate, event volume and stream connections.
5.
Failure behaviour for a worker crash, a lost client, a reconnect storm and a stuck step.
Follow-ups
Follow-up 1: queries that wait for a human, such as a clarifying question, for up to a day.
Follow-up 2: a user starts the same question twice by double-tapping, or the client retries after a timeout.
Follow-up 3: a single query must fan out to 20 parallel sub-agents and join their results.

steps: Represent the workflow as a durable state machine with task/step ids, inputs, budget, versioned prompts/models, artifacts and terminal conditions. Persist a completed step before scheduling its dependents.

Checkpoint long-running work, resume from committed steps and use compensating actions for partial external effects. A movie pipeline additionally needs asset/shot dependencies, continuity checks and reusable versioned outputs; a code-fix pipeline needs tests and review gates.
Measure task success, recovery, cost and user-visible correctness. Stop on budget exhaustion or repeated non-progress rather than running an unattended loop forever.

title: ML Model Design — Prompt-to-Design Generation
question:
ML Model Design — Prompt-to-Design Generation

Design a generative ML system that turns a natural-language description into a design, and walk through its full model lifecycle with the emphasis on data and evaluation.

Choose one of two output framings and justify the choice:

Concept image — a vision-language model that outputs a concept mock of the described screen.
Webpage HTML — a model that outputs renderable HTML/CSS for the described page.
Questions to answer
1.
Framing and requirements — the inputs and outputs, what a successful generation means, and the latency and cost targets.
2.
Training data — where (prompt, design) pairs come from, how you collect and label them at scale, and how you clean them.
3.

4.

5.

6.

title: ML Design: Recruiter Hiring Pipeline Assistant
question:
Recruiters each handle several open roles and hundreds of candidates at once, and their time, not the supply of candidates, is what limits hiring. Design an ML-powered assistant for a professional network that helps recruiters move candidates through the hiring pipeline (sourcing, outreach, screening, interview, offer) and get more done with the same hours. Keep each part brief: the goal is one coherent design, not every possible component.

Requirements
Users are recruiters, each handling several open roles and hundreds of candidates at the same time. Recruiter time is the scarce resource.
The assistant may suggest, rank, draft and remind. A recruiter makes every final decision about a candidate.
Assume the platform holds member profiles, job postings, recruiter actions, messages and the outcome of past hiring processes.
What to cover
1.
Problem framing and success metrics: who the users are, what hurts today, what the assistant does, and the metrics that tell you it works (efficiency, quality of hire, and guardrails).
2.
Funnel and drop-off analysis: define the pipeline stages, how you measure the drop-off between them, and how you decide where the assistant should intervene first.
3.
Data and labels: which signals and labels you use, how you handle delayed, missing and biased outcomes, and how you build training examples.
4.
Candidate-prioritization ranking model: the model that orders candidates for a recruiter, including features, objective, how it differs between stages, and how it copes with cold start.
5.
System architecture: from event ingestion to the screen the recruiter sees, covering offline and online components, latency and refresh.
6.
Evaluation: offline metrics and validation, then online experiments, including how you measure a recruiter-facing tool when outcomes arrive weeks later.
7.
Risks: fairness, feedback loops, privacy, and what you monitor after launch.
Deliverable

A structured design discussion that covers all seven parts, with the trade-offs you chose and the ones you rejected.

title: Design an LLM-Backed Customer-Service Chat System with Failure Handling
question:
Design a customer-service chat system in which an AI agent answers customers. The agent's replies are generated by an external LLM provider that your company does not operate, and the replies are streamed to the customer as they are generated.

Scale and assumptions
1.
Traffic: 50,000 conversations are active at peak. In an active conversation the customer sends a message about every 20 seconds.
2.
Replies: an average reply is about 300 tokens, and the provider streams about 50 tokens per second.
3.
Clients: customers use a web widget or a mobile app. Their networks can be slow or drop for seconds at a time.
4.
Provider: the external LLM API has rate limits, occasional elevated error rates, slow first tokens and streams that stop mid-reply. A second provider (or a second region of the same provider) is available as a fallback.
5.
Actions: the agent can call internal tools, for example to look up an order or issue a refund.
6.
Handoff: a conversation can be escalated to a human agent.
Parts to address
1.
Happy path, end to end: trace one customer message from the client to the agent, through the LLM call and any tool calls, and back to the customer as a streamed reply. Name every component, what it stores, and what the client sees at each step.
2.
Pub/sub message flow: how messages and streamed reply chunks are published and delivered to the customer's connection (and to a human agent's console when one joins). Cover what happens when the customer has more than one tab or device open.
3.
Failure handling (the main focus):
The LLM provider partially fails: a share of calls error out, calls are rate limited, or the first token does not arrive in time.
A stream is cut off in the middle of a reply.
The provider is down for minutes.
The customer's network breaks, during a send or during a streamed reply, and later reconnects.
4.
Retry policy: when and how to retry, including exponential backoff with jitter, a cap on the delay, a limit on total retries, and a deadline per customer turn. Show the expected delay of each retry.
5.
Client-side handling: what the client does on a failed send, a lost connection and a half-received reply, and what the customer sees.
Deliverables
1.
The architecture and the message flow for the happy path.
2.
The data model for conversations, messages and reply chunks.
3.
Capacity estimates: LLM calls per second and the number of open streams.
4.
A failure table: each failure, how it is detected, what the system does, and what the customer sees.
5.
The retry parameters you choose, with the numbers behind them.
Constraints
A customer must never be charged, refunded or otherwise acted on twice because of a retry.
A customer must never see the same message twice or see a reply with a gap in it.
Retries must not make a provider outage worse.

steps: Design a minimal retrieval-augmented question-answering system. Retrieve relevant evidence first, then generate an answer grounded in that evidence.
Ingest documents with stable ids, versions and access metadata; chunk them and build lexical and/or embedding indexes.
At query time apply authorization filters, retrieve candidates and rerank if needed. Supply bounded context with document identifiers to the generator.
Return evidence-linked answers or abstain when support is missing. Evaluate retrieval coverage separately from answer faithfulness and correctness.
Build an agent loop with explicit stop conditions. An agent alternates deciding what to do with receiving observations; the surrounding program must enforce limits.
Represent task state, available typed tools, execution history and a completion condition explicitly.
Validate each proposed tool call, execute with bounded time and record the observation. Distinguish read operations from consequential actions.
Stop on success, budget exhaustion, repeated failure or required human input; return an honest partial result if the objective is not reached.
Design tool schemas and validate LLM outputs. A tool response becomes useful only when its structure and meaning are checked by ordinary code.
Specify names, field types, required fields, bounds and enumerations; validate syntax before execution.
Perform semantic checks such as date ordering, inventory availability, authorization and allowed resource identifiers.
Return structured errors that allow a bounded repair attempt. Keep untrusted tool output separate from higher-priority instructions.
solution.example: If the correct paragraph is never retrieved, changing the answer prompt alone cannot solve that query.
solution.trap: Treating a fluent answer with citations as proof that the cited text supports the claim.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Keep evidence, decisions and side effects separate

For grounded generation, preserve a trace from authorized document versions to retrieved chunks to claims in the answer. Diagnose retrieval failures separately from unsupported generation: improving the prompt cannot recover evidence that never entered the context.

For an agent, maintain explicit state, typed tools, execution budgets and a completion predicate. A useful durable step record includes task id, step id, input/configuration version, status, output reference and idempotency key. Persist completion before releasing downstream work. A transcript alone does not encode enough to safely resume external effects.

A read-only model call and a payment or publication call have different recovery semantics. A timeout after a side effect means the outcome may be unknown; retrying with a new operation id can duplicate it. Query status or reconcile under the same id rather than assuming failure.

Enforce resource access and action authorization outside the language model. Retrieved text can contain imperative language; that does not make it a trusted instruction. Validate schemas **and meanings**: valid JSON with an unauthorized resource id is still an invalid request.

Measure end-to-end task success, evidence support, failure categories, latency and cost under fixed budgets. Evaluate with independent checks where possible. A successful tool call is not proof of a successful user outcome, and a fluent answer is not proof its citations support its claims.

title: ML System to Detect Harmful LLM Content
question: Design an ML system to detect harmful content produced by an LLM. The system feeds a content-moderation pipeline. Cover: data collection and labeling quality, model choice across modalities, evaluation under heavy class imbalance, deployment for both online and offline content, online monitoring, adversarial drift, and — the distinctive part of this round — the policy and human-in-the-loop dimension: how model predictions map to auto-action thresholds vs. human review queues, how labeling feedback closes the loop, and how the system stays aligned with evolving content policy. Discuss scalability, reliability, and the precision/recall trade-off across harm categories.

steps: Design multi-modal harmful-content detection. Use a calibrated triage system that combines automated decisions with human review capacity.
Define harm categories, policy versions and separate precision/recall targets per action and category.
Run cheap per-modality filters, then stronger joint models on uncertain cases; reserve pre-publication and asynchronous paths with separate latency budgets.
Prioritize a bounded review queue, audit decisions and retrain from reviewed labels with sampling-bias checks.
solution.example: A high-confidence severe violation can be blocked, while ambiguous content may receive limited distribution and human review under the specified policy.
solution.trap: Optimizing one aggregate accuracy metric while hiding catastrophic errors on a rare category.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Design the decision, not only the predictor

State which user action follows the model output, when the prediction occurs and which errors are costly. Then define labels and features using information available at that time. A feature recorded after the outcome is not made legitimate by being stored in the same table.

For a retrieval/ranking product, use a cascade: generate a broad eligible set, score a bounded candidate set, then apply policy and presentation rules. Evaluate retrieval recall separately because a ranker cannot rescue an item excluded upstream. Availability, permissions and budgets are hard constraints, not merely features a model may learn to respect.

Expected action utility can be written as

$$
a^*(x)=\arg\max_a\sum_y P(y\mid x)\,U(a,y).
$$

This makes clear why a probability metric and a product objective are different. The same calibrated probability may produce different actions when error costs change.

Describe a baseline, time/entity-aware validation, exposure logging and one controlled rollout. For a recommender, unexposed items are not automatically observed negatives. For moderation or fraud, mature labels and human-review capacity matter. Finish with a failure walkthrough: what happens when features are stale, the model is unavailable or the distribution changes? A simpler fallback with explicit monitoring is often more defensible than an elaborate system without an operational plan.

title: Designing a Harmful Content Detection System
question:
Design a system that detects harmful content on a large photo and video sharing social platform. Users upload images, videos and text (captions and comments); some of it is hate speech, harassment, nudity, self-harm or misinformation. The system must flag it automatically across all modalities, act on the clear cases, and send uncertain cases to human reviewers.

Requirements
1.
Handle multi-modal content: an image with its caption, a video with its comments, and text alone.
2.
Cover these harm classes: hate speech, harassment, nudity, child safety, self-harm or suicide, and misinformation.
3.
Provide two latency tiers. The pre-publish check on uploads returns within 2 seconds at p99, with the outcome block, allow, or publish with limited reach while the check continues. The post-publish check covers everything else, such as comments, edits and re-evaluation under new policies, and finishes within 5 minutes.
4.
Automated moderation with a fallback to human review: clear violations are actioned automatically, borderline items go to a review queue.
5.
Support model retraining with human feedback and new data.
6.
Allow auditing: every decision can be explained and reproduced later.
Scale and targets (design for these)
100 million uploads per day (images and short videos) and 1 billion comments per day.
Target precision of at least 95% for automatic removal. For the severe classes (child safety, nudity, self-harm) the target is at least 90% recall at that precision, where for self-harm the action is flagging for support and review rather than removal.
A reviewer team that can handle 200,000 items per day.
What to cover
1.
Data and labels: sources, label taxonomy, multi-label support, label quality.
2.
Architecture: ingestion, per-modality models, fusion, decision service, review queue, actions.
3.
Models: where to use cheap classifiers, and when to use large language models or vision-language models.
4.
Training and evaluation: offline metrics per class, online metrics, bias and fairness checks.
5.
Serving: latency budget and cost per item at the scale above.
6.
Human review: queue prioritization and feedback into training.
7.
Auditing: what is recorded for each decision.
8.
Monitoring, drift, and trade-offs.

title: Design an ML Fraud Detection System
question:
Design a machine learning system to detect fraudulent transactions on a payments platform. The round blends ML system design with traditional system design, with heavy emphasis on end-to-end architecture and how it serves at scale.

Cover both:

ML topics: data gathering/cleaning/preparation; model choice; handling class imbalance (fraud is rare); success metrics; deployment; post-launch maintenance/monitoring.
Infrastructure: scalability, reliability, throughput for a massive transaction volume; be ready to draw the full architecture (databases, servers, data flow).

steps: Design fraud or account-takeover detection. Predict risk at a concrete event and route it to an action whose cost is explicitly understood.
Collect time-valid device, account and behavior features with privacy and access controls.
Use a fast risk model and a policy layer for allow, challenge, review or block; tune thresholds to error costs and review capacity.
Evaluate on time-based splits with mature labels, account for adversarial adaptation and monitor false positives by user segment.
solution.example: A suspicious login can trigger a step-up challenge rather than an irreversible account block, reducing the cost of uncertain predictions.
solution.trap: Leaking post-investigation labels or future account events into training-time features.

title: Design an Account Takeover Prediction System
question:
Design a machine learning system to predict Account Takeover (ATO) risk for a payments platform. ATO occurs when an attacker steals login credentials or uses a fake identity to break into a real user's account. The prompt is deliberately open-ended — clarify rules and requirements up front.

The interview covers three areas:

Modeling (~20 min): feature engineering (login time/location/device, transaction amount and velocity, IP/network signals), preprocessing (missing values, scaling, categorical encoding), model choice and evaluation metrics, and risks (class imbalance, duplicate/leaky features, overfitting).

System (~15 min): architecture (ingestion, feature store, model serving, health monitoring), low-latency inference at high QPS, handling data-fetch delays, live model updates, and production monitoring of both prediction quality and system speed.

Business value (~15 min): proving impact (fewer compromised accounts, higher trust), the cost of false positives (blocking a legitimate user), and future improvements.

Follow-up on data splitting: how to train on heavily imbalanced data — oversampling, SMOTE, stratified sampling.

title: ML System Design: Search & Ranking
question:
Family of design prompts: Pin search, Pin ranking, home-feed retrieval, search input suggestions. Interviewers expect a candidate-generation -> ranking stage architecture with explicit embedding sourcing, loss choice (pair-wise vs point-wise), offline metrics, and candidate-pool sizing math.

Requirements

Design one of:

A search engine for Pins (the most common framing): candidate generation, ranking, query understanding, personalization.
Pin ranking / home feed: surface relevant pins to a user in real time, responsive to engagement.
Search input suggestions / typeahead: low-latency query autocompletion with personalization signal.
A recommender system end-to-end: data storage, candidate generation, ranking model serving.

The interviewer typically asks for explicit answers to: How do you efficiently generate candidates? What models / loss function (pair-wise vs point-wise vs list-wise)? What features and how are they constructed? Offline vs online metric? How many candidates pass to the ranker (justify the number)? Where is data stored / how are models served? For a 60GB GPU, how do you compute the serving batch size?

Notes
The standard reference architecture: two-tower retrieval (user tower, item tower; dot-product similarity) for candidate generation, plus a heavier ranker (DLRM / DCN / MMoE) for the top-N candidates. Pinterest's published PinSAGE / PinnerSAGE family is the relevant embedding work.
Candidate-count math: candidate pool is sized as inference_complexity_per_item x items_per_inference_batch x number_of_instances against the per-request latency budget. Be ready to derive it from a stated 100ms latency budget.
Batch size for a 60GB GPU: model weights + activation memory + intermediate buffers must fit; max_batch = (60GB - weights - KV) / activation_per_sample.
Embedding training is the most common driver: positive pairs (co-engaged pins, user-pin engagement), negative sampling (in-batch negatives, hard negatives), label-noise handling.
Pair-wise (BPR / RankNet) for ranking with implicit feedback; point-wise (cross-entropy on click) for retrieval when calibrated probabilities matter.

steps: Design a recommendation system from candidate generation to ranking. A cascade reduces a huge catalog to a small set worth scoring with expensive models.
Generate candidates using complementary signals such as collaborative, content and popularity retrieval.
Rank with user, item and context features, ensuring training features were available at event time.
Apply policy and diversity constraints, log exposures and outcomes, and evaluate retrieval recall, ranking utility and online guardrails separately.
Choose metrics for ranking and recommendation. The right metric should reflect the ordered choices users see and the value of a good recommendation.
For retrieval, inspect recall@K to ensure relevant items survive candidate generation.
For ranking, use an order-sensitive measure such as NDCG@K or a task-specific utility measure, and define relevance labels and position discounts.
Validate online impact with guardrails for latency, diversity, safety and long-term outcomes; correct or acknowledge exposure and selection bias.
solution.contract_notes: Evaluate retrieval recall, rank-order utility and end-to-end success separately; reranking cannot recover a relevant item the retrieval cutoff removed.
solution.example: Retrieve 1000 candidates from a million items, rerank 100, then display 10; each stage trades compute for selectivity.
solution.trap: Training only on clicked items and treating unexposed items as observed negatives.

title: ML System Design: Dynamic K in Retrieval Stage
question:
In a recommendation stack (retrieval, then ranking, then re-ranking), the retrieval stage hands a fixed number K of candidate items to the ranking stage for every request. A static K wastes ranking compute on easy requests and starves ranking on ambiguous ones. Design a model or system that chooses K dynamically for each request.

Requirements

Your design must cover these parts:

1.
Goal metric: define how you decide that the chosen K was right for a request, and which guardrail metrics (latency, ranking cost, engagement) bound it.
2.
Model output: decide whether the model predicts K directly or predicts a per-candidate quantity from which K is derived, and justify the choice, including where the training labels come from.
3.
Features: list the request-level, session-level, retrieval-stage and system-level signals the controller uses.
4.
Calibration and thresholds: explain how scores are made trustworthy enough to turn into a count, and how the threshold is tuned.
5.
Serving and safety: explain how worst-case latency is bounded, how the controller stays cheap, and how the learning loop is run.
6.
Evaluation and trade-offs: give an online experiment plan and compare static K with dynamic K, including failure modes.
Constraints
Ranking cost grows roughly linearly with K; p99 latency is a hard ceiling.
The controller adds negligible latency compared with the compute it saves.
A regression in downstream engagement must be caught before full rollout.

steps: When should you combine lexical retrieval, embeddings and reranking? Different retrieval signals capture different kinds of matching and fail in different ways.
Use lexical retrieval for exact terms, identifiers and uncommon names; use embeddings for semantic similarity and paraphrases.
Fuse candidate rankings using a defined rule such as reciprocal-rank fusion rather than adding incomparable raw scores blindly.
Rerank a manageable candidate set with a stronger scorer, and measure the gain against latency and cost.
Choose between exact and approximate nearest-neighbor search. Approximation trades some retrieval accuracy for faster or smaller search at scale.
Benchmark exact search as a correctness reference on a representative subset.
Choose an index and tune its search effort against recall, latency, memory and update frequency.
Evaluate downstream answer or recommendation quality, because a small recall loss can disproportionately affect rare important items.
solution.contract_notes: Choose K from an explicit quality/latency tradeoff rather than a fixed magic number. Train or calibrate a stopping rule on score gaps, query difficulty and marginal reranker benefit using held-out queries. Enforce minimum/maximum candidates and a hard deadline. Compare recall/answer success by query slice; a large first-score gap is a feature to validate, not proof of sufficient recall.
solution.example: A product code like “ZX-42” may benefit from exact matching even if a semantic encoder treats similar codes alike.
solution.trap: Reranking only two candidates after retrieval misses nearly all relevant documents.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Treat retrieval, filtering and ranking as separate stages

Choose the query language: prefix lookup, arbitrary substring search, lexical relevance and semantic similarity are different problems. An inverted index maps terms to document ids; a trie or finite-state prefix structure answers a different access pattern.

Normalize text consistently at indexing and querying time. Keep stable document ids, versions and deletion state. Apply authorization and required exclusion/eligibility rules before a truncation can remove all valid candidates; filtering an already tiny top list can return an unnecessarily empty result.

A lexical score can combine term frequency, document frequency and document-length normalization, while a reranker spends more work on a bounded candidate set. Evaluate candidate recall separately from ranking. An expensive reranker cannot select a document that retrieval never supplied.

For an exact-identifier query, lexical matching may be more dependable than semantic closeness; hybrid fusion needs compatible ranking semantics rather than blindly adding raw scores on different scales. Test empty queries, unseen terms, repeated terms, deletes and tied scores. For scale, benchmark realistic query/update distributions and freshness, not just a warmed cache with one popular query.

title: Video Recommendation
question:

Ranking: scoring model(s), features, multi-objective balancing.
Serving: request-time flow with bounded latency.

Service split (where boundaries sit), data flow (interaction -> event bus -> training data + features -> serving; training-serving skew), and event logging + observability as the central deep-dive (Kafka -> offline store -> training/feedback; metrics and monitoring).

title: Design App Store Search and Ranking
question:
Design the search and ranking system for the Apple App Store: a user types a query and receives a ranked list of relevant apps.

Requirements
1.
Scope and scale — state the catalog size, query volume, latency budget and objectives (relevance, install conversion, quality and anti-spam) you design for.
2.
Query understanding — how you normalize the query, detect its language, embed it, and classify its intent (navigational vs. exploratory).
3.
Retrieval — how you produce a candidate set of a few hundred apps from millions, covering both exact and semantic matches.
4.
Ranking — the model, the features it uses (from the sources below), and the training objective.
5.
Feature freshness and serving — how static and fast-changing features are computed, stored and served within the latency budget.
6.
Risks and trade-offs — cold-start apps, spam and keyword stuffing, optimizing clicks vs. installs, and privacy limits on user features.
Available feature sources
Static app features (recomputed when the app is updated): title, subtitle, description, category, keywords, icon and preview-image embeddings, price, in-app-purchase presence, developer reputation.
Dynamic app features (updated every minute): rating, review count, install velocity, recent click-through and uninstall rates.
Query features: normalized tokens, language, query embedding, inferred intent, query popularity.
Query-app interaction features: BM25 score, semantic cosine similarity, historical click-through and install rate for the (query, app) pair, lexical overlap.
User and context features (subject to privacy constraints): locale, device, prior downloads, cohort.
Constraints
Catalog of several million apps; end-to-end latency of roughly 200 ms per query.
Deliverable

A design that answers parts 1–6: the pipeline stages, the features and model used at each stage, and the main trade-offs.

steps: Design a recommendation system from candidate generation to ranking. A cascade reduces a huge catalog to a small set worth scoring with expensive models.
Generate candidates using complementary signals such as collaborative, content and popularity retrieval.
Rank with user, item and context features, ensuring training features were available at event time.
Apply policy and diversity constraints, log exposures and outcomes, and evaluate retrieval recall, ranking utility and online guardrails separately.
Choose metrics for ranking and recommendation. The right metric should reflect the ordered choices users see and the value of a good recommendation.
For retrieval, inspect recall@K to ensure relevant items survive candidate generation.
For ranking, use an order-sensitive measure such as NDCG@K or a task-specific utility measure, and define relevance labels and position discounts.
Validate online impact with guardrails for latency, diversity, safety and long-term outcomes; correct or acknowledge exposure and selection bias.
solution.contract_notes: App search needs query intent, lexical matching, locale/device compatibility and quality signals. A popular irrelevant app should not outrank an exact legitimate match merely because it has more installs.
solution.example: Retrieve 1000 candidates from a million items, rerank 100, then display 10; each stage trades compute for selectivity.
solution.trap: Training only on clicked items and treating unexposed items as observed negatives.
