title: Build a Simplified Image-Text Retrieval Training and Evaluation Pipeline
question:
eBay uses multimodal intelligence (image + text) to retrieve relevant products for a user's text query. Build a simplified image-text retrieval model training and evaluation pipeline.

What you are given
A dataset of product images (assume one image per product)
Product title/description text for each product
Query text with associated positive product IDs
Image encoder: resnet50
Text encoder: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2
What to implement

Image and text embedding models

Use resnet50 to extract image features, then a trainable projection head to map them into a shared embedding space of dimension D.
Use all-MiniLM-L6-v2 to extract text features, then a trainable projection head to map them into the same embedding space.
Apply L2 normalization to the final embeddings so cosine similarity can be used for retrieval.

A joint-embedding loss function

Implement a contrastive objective that aligns query text with its positive product (image and/or product text representation).
Must support in-batch negatives.
You may choose InfoNCE / softmax cross-entropy / triplet loss, etc., but provide a runnable implementation.

Retrieval evaluation

Given a query text, score all products by similarity (e.g., cosine similarity) and return Top-K product IDs.
Implement an offline evaluation over a set of queries, computing Top-K quality such as Recall@K.
Constraints / requirements
Use Python (PyTorch recommended).
Include a training loop (forward, loss, backprop, optimizer step).
Evaluation must be callable independently and return Top-K results.
Describe/implement how you build training batches (at minimum query-positive-product pairs).
Deliverables
Clean code structure (clear classes/functions).
A minimal runnable example (you may mock data with random tensors; the interfaces and data flow must be realistic).
Example
Input:  query="red nike shoes", k=5, (products: precomputed embeddings)
Output: top_k=[103, 998, 42, 77, 501]

steps: Design image-text retrieval. Learn or use embeddings that place matched images and text near each other, then search and rerank efficiently.
Build cleaned matched-pair data with duplicate and entity-aware evaluation splits.
Train dual encoders with an appropriate contrastive objective, then precompute catalog embeddings and build an index.
Evaluate recall@K, hard-negative behavior, latency and subgroup performance; use a stronger reranker if the quality gain justifies cost.
Implement symmetric InfoNCE loss. A matched query/key pair should score above other examples in the batch, in both retrieval directions.
Normalize q and k along the embedding dimension and require temperature>0.
Compute logits=q@kᵀ/temperature; the correct key for query i is index i. Use stable cross-entropy across each row.
Average query-to-key and key-to-query cross-entropies. Keep the computation differentiable in a training implementation and define how duplicate positives are treated.
Choose hard negatives for a retrieval model. Useful negatives are challenging non-matches, not mislabeled positives selected for looking similar.
Start with in-batch or random negatives as a baseline.
Mine high-scoring incorrect candidates, filter known duplicates and alternative valid answers, and control the negative mixture.
Evaluate on unseen queries and inspect whether the model learns real distinctions or shortcuts from mining artifacts.
solution.example: A text query retrieves candidate images by embedding similarity, while a pairwise reranker checks the top candidates more carefully.
solution.trap: Splitting near-duplicate images across training and test or interpreting false negatives as unrelated pairs automatically.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Derive the diagonal contrastive targets

For matched query/key rows $(q_i,k_i)$, normalize each nonzero vector and form a batch similarity matrix

$$
S_{ij}=\frac{\tilde q_i^\top\tilde k_j}{\tau},\qquad
L_{q\to k}=-\frac1B\sum_i\log\frac{e^{S_{ii}}}{\sum_j e^{S_{ij}}}.
$$

The key-to-query loss uses $S^\top$; the symmetric objective is $(L_{q\to k}+L_{k\to q})/2$. Temperature controls logit sharpness and gradient scale. Normalizing first makes this interpretation independent of arbitrary positive embedding scale.

A batch of one has zero loss because the only key is the positive. That is a warning about absent negatives, not evidence of perfect semantic retrieval. Likewise, repeated or alternative true matches can be wrongly penalized as negatives by a diagonal-only target.

Use stable log-softmax/cross-entropy rather than manually exponentiating large scores. A NumPy implementation is a forward numerical reference; training needs the equivalent differentiable operations so gradients flow into both intended branches. A deliberately detached momentum branch is a different architecture decision, not an accidental conversion to NumPy.

Test swapping $q$ and $k$, positive row scaling, small temperature and zero-norm input policy. If negatives are gathered across workers, adjust each positive index and specify whether gradients cross that collective. More negatives can help discrimination, but label correctness and negative distribution are at least as important as the raw batch count.

title: Implement a Vision Transformer (ViT) from Scratch
question:
Implement a Vision Transformer (ViT) from Scratch

Implement the forward pass of a Vision Transformer image classifier using only NumPy. The model cuts an image into square patches, turns every patch into a token, adds one extra classification token (CLS) and a learned position embedding, runs the tokens through a stack of pre-norm transformer encoder blocks, and predicts the class from the final CLS token. The weights are given; you write the computation.

What to implement
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1): ...
def layer_norm(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5): ...
def gelu(x): ...
def patch_embed(images, w, b, patch_size): ...
def multi_head_attention(x, w_qkv, b_qkv, w_out, b_out, num_heads): ...
def encoder_block(x, p, num_heads): ...
def vit_forward(images, params, patch_size, num_heads): ...

Do not use any deep-learning library or ready-made attention or transformer layer; only NumPy. B is the batch size, N the number of patches, D the embedding size.

Rules
1.
softmax(x, axis): subtract the maximum along axis before exponentiating, so large inputs do not overflow.
2.
layer_norm(x, gamma, beta, eps): normalize over the last axis: (x - mean) / sqrt(var + eps) * gamma + beta, with the biased variance (divide by the count).
3.
gelu(x): the tanh form 0.5 * x * (1 + tanh(sqrt(2 / pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x^3))).
4.
patch_embed(images, w, b, patch_size): images has shape (B, C, H, W) with H and W divisible by P = patch_size. Patches are taken row by row (left to right, then top to bottom), and the pixels of one patch are flattened in (C, P, P) order into a vector of length C*P*P. The result is flat @ w + b with w of shape (C*P*P, D), shape (B, N, D), N = (H/P) * (W/P).
5.
multi_head_attention(x, ...): x has shape (B, N, D). Compute qkv = x @ w_qkv + b_qkv with w_qkv of shape (D, 3D). Columns [0, D) are the queries, [D, 2D) the keys, [2D, 3D) the values. Head h uses columns [h*d, (h+1)*d) of each, where d = D / num_heads. Per head, the attention weights are softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) over the keys (no mask), and the head output is the weights times V. Concatenate the heads in order and return concat @ w_out + b_out, shape (B, N, D).
6.
encoder_block(x, p, num_heads) is pre-norm with residual connections: x = x + attention(layer_norm(x)), then x = x + mlp(layer_norm(x)), where mlp(h) = gelu(h @ fc1_w + fc1_b) @ fc2_w + fc2_b. The dictionary p has the keys ln1_g, ln1_b, qkv_w, qkv_b, proj_w, proj_b, ln2_g, ln2_b, fc1_w, fc1_b, fc2_w, fc2_b.
7.
vit_forward(images, params, patch_size, num_heads): embed the patches with params["patch_w"], params["patch_b"]; put the CLS vector params["cls"] (shape (D,)) in front of the tokens as token 0; add params["pos"] (shape (N+1, D)); apply the blocks in params["blocks"] (a list of dictionaries as in rule 6); apply layer_norm with params["ln_g"], params["ln_b"]; and return the logits of token 0: token0 @ params["head_w"] + params["head_b"], shape (B, num_classes).
Examples

Example 1: images of shape (2, 3, 16, 16), patch_size = 4, D = 8, 10 classes. patch_embed returns shape (2, 16, 8), the sequence has 17 tokens after the CLS token is added, and vit_forward returns shape (2, 10).

Example 2: layer_norm(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), 1.0, 0.0, eps=0.0) returns [-1.2247, 0.0, 1.2247]. The mean is 2 and the biased variance is 2/3.

Example 3: images = [[[[1, 2], [3, 4]]]] (one image, one channel, 2 x 2 pixels), patch_size = 1, w = [[2.0]], b = [1.0] returns [[[3.0], [5.0], [7.0], [9.0]]]. Each pixel is a patch and is mapped to 2 * pixel + 1, in row-major order.

Constraints
1 <= B <= 8; images up to 224 x 224; 1 <= C <= 3.
D is divisible by num_heads; D <= 768; up to 12 blocks.
The inputs and the parameters are not modified.

steps: Implement the forward structure of a Vision Transformer. A ViT turns image patches into a sequence processed by Transformer blocks.
Split an image into non-overlapping patches, requiring compatible image dimensions or an explicit padding policy.
Flatten each patch, project it into the model dimension and add position information and any classification token.
Run normalization, attention and FFN blocks, then use the specified pooling/head. Trace every reshape to preserve patch order.
solution.example: A 32-by-32 RGB image with 8-by-8 patches gives 16 patch tokens of 192 input features each, before projection.
solution.trap: Mixing channels and patch positions during reshape or silently discarding image borders.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Build the computation before optimizing it

Start by saying which axis represents examples, positions, heads and features. With batch size $B$, query length $T_q$, key length $T_k$ and head width $d_k$, a head receives $Q\in\mathbb R^{B\times T_q\times d_k}$ and $K\in\mathbb R^{B\times T_k\times d_k}$. Values may have a different final width $d_v$. The essential operation is

$$
S=\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M,\qquad
P_{ij}=\frac{\exp(S_{ij}-m_i)}{\sum_j\exp(S_{ij}-m_i)},\qquad O=PV.
$$

Here the transpose affects the final two axes, $m_i=\max_j S_{ij}$ is a row maximum, and $M$ contains zero for allowed positions and $-\infty$ for forbidden ones. Each query produces one distribution **over keys**, so summing the wrong axis changes the operation even when the output shape looks plausible.

For a tiny check, give a query access to exactly one key. Its output must equal that key's value, regardless of the score. Then change a forbidden future token: earlier causal outputs must remain unchanged. These checks expose mistakes that a random shape test misses.

Explain the limitation of the simple implementation. Explicitly materializing $P$ uses $O(T_qT_k)$ score storage per head. A reference implementation is useful for correctness; a tiled kernel can avoid that materialization while preserving the mathematical attention operation. Generation additionally needs correct target shifts, positions and cache state, not just a working matrix multiplication.

title: Tiny Next-Token Prediction Model (PyTorch Fill-In)
question:
Fill in the TODOs of a tiny PyTorch skeleton so a feed-forward (no recurrence, no attention) model trains for next-token prediction conditioned only on the current token.

1.
DataLoader — wrap SyntheticDataset(num_samples, seq_len, vocab_size) with DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=True).
2.
Model — Embedding(vocab_size, hidden_dim) → Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim) → ReLU → Linear(hidden_dim, vocab_size).
3.
forward(x) — return logits of shape (batch, seq_len, vocab_size).
4.
Input/target prep — given sequences (batch, seq_len), set inputs = sequences[:, :-1], targets = sequences[:, 1:]; flatten so cross-entropy sees (batch·(seq_len-1), vocab_size) and (batch·(seq_len-1),).
5.
Training loop — forward, cross-entropy, backward, optimizer step (Adam is fine).

Hidden tests check that loss strictly decreases on a fixed seed and that the input/target shift is correct.

steps: Why is a next-token model trained with shifted targets? At position t, the model sees tokens through t and predicts token t+1. The target shift makes the training task match autoregressive generation.
Given tokens [x0,x1,x2,x3], use inputs [x0,x1,x2] and targets [x1,x2,x3], unless the library performs this shift internally.
Apply a causal mask to prevent access to later input positions. Use cross-entropy over vocabulary logits without an extra softmax first.
For instruction tuning, mask unwanted target positions after aligning the shift. Divide by the count of supervised targets, not padded sequence length.
Debug a miniature GPT that fails to learn. Localize the first broken invariant rather than changing many hyperparameters at once.
Check shifted labels, causal masking, tensor axes, vocabulary bounds and padding/loss masks on a tiny batch.
Check train/eval mode, gradient presence, optimizer steps and parameter changes. Overfit a tiny dataset with dropout disabled as a diagnostic.
Compare against a simple trusted baseline; then test generation and caching separately. Record one controlled change and its effect at a time.
solution.example: If a prompt ends at input position 3 and the first answer is token 4, the prediction at position 3 is the first supervised answer target.
solution.trap: Shifting twice because both a data collator and the model's loss already shift labels, or supervising the wrong prompt boundary.

title: Prompt sampling
question:
Part 1: Implement a llm sampler class that consists of tokenize, detokenize, sampler function, and think of strategies to parallelize the task. This part aims to test your ability to write clear classes, and your understanding of parallel computing such as processes and threads.

Part 2: Implement a function that computes the rewards given the samples, the reward function is given as the function with string input and output integers. Find a way to calculate the mean reward and the bootstrapped 99% confidence interval.

steps: Separate tokenize, model sampling, detokenize and reward evaluation behind explicit interfaces, with seeds and generation limits in configuration.

Batch model work where supported; use threads for independent I/O calls and processes only when CPU-bound work and serialization costs justify them. Preserve the association between prompt, sample, seed and reward.

Compute the sample mean over the stated unit. For a bootstrap 99% percentile interval, resample independent units with replacement, recompute the mean many times, and use empirical 0.5% and 99.5% quantiles.

If several samples share one prompt, cluster-resample prompts when inference targets variability across prompts. Report the number of prompts/samples, seed, bootstrap convention and limitations of tiny or dependent data.
solution.example: Rewards [0,1,1,0] have mean 0.5. The interval depends on sample size and resampling unit; taking the mean of per-thread means can be wrong when thread sample counts differ.
solution.trap: Treating generated samples from the same prompt as unrelated independent tasks without checking the inferential target.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Define the candidate set before sampling

Sampling has three operations: choose retained tokens, normalize their scores, and draw a vocabulary id. With temperature $\tau>0$ and retained set $S$,

$$
P(i\mid i\in S)=\frac{\exp(z_i/\tau)}{\sum_{j\in S}\exp(z_j/\tau)}.
$$

Top-$k$ defines $S$ as the $k$ largest logits. Temperature changes the distribution within that fixed set but does not change its ordering for positive $\tau$. With logits $[1,2,0.5,4]$ and $k=2$, only original ids 1 and 3 may be returned. A local index zero in the two-element candidate array is not necessarily vocabulary id zero.

For top-$p$, first sort probabilities $p_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge p_{(V)}$ and choose

$$
k^*=\min\left\{k:\sum_{j=1}^k p_{(j)}\ge p\right\}.
$$

Include the token that crosses the threshold, then renormalize. For $[0.6,0.25,0.15]$ and threshold $0.8$, retain the first two tokens, whose mass is $0.85$. Keeping only the first would fail the requested coverage.

A readable reference sorts in $O(V\log V)$; partial selection can improve top-$k$ selection cost but needs a deliberate equal-score rule. Use an explicit random generator to reproduce experiments. Test $k=1$, $k=V$, $p=1$, very small positive $p$ and tied logits. A fixed seed does not guarantee identical sequences after a change in floating-point reduction or the number/order of random draws.

title: Compute the Distribution of LLM Decoding Stopping Time and Build a Strategy Against Adversaries
question:
Problem: Model the Distribution of LLM Decoding Stopping Time and Implement a Minimax Strategy Against Adversaries

In a simplified LLM decoding process, at each step the model may emit a special token <STOP> and terminate. You must do two things.

Part A: Stopping-Time Distribution

Given a maximum length N (generation runs for at most N tokens; if it does not stop early, it is forced to stop at N) and a per-step stop probability sequence:

At step t (1-indexed), the probability of emitting <STOP> is p[t] (0 <= p[t] <= 1)
If it does not stop at step t, it proceeds to step t+1

Compute:

For all t = 1..N, the stopping-time probability P(T=t)
The expected stopping time E[T]

Note: If <STOP> is never emitted by step N, define T=N (forced stop).

Part B: Strategy Against Adversaries

There are multiple adversaries. Each adversary corresponds to a different mechanism that influences p[t] and/or the payoff. After observing p[1..N] (or its parametric form), your program must choose a decision (e.g., a cutoff step k, an early-stop policy, or an action a) to maximize the worst-case (minimax) expected reward.

Implement a program that takes:

N
p[1..N]
parameters for M adversaries (each defines a possible p[t] and/or reward function)
a reward function reward(decision, T, adversary)

Output:

the chosen decision
the expected reward under the worst adversary
I/O Spec

You must clearly specify:

stdin input format
stdout output format
constraints (N, M) and complexity requirements

Provide at least 5 test cases including edge cases.

Example

Input:

...

Output:

...

steps: Let survival s_1=1. For t<N set P(T=t)=s_t*p_t and s_(t+1)=s_t*(1-p_t). Assign P(T=N)=s_N, absorbing both an actual stop and forced termination at N; this final mass does not need an extra p_N factor.
Compute E[T]=sum_t t*P(T=t), or equivalently sum_t s_t. Use stable accumulation and verify total probability is one, including p=0/1 boundaries.

For each fully specified decision a and adversary m, compute expected payoff sum_t P_m(T=t)*reward(a,t,m). Choose the decision maximizing the minimum of those expectations; define deterministic tie-breaking.

Time is O(M*A*N) for explicit finite action/adversary lists, plus distribution construction. The prompt does not define a unique decision/reward interface, so state a concrete schema rather than claiming one universal numerical minimax answer.
solution.example: N=3 and p=[0.5,0.5,anything] gives masses [0.5,0.25,0.25], expectation 1.75. If every early p is zero, T=N surely.
solution.trap: Losing survival mass at the forced-stop boundary or averaging adversaries when the requested criterion is worst-case.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Name the random experiment and condition on the right event

Write the sample space and independence assumptions before counting. Bayes' rule reverses conditioning:

$$
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)},\qquad P(B)>0.
$$

A $90\%$ detection rate is not a $90\%$ probability that an alert is genuine. Prevalence and false-positive rate determine the latter. Work expected counts in a hypothetical population when the formula feels abstract.

For waiting-time and random-walk exercises, first-step analysis often gives a solvable recurrence:

$$
h(s)=1+\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s)h(s'),\qquad h(s)=0\text{ at absorbing states}.
$$

Specify what counts as one step: two particles moving once each may cost two coin flips but only one elapsed second. At a forced horizon, all surviving probability mass must be assigned to the final stopping time.

For expected counts, indicator variables and linearity do not require independent indicators. For uncertainty or variance, dependence does matter. Check normalization, limiting cases and a small enumeration. Simulation is useful validation but not a replacement for a requested exact derivation; conversely, a neat-looking fraction should not be asserted merely because a numerical estimate is close to it.

#### Put the result in mathematical notation

Let $s_1=1$ and $s_{t+1}=s_t(1-p_t)$. Then
$$P(T=t)=s_tp_t\quad(t<N),\qquad P(T=N)=s_N,\qquad
\mathbb E[T]=\sum_{t=1}^N s_t.$$
The final mass includes every surviving path. For finite actions and adversaries,
$$a^*=\arg\max_a\min_m\sum_t P_m(T=t)R(a,t,m).$$
Averaging adversaries solves a different problem from the requested worst-case criterion.

title: Classifier Analysis
question:
Classification Analysis: Loss Bounds and Calibration

We train an image classifier on the 10-digit MNIST dataset for many epochs and study what happens once it overfits. You bound the cross-entropy loss, predict the shape of the training curves, and implement a calibration metric called Average Calibration Error (ACE).

Setup

The classifier is an MLP with three hidden layers of 1024 ReLU units (784 -> 1024 -> 1024 -> 1024 -> 10), trained with Adam (learning rate 3e-4, batch size 256) for 50 epochs on 50,000 training images. After every epoch the run records the mean loss, the accuracy and the ACE on the training set and on the 10,000 test images. You do not need to run the training: Questions 3 to 5 are answered from what you know about overfitting and from the definition of ACE.

The confidence of an example is the probability the model assigns to the class it predicts (the arg-max class). Its log is logprob; the accuracy acc of an example is 1 if the prediction is correct and 0 otherwise.

1. Bounds of the cross-entropy loss

For one example with true class c, the loss is -log(p_c), where p is the softmax output over the 10 classes.

1.
Question 1. Give the tightest lower and upper bound of the loss of a single example when the prediction is correct (accuracy = 1), and when it is wrong (accuracy = 0).
2.
Question 2. A data set has n examples, exactly k of them misclassified, and the loss is the mean over the examples. Give the bounds of the mean loss for k = 0, for k = 1 (accuracy close to 1) and for k = n - 1 (accuracy close to 0), and say which bounds are finite.
2. Expected training curves
3.
Question 3. While the model trains, what do you expect the curves of train and test loss and accuracy to look like?
4.
Question 4. After training ends, explain what happens to the test loss and the test accuracy, and why.
3. Implement ACE

ACE measures how well the confidence of the model matches its accuracy.

1.
The confidence of an example is exp(logprob), a number in (0, 1].
2.
Split [0, 1] into m_bins equal-width bins: bin m covers [m/m_bins, (m+1)/m_bins). A confidence of exactly 1.0 belongs to the last bin.
3.
For every non-empty bin B, acc(B) is the mean accuracy and conf(B) the mean confidence of the examples in it.
4.
ACE = mean over the non-empty bins of |acc(B) - conf(B)|. Empty bins are skipped: they are not counted as zero and they are not in the denominator.
5.
With no examples, return 0.0.

Implement:

def ace_calc(logprobs: np.ndarray, accs: np.ndarray, m_bins: int = 15) -> float:

logprobs and accs are arrays of the same length n; logprobs[i] <= 0 and accs[i] is 0 or 1. The function returns a Python float.

Examples

Example 1: m_bins = 5, confidences [0.9, 0.95, 1.0, 0.5, 0.55] (so logprobs = np.log(confidences)), accs = [1, 1, 1, 0, 1] returns 0.0375. The first three fall in bin 4 (acc 1.0, conf 0.95, gap 0.05). The last two fall in bin 2 (acc 0.5, conf 0.525, gap 0.025). The other three bins are empty, so ACE = (0.05 + 0.025) / 2.

Example 2: m_bins = 15 (the default), confidences [0.99, 0.30], accs = [1, 0] returns 0.155. The confidences fall in bins 14 and 4 (gaps 0.01 and 0.30), so ACE = (0.01 + 0.30) / 2.

Example 3: logprobs = [0.0, 0.0], accs = [1, 1] returns 0.0. Both confidences are exactly 1.0, they share the last bin, and acc = conf = 1.

Constraints
0 <= n <= 10^6
1 <= m_bins <= 1000
4. Interpret the ACE curves
5.
Question 5. Interpret the curves of loss, accuracy and ACE over the epochs.
1.
Why does the training ACE approach 0?
2.
What happens to the test ACE?
3.
Why is the ACE curve spiky between epochs?
5. Improve the metric
6.
Question 6. Propose improvements or alternatives to ACE. Consider printing or plotting how the bin populations change over the epochs.

steps: Why can cross-entropy worsen while accuracy stays unchanged? Accuracy uses the chosen class; cross-entropy also measures how much probability the model assigns to the true class.
Separate correct and incorrect predictions and inspect confidence changes.
For a true-class probability p, loss is -log(p), which grows without bound as p approaches zero.
Track validation loss, accuracy and calibration together; consider early stopping or calibration using a separate validation set.
Bound cross-entropy when a prediction is correct or incorrect. The label probability is constrained by whether it is the largest class probability, not merely by the number of classes.
For C classes and a correct argmax, p_true>=1/C, so 0<=loss<=log(C), subject to tie conventions.
For an incorrect argmax, p_true<=1/2 and loss>=log(2), with the lower bound an infimum when strict inequality is required.

There is no finite upper bound for an incorrect prediction as p_true approaches zero. For N examples with k errors, the mean-loss lower bound is (k/N)*log(2). If k=0 the upper bound is log(C); if k>0 there is no finite upper bound.
Calculate average calibration error from confidence bins. Calibration compares predicted confidence with observed correctness; it is different from classification accuracy.
Convert predicted-class log probabilities to confidence with exp(logprob), then assign equal-width bins in [0,1].
Put confidence exactly 1 in the last bin. For each non-empty bin compute abs(mean_accuracy-mean_confidence).
For this ACE definition, average gaps equally across non-empty bins and return zero for no examples. A sample-weighted version is a different metric.
solution.example: An already-wrong example whose true-class probability falls from 0.1 to 0.001 keeps the same error count while loss grows from 2.303 to 6.908.
solution.trap: Concluding that accuracy and confidence quality must improve or degrade together.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Specify which calibration error you mean

Confidence here is the probability of the **predicted** class, not necessarily the true class. If its stored value is log confidence $\ell_i$, recover $c_i=e^{\ell_i}$ and let $a_i\in\{0,1\}$ indicate correctness.

Split $[0,1]$ into $M$ equal-width bins, placing exactly $1$ in the final bin. For nonempty bins $\mathcal B_+$, this exercise defines

$$
\operatorname{ACE}=\frac1{|\mathcal B_+|}\sum_{b\in\mathcal B_+}
\left|\frac{\sum_{i\in b}a_i}{n_b}-\frac{\sum_{i\in b}c_i}{n_b}\right|.
$$

Every nonempty bin receives equal weight. A population-weighted ECE instead weights each gap by $n_b/N$ and is a different statistic. Empty bins are omitted rather than counted as zero-error bins.

For confidence values $[0.9,0.95,1,0.5,0.55]$ and correctness $[1,1,1,0,1]$ at five bins, the first group has accuracy $1$ and mean confidence $0.95$, gap $0.05$; the second has accuracy $0.5$ and confidence $0.525$, gap $0.025$. ACE is $(0.05+0.025)/2=0.0375$.

Show bin counts alongside the number. Small bins and examples crossing a boundary can make the curve spiky even without a large change in the model. Use independent calibration/evaluation data and inspect proper scores such as log loss too; one binned metric is not a complete account of probability quality.

title: Implement Binary Focal Loss
question:
Given n binary classification samples, true labels y_i ∈ {0,1}, and predicted probabilities p_i for the positive class, implement Binary Focal Loss.

For each sample:

If y_i = 1, then p_t = p_i, alpha_t = alpha.
If y_i = 0, then p_t = 1 - p_i, alpha_t = 1 - alpha.

The per-sample loss is:

loss_i = - alpha_t * (1 - p_t)^gamma * log(p_t)

To avoid log(0), clip probabilities to [1e-15, 1 - 1e-15].

Input Format
n gamma alpha reduction
y_1 y_2 ... y_n
p_1 p_2 ... p_n

Where reduction is one of mean, sum, or none:

mean outputs the average loss.
sum outputs the total loss.
none outputs every sample's loss.
Output Format
If reduction is mean or sum, print one float rounded to 6 decimal places.
If reduction is none, print n floats separated by spaces, each rounded to 6 decimal places.
Constraints
1 <= n <= 100000
0 <= gamma <= 10
0 <= alpha <= 1
0 <= p_i <= 1
Example

Input:

3 2.0 0.25 mean
1 0 1
0.9 0.1 0.2

steps: Implement numerically stable binary focal loss. Focal loss reduces the contribution of already-easy examples by multiplying binary cross-entropy by (1-p_true)^gamma.
Given a binary label y and logit z, compute stable BCE as logaddexp(0,z)-y*z.
Let log_p_true=-BCE and compute 1-p_true stably as -expm1(log_p_true).
Multiply BCE by that factor raised to gamma and by alpha for positives or 1-alpha for negatives, if alpha weighting is specified. State the reduction.
Differentiate binary focal loss conceptually. Its gradient includes both cross-entropy's gradient and the derivative of the focusing weight.
Write L=(1-p_t)^gamma*(-logp_t), with any class weight explicit.
Apply the product rule: changing the logit changes the BCE term and the modulation term.
Use a stable differentiable implementation and compare gradients with finite differences rather than multiplying BCE gradients by a fixed-looking weight.
solution.example: At gamma=0, focal modulation is one, so the result reduces to ordinary BCE with the chosen alpha weighting.
solution.trap: Applying focal loss twice to already-probability-transformed scores or confusing it with calibration improvement.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Derive a local rule, then apply the chain rule

Treat a layer as a function with a declared input and output shape. Write the scalar loss and its reduction first: a sum, mean over rows and mean over all elements produce different gradient scales. For an affine layer $Y=XW+b$ with upstream gradient $G=\partial L/\partial Y$,

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X}=GW^\top,\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=X^\top G,\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=\sum_i G_{i,:}.
$$

The bias sum is over all leading positions where the same bias was reused. Do not average again if $G$ already contains the mean-loss factor. For example, with one row $x=[2,3]$ and scalar upstream derivative $4$, the weight derivative is $[8,12]$.

Cache the forward values needed by the derivative; compute all gradients before updating parameters. Updating $W$ midway would make the earlier-layer derivative use a different function from the one evaluated forward.

Check a scalar objective using central differences:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_j}\approx
\frac{L(\theta+h e_j)-L(\theta-h e_j)}{2h}.
$$

Use float64 and several sensible $h$ values. An arbitrarily tiny $h$ loses the difference to rounding, while a large one measures curvature rather than a local derivative. Avoid ReLU's kink at zero during this check, and test inputs, weights and biases separately.

title: Implement Softmax
question:
You may not use any third-party libraries.

Given an array x of n real numbers, implement the softmax function:

softmax(x_i) = exp(x_i) / sum(exp(x_j)), j = 0..n-1

To avoid overflow, use the equivalent form:

softmax(x_i) = exp(x_i - max(x)) / sum(exp(x_j - max(x)))

Print every softmax value rounded to 6 decimal places.

Input Format
n
x_0 x_1 ... x_{n-1}
Output Format

Print one line containing n decimal values.

Constraints
1 <= n <= 1000
-1000 <= x_i <= 1000
Example

Input:

3
1 2 3

Output:

0.090031 0.244728 0.665241

steps: Implement stable softmax and log-softmax. A common logit shift leaves the probability distribution unchanged, so subtract a maximum before exponentiation.
Convert finite logits to a floating array and choose the class axis explicitly.
Set z=x-max(x), then softmax=exp(z)/sum(exp(z)). Compute log-softmax directly as z-log(sum(exp(z))).
Test shift invariance, normalization and very large logits. Define a separate policy for negative-infinity masks rather than silently accepting an all-masked row.
Derive the softmax cross-entropy gradient. The fused gradient is predicted probability minus target probability.
Write L=-sum(y_j*logp_j), with targets summing to one.
Differentiate logp_j=z_j-logsumexp(z), yielding dL/dz_i=p_i-y_i.
Apply the chosen batch or mask reduction afterward and preserve zero gradients for excluded examples.
solution.example: Logits [1000,1001] give the same probabilities as [0,1], approximately [0.269,0.731].
solution.trap: Computing log(softmax) when tiny probabilities may underflow to zero.

title: Implement a Two-Hidden-Layer MLP with Backpropagation in NumPy
question:
Implement a Two-Hidden-Layer MLP with Backpropagation in NumPy

Build a small fully connected neural network for regression from scratch, using only NumPy. It maps a 10-number input to one predicted number through two ReLU hidden layers. You write the forward pass, the mean squared error loss, the backward pass that returns every gradient, and a gradient descent step. No deep learning library is allowed.

What to implement

A class MLP with:

__init__(self, input_dim=10, h1=64, h2=32, output_dim=1, seed=0): given in the starter. It stores the parameters in self.params, a dict with "W1" (input_dim, h1), "b1" (h1,), "W2" (h1, h2), "b2" (h2,), "W3" (h2, output_dim) and "b3" (output_dim,). Weights are drawn as rng.standard_normal(shape) * 0.01 with rng = np.random.default_rng(seed), in the order W1, W2, W3; biases start at zero.
forward(self, x) -> np.ndarray: x has shape (B, input_dim); return the predictions, shape (B, output_dim).
loss(self, x, y) -> float: the mean squared error between forward(x) and y (shape (B, output_dim)).
backward(self, x, y) -> dict: the gradient of loss(x, y) with respect to every parameter, as a dict with the same six keys and shapes as self.params. It must not change the parameters.
step(self, grads, lr) -> None: gradient descent, replacing every parameter p with p - lr * grads[name].
Rules
1.
The network is z1 = x W1 + b1, a1 = ReLU(z1), z2 = a1 W2 + b2, a2 = ReLU(z2), y_pred = a2 W3 + b3. The output layer has no activation.
2.
ReLU(z) = max(z, 0). Its derivative is 1 where z > 0 and 0 where z <= 0 (so 0 at exactly 0).
3.
The loss is mean((y_pred - y) ** 2) over all B * output_dim entries.
4.
forward, loss and backward do not modify x, y or self.params.
Examples

Both examples use a tiny network, MLP(input_dim=2, h1=2, h2=2, output_dim=1), with these parameters:

W1 = [[1, -1], [2, 1]]    b1 = [0, 0.5]
W2 = [[1, 0], [-1, 1]]    b2 = [0, -1]
W3 = [[2], [1]]           b3 = [0.5]

Example 1: x = [[1, 2], [1, -1]], y = [[7], [1.5]].

forward(x) gives [[8], [0.5]]. For the first row, z1 = [5, 1.5] and z2 = [3.5, 0.5], so the output is 2 * 3.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 8. The second row has z1 = [-1, -1.5], so both hidden layers are off and the output is just b3.
loss(x, y) is 1.0: the errors are +1 and -1.
backward(x, y) gives W3 = [[3.5], [0.5]], b3 = [0], W2 = [[10, 5], [3, 1.5]], b2 = [2, 1], W1 = [[2, -1], [4, -2]], b1 = [2, -1]. Only the first row contributes to the hidden-layer gradients, and the two output errors cancel in b3.
After step(grads, 0.1), W1 is [[0.8, -0.9], [1.6, 1.2]].

Example 2: change b2 to [1, 0] and use x = [[1, -0.5]], y = [[1.5]].

z1 = [0, -1] and z2 = [1, 0], so forward(x) gives [[2.5]] and the loss is 1.0.
backward gives b3 = [2], W3 = [[2], [0]], b2 = [4, 0], and zeros for W2, W1 and b1. The units with a pre-activation of exactly 0 pass no gradient (rule 2).
Constraints
1 ≤ B ≤ 1000; all dimensions are between 1 and 128.
Inputs are float arrays. Use vectorised NumPy (matrix products), not Python loops over samples.

steps: Write a two-hidden-layer MLP and derive backpropagation. Cache local intermediate values, then apply the chain rule in the reverse order of the forward computation.
Use Z1=XW1+b1, A1=ReLU(Z1), Z2=A1W2+b2, A2=ReLU(Z2), Yhat=A2W3+b3.
For mean squared error over all N*C outputs, dY=2*(Yhat-Y)/(N*C). Compute dW3=A2ᵀ*dY and db3=sum(dY), then propagate through W3 and the ReLU masks.
Repeat for the earlier layers. Keep parameter updates separate from gradient calculation and check a small network numerically.
Why does zero initialization fail in a hidden layer? Identical hidden units can receive identical gradients and remain redundant instead of learning different features.
Trace the forward activations of two units with equal incoming weights and biases.
Show that their backward gradients are equal under symmetric outgoing connections, so gradient descent preserves symmetry.
Use an initialization that breaks symmetry with a scale appropriate to activation and fan-in; zero biases can still be reasonable.
solution.example: For a dense layer X:(4,3), W:(3,2), dY:(4,2), dW has shape (3,2) and dX has shape (4,3).
solution.trap: Dividing by batch size twice, or updating a weight before using its original value in an earlier gradient.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Walk backward through the exact scalar objective

Use row-major examples and explicitly name every activation:

$$
Z_1=XW_1+b_1,\ A_1=\operatorname{ReLU}(Z_1),\quad
Z_2=A_1W_2+b_2,\ A_2=\operatorname{ReLU}(Z_2),\quad
\hat Y=A_2W_3+b_3.
$$

For $N$ examples and $C$ target coordinates, define $L=\|\hat Y-Y\|_F^2/(NC)$. The output derivative is therefore

$$
G_3=\frac{2}{NC}(\hat Y-Y),\qquad
\nabla_{W_3}L=A_2^\top G_3,\quad
\nabla_{b_3}L=\sum_iG_{3,i,:}.
$$

Propagate through the matrix and activation in reverse order:

$$
G_2=(G_3W_3^\top)\odot\mathbf1[Z_2>0],\qquad
\nabla_{W_2}L=A_1^\top G_2,
$$

then repeat for layer one. The ReLU mask belongs to the **preactivation** of the corresponding layer. Bias derivatives sum across reused batch positions, and no additional mean should be introduced after the $1/(NC)$ already in $G_3$.

For $X$ shaped $(4,3)$ and $W_1$ shaped $(3,5)$, $Z_1$ is $(4,5)$, $\nabla W_1$ is $(3,5)$ and $\nabla X$ is $(4,3)$. Check these shapes before compacting expressions.

Compute all gradients before updating weights, and compare each parameter tensor with a central-difference reference on a tiny non-boundary example. Shape agreement alone misses wrong transpose/reduction choices. A constant or symmetric initialization can also prevent useful hidden-unit differentiation; a correct backward pass does not guarantee an effective training configuration.

title: Debug an NLP Classifier Training Pipeline (BERT + Linear)
question:
Task: Debug an NLP Classifier Training Pipeline (BERT + Linear)

You are given a training codebase skeleton for text classification (you may choose a PyTorch or TensorFlow implementation). The high-level components include:

Dataset
DataLoader
Customized Model   (Transformer/BERT + a few Linear layers)
Trainer            (similar to HuggingFace Transformers)
Evaluation
AUC metric

The code contains multiple bugs that prevent training/evaluation from running correctly or produce incorrect metrics. Your task is to debug and fix the pipeline within a limited time.

Issues you are expected to identify and fix (cover at least these areas)

1. Dataset / label parsing

The dataset parses label as a string.
Training expects labels in a numeric form usable by the loss function (e.g., int / tensor).

2. One-hot encoding bug

A one-hot encoding snippet is provided and can replace the current label logic.
However, the provided one-hot implementation has a dimension/shape mismatch that must be fixed.

3. Incorrect use of model output (last_hidden_state)

The model uses a BERT/Transformer output for classification.
The current usage of last_hidden_state is incorrect, leading to wrong shapes or an invalid classifier head input. Fix it (e.g., choose an appropriate pooling strategy or token representation).

4. Loss bug: applying Softmax before CrossEntropy

The implementation applies softmax before cross entropy loss.
Fix it to follow the correct usage for the chosen framework.

5. AUC metric input/parameter bug

The AUC computation has incorrect inputs and/or key parameters, causing errors or wrong results.
Fix the AUC call so it matches the binary or multiclass setting.

6. Training detail checks

Verify dropout behavior (train vs eval mode).
Verify no incorrect requires_grad settings that freeze parameters unintentionally.
Deliverables
1.
A corrected pipeline that trains without crashing and reports a valid AUC.
2.
For each bug: the symptom, the root cause, and the fix.
3.
A sanity check showing the fixed pipeline learns (for example, overfitting one small batch).

steps: A classifier's loss does not decrease. What do you check first? Use a small controlled problem to distinguish a broken training loop from a difficult learning task.
Check target encoding, logits/loss compatibility, preprocessing, train mode, optimizer parameters and zero_grad/backward/step order.
Inspect finite activations and gradients, then confirm that parameters change. Try overfitting a tiny batch.
Once basic learning works, sweep learning rate and compare a simple baseline; change one factor at a time.
Fit a baseline on messy tabular data without leakage. Build a trustworthy split and simple baseline before sophisticated feature engineering.
Define the target, prediction time and unit of independence, then split by time or group if required.
Fit imputation, scaling and category encodings on training folds only. Start with a dummy baseline and a regularized linear or small tree model.
Evaluate slices, missingness patterns and calibration; document features unavailable at decision time and remove them.

Use raw classification logits with cross-entropy and integer class labels; ensure encoder/head parameters are in the optimizer if intended. Verify device placement, train/eval state and gradient flow. Pooling a padding token or feeding probabilities into a logits loss are independent bugs that a tiny-batch overfit test can reveal.
solution.example: Passing softmax probabilities into a loss expecting logits applies a second normalization and can produce weak or misleading gradients.
solution.trap: Blaming insufficient model size before proving that the optimizer is updating the intended parameters.

$$

\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=\sum_i G_{i,:}.
$$

The bias sum is over all leading positions where the same bias was reused. Do not average again if $G$ already contains the mean-loss factor. For example, with one row $x=[2,3]$ and scalar upstream derivative $4$, the weight derivative is $[8,12]$.

Check a scalar objective using central differences:

$$

$$

title: Understanding Logistic Regression: Mechanism and Applications
question:
Understanding Logistic Regression: Mechanism and Applications

Describe logistic regression, explain how it works and its applications.

def solution():
# Read data from standard input
# Write your code here
pass

steps: Explain logistic regression from scores to gradients. Logistic regression models binary probability with a linear score passed through a sigmoid.
Compute z=xᵀw+b and p=sigmoid(z); p/(1-p)=exp(z), so the log odds are linear.
Fit weights by minimizing binary cross-entropy, preferably calculated from logits for stability.
The score gradient is p-y, giving weight gradient Xᵀ(p-y)/N under mean reduction. Choose the classification threshold using validation costs and metrics.
solution.example: A logit of 0 means p=0.5; a logit of log(3) means p=0.75 and odds 3:1.
solution.trap: Calling sigmoid a hard threshold, or assuming a threshold of 0.5 is optimal for every cost structure.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Connect the model, objective and evaluation split

A model class states what relationships can be represented; the objective states which errors training penalizes; the split estimates where those relationships generalize. These are separate choices. For binary logistic regression,

$$
z_i=x_i^\top w+b,\qquad p_i=\sigma(z_i),\qquad
L=\frac1N\sum_i\left[\log(1+e^{z_i})-y_i z_i\right]+\lambda R(w).
$$

Compute the softplus term stably from logits. The derivative of the unregularized per-example loss with respect to its score is $p_i-y_i$. A decision threshold changes actions but does not refit the probability model.

Inspect a simple baseline and training/validation curves before diagnosing high bias or variance. Low training error and poor validation performance may indicate overfitting, entity leakage, an inappropriate split or a genuine distribution change. The remedies differ: regularization does not repair a broken future-information boundary.

Fit scaling, imputation and encoders within training folds. For repeated users, grouped validation can be necessary; for forecasting, preserve the direction of time. Include class imbalance, calibration and subgroup errors rather than reporting only one accuracy number. A model can improve ranking while becoming worse as a probability estimate, and a statistically better estimate can still produce worse decisions at an unsuitable operating threshold.

title: L1 L2 Regularization
question: What are L1 and L2 regularization? What are the differences between them?

steps: Compare L1 and L2 regularization. Both penalize large coefficients, but their geometry produces different coefficient patterns.
Add lambda*sum(abs(w)) for L1 or a stated lambda-scaled squared norm for L2.
L1 can produce exact zeros with suitable optimization, aiding sparse selection; L2 usually shrinks coefficients smoothly and stabilizes correlated predictors.
Standardize features using training statistics, tune lambda on validation data and state whether the intercept is penalized.
solution.example: With two almost identical predictors, L1 may choose one unstably while L2 spreads weight across both.
solution.trap: Interpreting a selected correlated feature as uniquely causal, or comparing unscaled coefficients across different units.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Why one penalty creates zeros and the other usually does not

State the loss convention before comparing penalty coefficients. With a mean data loss, one possible pair of objectives is

$$
J_1(w)=\frac1N\sum_i\ell_i(w)+\lambda\|w\|_1,
\qquad
J_2(w)=\frac1N\sum_i\ell_i(w)+\frac\lambda2\|w\|_2^2.
$$

L2 contributes derivative $\lambda w$, continuously shrinking larger coefficients. L1 has subgradient $\lambda\operatorname{sign}(w_j)$ away from zero and an interval $[-\lambda,\lambda]$ at zero. That interval can balance the data gradient while the coefficient remains **exactly zero**.

A one-coordinate example makes the distinction concrete. For the quadratic data term $\tfrac12(w-z)^2$, the solutions are

$$
w_{\rm L1}=\operatorname{sign}(z)\max(|z|-\lambda,0),\qquad
w_{\rm L2}=\frac{z}{1+\lambda}.
$$

With $z=0.8$ and $\lambda=1$, L1 gives zero and L2 gives $0.4$. These closed forms describe this specific separable objective; arbitrary correlated-design regression is not solved by independently applying them to the raw targets.

Scale features using training-only statistics, otherwise coefficient magnitude reflects units as well as influence. Usually state separately whether the intercept is penalized. For correlated predictors, L1 can choose one somewhat arbitrarily, whereas L2 often distributes weight and stabilizes predictions. Neither sparse selection nor a large coefficient establishes causality.

**When to use.** L1 is useful when sparsity itself helps interpretation or deployment; L2 is a strong stability baseline. Tune the penalty within the validation procedure and compare the actual predictive/operational objective. Elastic net combines both penalties rather than claiming one is universally superior.

title: Handling Imbalance Data
question: For imbalance data, if you apply down sampling to the training data, should you also down sample the test data?

steps: Why can high accuracy hide failure on imbalanced data? A model can achieve high accuracy by predicting the common class while missing nearly all important rare events.
Inspect class prevalence, the confusion matrix and per-class precision/recall.
Choose a metric connected to the decision: PR behavior for rare-event retrieval, calibration for probability-based decisions, and explicit cost curves for thresholds.
Try class weights, resampling or focal loss carefully, validating on the natural deployment distribution and recalibrating when needed.
Check calibration and choose a decision threshold. A probability estimate and the action taken from it are separate design choices.

Fit a calibration transform only on held-out predictions if needed, then choose a threshold using explicit costs or operational capacity.
Evaluate the entire calibrated-and-thresholded pipeline on untouched test data and important slices.

title: Understanding Linear Regression and Multicollinearity Issues
question:
Understanding Linear Regression and Multicollinearity Issues

Describe linear regression and explain why variables should not have multicollinearity.

steps: Explain multicollinearity and stable least squares. Correlated predictors can make coefficient estimates unstable even when predictions remain useful.
Write the least-squares objective ||Xw-y||²; inspect rank or singular values of X.
Use QR or SVD-based least squares rather than explicitly inverting XᵀX. Centering and scaling can help conditioning.
Use ridge if shrinkage is appropriate, and distinguish predictive stability from interpretation of individual coefficients.
Derive ridge regression and its effect on conditioning. Ridge penalizes large weights and reduces sensitivity along weakly identified feature directions.
For objective ||Xw-y||²+lambda*||w||², set its gradient to zero.
Solve (XᵀX+lambda*I)w=Xᵀy, keeping intercept treatment explicit.
Use a numerical solve rather than an explicit inverse, and tune lambda using held-out data.
solution.example: If one column is exactly twice another, several coefficient pairs produce the same predictions. The individual coefficients are not identifiable without an extra convention.
solution.trap: Taking a numerical inverse and treating enormous coefficients as strong evidence of real effects.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Prefer projections and stable solves to memorized inverses

Least squares finds the projection of the response onto the feature space:

$$
\hat\beta=\arg\min_\beta\|X\beta-y\|_2^2,
\qquad X^\top X\hat\beta=X^\top y.
$$

The normal equations explain the mathematics, but explicitly forming $(X^\top X)^{-1}$ is usually a poor numerical implementation. Squaring the condition number can amplify instability. QR or SVD-based least-squares routines expose rank and near-dependence more reliably.

For two datasets with the same feature definitions, sufficient statistics add:

$$
S=X_1^\top X_1+X_2^\top X_2,\qquad
 t=X_1^\top y_1+X_2^\top y_2.
$$

Solving the pooled problem is not equivalent to averaging the two coefficient vectors. Rows carry different directional information, not only different sample counts.

State centering, intercept and regularization conventions. With ridge, the penalized directions satisfy $(X^\top X+\lambda I)\beta=X^\top y$, but an unpenalized intercept needs separate treatment. Distinguish coefficient identification from predictive usefulness: correlated columns can make individual coefficients unstable while their combined predictions remain fairly stable. Validate forecasts on independent data; impressive training fit, including interpolation of noise, is not evidence of a real predictive relation.

title: Implement K-Means from Scratch
question:
Implement the K-Means algorithm from scratch.

Implement a K-Means clustering algorithm from scratch. The algorithm should take the following parameters: a list of 2D data points data_points, an integer k indicating the number of clusters, and max_iterations, the maximum number of iterations. The output should be a list of integers, where each integer represents the cluster label of the corresponding data point in data_points.

Example input:

[[1.0, 2.0], [1.5, 1.8], [5.0, 8.0], [8.0, 8.0], [1.0, 0.6], [9.0, 11.0]]

Output:

[0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1]

Data scale:

data_points contains up to 1000 2D points.
k ranges from 1 to 10.
max_iterations defaults to 300.
Example
Input
[[1.0, 2.0], [1.5, 1.8], [5.0, 8.0], [8.0, 8.0], [1.0, 0.6], [9.0, 11.0]], 2

steps: Implement k-means with convergence and empty clusters. Alternate assigning points to their closest centers and moving each center to the mean of its assigned points.
Initialize k distinct data indices under an explicit random seed, requiring 1<=k<=N.
Compute squared distances, assign closest centers and recompute non-empty means. For an empty cluster, retain its center or explicitly reseed it.
Stop on a center-shift tolerance or iteration cap, then recompute labels for the returned centers. Compare objective values, not center ordering, across implementations.
Choose the number of k-means clusters. There is rarely one objectively correct k; the useful resolution depends on geometry and the downstream task.
Compare objective curves across k, using several initialization seeds.
Inspect cluster stability, silhouette behavior, sizes and representative examples, and standardize features if appropriate.
Validate usefulness for the real decision; do not choose a visually neat elbow without checking whether clusters are meaningful.
solution.example: For [0,1,9,10] with k=2 and sensible initialization, centers converge to 0.5 and 9.5.
solution.trap: Taking the mean of an empty slice, stopping with labels from old centers, or assuming a local optimum is globally best.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Choose the geometry before the update rule

An algorithm's center update follows its objective. Squared Euclidean clustering uses means:

$$
J_2=\sum_i\|x_i-\mu_{c_i}\|_2^2.
$$

For fixed assignments, differentiating with respect to a center sets it to its members' arithmetic mean. Manhattan distance instead uses coordinatewise medians:

$$
J_1=\sum_i\|x_i-m_{c_i}\|_1.
$$

For points $0,2,10$, the squared-error center is $4$, while the absolute-distance center is $2$. Swapping these updates silently solves a different problem.

Alternating nearest-center assignment and an exact fixed-cluster update cannot increase the chosen objective, but it need not reach a global optimum. State initialization, empty-cluster handling, deterministic ties and a stopping rule. Recompute assignments for returned centers after the last update.

For retrieval, state normalization, similarity and relevance labels. Cosine and raw dot product rank differently when embedding norms vary. Index approximation must be evaluated using recall and downstream quality, not latency alone. Negative examples can actually be valid alternative matches; audit this before interpreting a lower contrastive loss as better semantics. Evaluate cluster/retrieval stability across seeds and important slices rather than trusting a visually attractive plot.

title: KNN Classification From Scratch
question:
Data Science coding task (leaf dataset, 3 classes). The original assignment is a Jupyter-notebook workflow: load train.csv (feature columns feature_0..feature_2, integer label with 3 classes), split into train/validation, implement KNN from scratch (no built-in KNN trainer), report validation accuracy, predict on test.csv, write predictions.csv preserving row order, then tune K (optionally with cross-validation).

This gradable version isolates the core algorithm — KNN classification from scratch:

Function
knn_predict(train_features, train_labels, test_features, k) -> list[label]
train_features: list of numeric feature vectors.
train_labels: integer class labels aligned with train_features.
test_features: feature vectors to classify.
k: number of neighbours.

Use Euclidean distance. Return the majority label among the k nearest training points for each test row. Tie-breaking: on a voting tie, return the smallest class id.

Example
train_features = [[0,0,0],[1,1,1],[2,2,2]]
train_labels   = [0, 1, 2]
test_features  = [[1,1,1]],  k = 1
-> [1]
Notes
Do not use a built-in KNN implementation.
Euclidean distance; smallest-class-id tie-break.

steps: Implement k-nearest-neighbor classification. Store the training examples; for a query, predict from the labels of the nearest k examples under a chosen distance.
Fit feature transformations on training data only and apply the same transformation to queries.
Compute query-to-training squared distances, choose k neighbors, and count their labels or use defined distance weights.
Specify tie-breaking and k bounds. For many queries use batching or a search index; the brute-force baseline costs O(ND) per query before selection overhead.
solution.example: Neighbors with labels [A,A,B] predict A for k=3. With k=2 and labels [A,B], a deterministic tie rule is required.
solution.trap: Comparing unscaled features with incompatible units or including the test point as its own training neighbor.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Derive a local rule, then apply the chain rule

Treat a layer as a function with a declared input and output shape. Write the scalar loss and its reduction first: a sum, mean over rows and mean over all elements produce different gradient scales. For an affine layer $Y=XW+b$ with upstream gradient $G=\partial L/\partial Y$,

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X}=GW^\top,\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=X^\top G,\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=\sum_i G_{i,:}.
$$

The bias sum is over all leading positions where the same bias was reused. Do not average again if $G$ already contains the mean-loss factor. For example, with one row $x=[2,3]$ and scalar upstream derivative $4$, the weight derivative is $[8,12]$.

Cache the forward values needed by the derivative; compute all gradients before updating parameters. Updating $W$ midway would make the earlier-layer derivative use a different function from the one evaluated forward.

Check a scalar objective using central differences:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_j}\approx
\frac{L(\theta+h e_j)-L(\theta-h e_j)}{2h}.
$$

Use float64 and several sensible $h$ values. An arbitrarily tiny $h$ loses the difference to rounding, while a large one measures curvature rather than a local derivative. Avoid ReLU's kink at zero during this check, and test inputs, weights and biases separately.

title: Compute Euclidean Distance Between Two Tensors
question:
Given two tensors of shape [B, N, 100] and [B, M, 100], compute the Euclidean distance between them so the output is a tensor of shape [B, N, M].

For every batch b, output out[b][i][j] is the Euclidean distance between the vector A[b][i] and the vector B[b][j] (each of length D = 100).

Example
Input: A = [[[1]*100]*3]*2, B = [[[2]*100]*4]*2

Here A is a batch of 2, each holding 3 vectors of one hundred 1s; B is a batch of 2, each holding 4 vectors of one hundred 2s. Every pairwise distance equals sqrt(100 * (2-1)^2) = 10, so the output has shape [2, 3, 4] and every entry is 10.0.

For X:(N,D), Y:(M,D), the result is (N,M). A direct reference uses X[:,None,:]-Y[None,:,:].
A lower-memory algebraic version computes squared distances as norm(X)²+norm(Y)²-2X@Yᵀ, clamping tiny negative roundoff to zero.
Take square roots only if actual distances are needed. Block the computation when N*M is too large; no formula removes the output-size cost.

title: Baseline Classifier on a Messy Tabular Dataset
question:
You are given a tabular dataset for a binary classification task, loaded into a pandas DataFrame df with a label column target. The data is deliberately messy: some numeric columns have missing values, some categorical columns spell the same category in several ways (for example "NY", "ny ", "New York"), one column mixes numbers and strings, and an identifier column is present. Build a clean, working baseline classifier end to end and explain your choices.

What to deliver
1.
Profile the data. Inspect types, missing-value counts, cardinality of each categorical column and the class balance of target. State which columns you will drop, which you will fix and why (including any column that must not be a feature).
2.
Clean the data. Handle missing values by column type, normalise inconsistent category spellings, and coerce the mixed-type column to a single type. Say what you do with values that cannot be converted.
3.
Split before transforming. Create a train/test split first (stratified when the classes are imbalanced), and fit every imputer, encoder and scaler on the training part only.
4.
Train the simplest sufficient model. Use a model such as logistic regression or a shallow decision tree on a small, justified set of features. Explain why you did not start with a larger ensemble or a grid search.
5.
Evaluate on the held-out set. Report accuracy, a confusion matrix and precision and recall for the minority class. Say which number you would lead with and why accuracy alone can mislead.
6.
Justify and extend. Explain what each pitfall would have cost (leakage, an ID column used as a feature, mean-imputing a categorical column), and what you would add next for a setting where interpretability and monitoring matter.
Constraints
Use pandas and scikit-learn only; the whole pipeline should run top to bottom on the dataset.
Report numbers from the held-out split, never from the training data.

title: Bias-Variance Trade-off: Diagnose and Fix a Model
question:
A model you trained for a credit-risk task performs worse than expected. Use the bias-variance trade-off to explain why a model can fail in two opposite ways, how you would tell which one you are facing, and what you would change in each case.

Requirements

Answer all five parts.

1.
Definitions. Define bias and variance of a learned model, and state the decomposition of expected squared prediction error into bias, variance and irreducible noise.
2.
Failure examples. Give one concrete example of a high-bias model and one of a high-variance model, and say how each looks in the training error and the validation error.
3.

4.

5.
Remedies. For each failure type, list at least two changes you would try and explain why each one moves the model along the trade-off, including how L2 regularisation, dropout and early stopping reduce variance at a small cost in bias.

title: Experiment Design: Switchback and CI Interpretation
question:
Scientist onsite round — a reasoning prompt, not coding. Pick a metric (e.g. ETA vs session conversion) and design an experiment to measure a causal effect on Uber's marketplace.

Cover: metric definition, choice of experimentation framework (A/B vs switchback), treatment/bucket design and guardrails, rollout strategy, and confidence-interval interpretation for ratio metrics. Be fast and precise in defining the metric.

steps: Design a switchback experiment for a shared marketplace. Time-block treatment assignment can reduce simultaneous cross-treatment interference, but introduces time effects and carryover concerns.
Define the interacting unit, such as a region-time block, and randomize a balanced treatment schedule.
Choose block length and washout periods based on system response and persistence, not convenience alone.
Analyze at the assignment unit with time and region structure, checking carryover and enough independent blocks.
Interpret a confidence interval that includes zero. The interval describes uncertainty under a sampling procedure; it does not prove no meaningful effect exists.
State the estimated effect and interval in practical units.
Compare the entire interval with the smallest meaningful benefit and acceptable harm, not just zero.
Check power, design and uncertainty assumptions before deciding to launch, gather more data or reject the change.
solution.example: Alternating dispatch policies within one shared fleet by individual rider can contaminate both arms; region-time assignments may fit better.
solution.trap: Treating thousands of rides inside one time block as thousands of independent randomized units.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Establish what the number actually estimates

Write the population, unit of analysis, outcome window and denominator next to the metric. A per-user mean and a per-impression mean answer different questions. A global mean over unequal batches is

$$
\bar\ell=\frac{\sum_b\sum_{i\in b}\ell_i}{\sum_b n_b},
$$

not generally the unweighted mean of batch means. Workers should reduce numerators and denominators separately when reporting that metric.

Use a comparison with matched examples, mature labels and unchanged definitions. For uncertainty, resample independent units; repeated events within a user or prompt are not automatically independent. title: Stratified Sampling from Class-Bucketed Data
question:
Build a sampler for a labelled dataset that is stored in one bucket of examples per class. A draw must return a class label together with one example of that class, and every class must be equally likely to be the one returned, however many examples its bucket holds. This is the sampler you would use to build class-balanced training batches.

What to implement

stratified_sample(training, rng=None) -> tuple[str, object]

training: a dict that maps a class label (str) to the list of examples of that class, for example {"cat": [...], "dog": [...], "fox": [...]}.
rng: an optional random.Random instance. Use it for every random choice, so a seeded generator makes the draw repeatable. When it is None, use the module-level random.
Return (class_label, example).
Rules
1.
The probability that the returned label is a given class is the same for every class that has at least one example (1/K for K such classes), whatever the bucket sizes.
2.
Given the class, every example in its bucket is equally likely.
3.
A class whose bucket is empty is never returned and does not count towards K.
4.
If no class has any example (including an empty dict), raise ValueError.
5.
Do not modify training.
Examples
1.
{"cat": [1, 2, 3, 4], "dog": ["d"]}: the label is "cat" with probability 1/2 and "dog" with probability 1/2. If it is "cat", each of 1, 2, 3, 4 has probability 1/4; if it is "dog", the example is "d". Drawing uniformly over all five examples would instead return "cat" 80% of the time, which is not what is wanted here.
2.
{"a": [], "b": [7], "c": []} always returns ("b", 7).
3.
{"a": [], "b": []} raises ValueError.
Constraints
Up to 10^3 classes and 10^6 examples per class; each draw takes O(K) time and O(K) extra space, where K is the number of classes.

steps: Create stratified samples from class buckets. Sampling rules must specify desired class proportions, replacement and rounding behavior.
Compute class quotas from target proportions and requested size using a deterministic remainder-allocation rule.
Sample within buckets using a seeded generator, respecting available counts or explicitly allowing replacement.
Preserve or record inclusion probabilities if the sample will be used for population estimation.
solution.example: For 10 examples at proportions [0.55,0.45], quotas cannot both be exact; a stated tie/rounding rule must allocate the final unit.
solution.trap: Assuming an intentionally balanced sample has the original population prevalence.

$$

not generally the unweighted mean of batch means. Workers should reduce numerators and denominators separately when reporting that metric.

title: Clean Noisy Human Labels by Scoring Annotator Reliability
question:
Clean Noisy Human Labels by Scoring Annotator Reliability

A team trains a binary classifier that flags identity_attack comments: negative or hateful comments that target someone because of their identity. Each training comment was labelled by several human annotators, and some annotators are careless. Your job is to measure how reliable each annotator is and use that to clean the training labels. Then show that a classifier trained on the cleaned data beats one trained on every raw label.

What to implement

Every row is a dict {"prompt_id": str, "rater_id": str, "embedding": list[float], "label": 0 or 1}. The train set has one row per annotation, so a prompt appears once per annotator who labelled it, always with the same embedding.

1.
dataset_stats(train) -> dict: return {"num_raters": int, "num_prompts": int, "label_counts": {0: int, 1: int}, "embedding_dim": int}. These are the numbers of distinct raters and prompts, the number of rows with each label (both keys always present), and the embedding length (0 for an empty train set).
2.
majority_labels(train) -> dict: map each prompt_id to the label given by more than half of its annotations, or None if neither label has more than half (a tie).
3.
rater_agreement(train, majority) -> dict: map each rater_id to the share of that rater's rows whose label equals the prompt's majority label. Skip rows whose prompt has majority None; leave out a rater with no rows left.
4.
assign_pools(agreement, expert_min=0.90, decent_min=0.70) -> dict: map each rater to "expert" if agreement ≥ expert_min, else "decent" if agreement ≥ decent_min, else "spammer".
5.
filter_reliable(train, pools) -> list[dict]: the rows whose rater is "expert" or "decent", in their original order. Raters missing from pools are dropped.
6.
weighted_consensus(train, agreement) -> list[dict]: one row per prompt, in order of the prompt's first appearance in train, as {"prompt_id", "rater_id": "consensus", "embedding", "label"}. Give each rater the weight max(0, 2 * agreement - 1) (0 for a rater missing from agreement). The label is 1 if the weighted share of 1-votes is above 0.5, otherwise 0. Drop a prompt whose raters all have weight 0.

None of the functions may modify its inputs.

Given in the starter (do not change them):

make_dataset(seed=0) returns (train, test, true_pool). train has 600 prompts with 5 annotations each from 22 raters; test has 400 prompts with gold labels; true_pool is every rater's hidden pool (use it only to check your work).
train_and_evaluate(train_rows, test_rows) fits a logistic regression on the rows' embeddings and labels and returns {"accuracy": float, "f1": float} on the test rows.
Examples

Example 1. Raters A, B and C label three prompts:

prompt  A  B  C
p1      1  1  0
p2      0  0  1
p3      1  -  0
majority_labels gives {"p1": 1, "p2": 0, "p3": None}: p3 is a 1-1 tie.
rater_agreement gives {"A": 1.0, "B": 1.0, "C": 0.0}: p3 is skipped, and C disagrees on both remaining prompts.
assign_pools gives A and B "expert" and C "spammer", so filter_reliable keeps the five rows from A and B.
weighted_consensus gives labels 1, 0, 1 for p1, p2, p3. C's weight is max(0, 2 * 0 - 1) = 0, so p3 takes A's label.

Example 2. One prompt, A says 0, B and C say 1, with agreement A = 1.0, B = 0.6, C = 0.6. The weights are 1.0, 0.2 and 0.2, so the weighted share of 1-votes is 0.4 / 1.4 ≈ 0.29 and the label is 0. A plain majority vote would say 1.

Example 3. On make_dataset(0), assign_pools(rater_agreement(train, majority_labels(train))) equals true_pool. The classifier trained on all 3,000 annotations scores accuracy 0.855 and F1 0.772. Trained on filter_reliable rows it scores 0.94 and 0.881, and on weighted_consensus rows 0.94 and 0.882.

Constraints
Up to 10^5 rows, 10^3 raters and 10^4 prompts; labels are 0 or 1.
Each function should run in O(number of rows) time, apart from building its output.
Follow-up discussion
1.
Besides careless annotators, what difficulties come up with human-labelled data (for example ambiguous guidelines, systematic bias of a group of raters, class imbalance, raters who disagree in good faith)?
2.
A rater's own vote is part of the majority that rater is scored against. Why does that inflate agreement, and how would you fix it?
3.
The pool thresholds were picked by hand. How would you choose them, or avoid them?

steps: Clean noisy annotations using rater agreement. Estimate which annotators agree with a provisional consensus, but recognize that the consensus itself can be biased.
Group annotations by prompt; form a majority label, marking ties as unresolved.
For each rater, measure agreement only on resolved prompts. Assign reliability tiers or continuous weights, then filter or aggregate annotations according to the specified thresholds.
Train identical baseline and cleaned-data models and compare on independent gold labels. Include a leave-one-rater-out consensus variant to reduce self-inclusion bias.
solution.contract_notes: For the weighted consensus variant, use w=max(0,2*agreement-1), drop all-zero-weight prompts, predict 1 only when the weighted positive fraction is greater than 0.5, and preserve first-prompt order. Keep tie-majority prompts out of agreement denominators and leave raters with no resolved votes unscored. Never mutate input rows; compare cleaned and raw training on the independent gold test set.
solution.example: If A and B vote 1 and C votes 0 on two prompts, C has agreement zero with their majority; that does not prove A and B are correct.
solution.trap: Evaluating on labels generated by the same consensus used for cleaning, or assuming minority annotators are necessarily careless.
