Design an end-to-end A/B testing / experimentation platform: experiment configuration, traffic / bucket allocation, and metrics collection. A collaborative round that goes deep into trade-offs.

SWE ab-testing metrics experiment-design

Design an end-to-end A/B testing / experimentation platform. Cover at least:
Experiment configuration: defining experiments, variants, and targeting.
Traffic allocation: assigning users to buckets / variants with stable, deterministic assignment.

question:
Research-track take-home. You get a self-contained ML problem to solve in ~4 hours in your own environment (local IDE or Colab), immediately followed by a 40-minute live review where you present results and field questions.

title: QR Take-Home Data Project & Presentation
question:
You are given a table of time-stamped market data (prices and a few candidate predictors) and asked to build a predictive model of future returns, then explain and defend the work to a panel of reviewers. Describe how you would carry out the whole project and which choices you would defend.

title: Implement a Basic Tokenizer and Train a Simple LLM-like Model in a Notebook Case Study
question:
Implement a Basic Tokenizer and Train a Simple Language Model

Build a small end-to-end language-model pipeline: tokenize text, encode tokens to ids, decode ids back to text, and train a next-token model whose loss decreases.

Implement the class SimpleTokenizer and the function train_bigram using NumPy only (no deep-learning framework).

Requirements
1.
tokenize(text) — split text into word tokens on whitespace. A string returns List[str]; a list of strings returns List[List[str]]. Runs of whitespace collapse, and the result is deterministic.
2.
build_vocab(texts) — from a list of strings, build vocab (token -> id) and inv_vocab (id -> token). Id 0 is reserved for the unknown token "<unk>"; the other tokens get ids in order of first appearance. Return vocab.
3.
word_to_token(text) (encoding) — map a string to a list of ids, or a list of strings to a list of id lists. A token that is not in the vocabulary maps to the <unk> id.
4.
token_to_word(ids) (decoding) — map a list of ids to a space-joined string, or a list of id lists to a list of strings. An unknown id decodes to <unk>.
5.
train_bigram(token_ids, vocab_size, epochs=200, lr=0.5, seed=0) — train a bigram next-token model: a vocab_size x vocab_size weight matrix W (initialized from a normal distribution with standard deviation 0.01 and the given seed) whose row x holds the logits of the token that follows x. Each epoch computes the mean cross-entropy over all (current, next) pairs and takes one plain SGD step on its gradient. Return (W, losses), where losses holds the loss of each epoch.
Input / Output
Texts are Python strings; ids are non-negative integers.
train_bigram takes the id sequence of a training text and returns the trained matrix and the per-epoch losses.
Constraints
Decoding the encoding of in-vocabulary text returns the whitespace-normalized text.
Training must reduce the loss: losses[-1] < losses[0].
Example
tok = SimpleTokenizer()
tok.tokenize("the  cat   sat")       ->  ["the", "cat", "sat"]
tok.tokenize(["a b", "c"])           ->  [["a", "b"], ["c"]]
tok.build_vocab(["the cat sat on the mat", "the dog sat on the log"])
->  {"<unk>": 0, "the": 1, "cat": 2, "sat": 3,
"on": 4, "mat": 5, "dog": 6, "log": 7}
tok.word_to_token("the cat elephant") ->  [1, 2, 0]
tok.token_to_word([1, 2, 3])         ->  "the cat sat"

ids = tok.word_to_token("the cat sat on the mat the dog sat on the log")
W, losses = train_bigram(ids, 8)     # losses[0] ~ 2.08, losses[-1] ~ 0.59

steps: Implement a deterministic toy tokenizer, then explain what BPE adds. A tokenizer turns text into a reproducible token sequence; BPE learns reusable merges beyond individual symbols.
Define the base alphabet and normalization policy, including whitespace and unknown characters.
For BPE training, repeatedly count adjacent pairs, choose the most frequent under a deterministic tie rule, merge non-overlapping occurrences and update the vocabulary.
At encoding time apply learned merge ranks, not a fresh frequency count on each document. Keep decoding and special-token handling explicit.

Why is a next-token model trained with shifted targets? At position t, the model sees tokens through t and predicts token t+1. The target shift makes the training task match autoregressive generation.
Given tokens [x0,x1,x2,x3], use inputs [x0,x1,x2] and targets [x1,x2,x3], unless the library performs this shift internally.
Apply a causal mask to prevent access to later input positions. Use cross-entropy over vocabulary logits without an extra softmax first.
For instruction tuning, mask unwanted target positions after aligning the shift. Divide by the count of supervised targets, not padded sequence length.
Debug a miniature GPT that fails to learn. Localize the first broken invariant rather than changing many hyperparameters at once.
Check shifted labels, causal masking, tensor axes, vocabulary bounds and padding/loss masks on a tiny batch.
Check train/eval mode, gradient presence, optimizer steps and parameter changes. Overfit a tiny dataset with dropout disabled as a diagnostic.
Compare against a simple trusted baseline; then test generation and caching separately. Record one controlled change and its effect at a time.
solution.example: Starting from a a a a, merging pair (a,a) non-overlapping produces aa aa, not three overlapping replacements.
solution.trap: Confusing longest-prefix matching over a fixed vocabulary with a complete BPE training algorithm.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Build the computation before optimizing it

Start by saying which axis represents examples, positions, heads and features. With batch size $B$, query length $T_q$, key length $T_k$ and head width $d_k$, a head receives $Q\in\mathbb R^{B\times T_q\times d_k}$ and $K\in\mathbb R^{B\times T_k\times d_k}$. Values may have a different final width $d_v$. The essential operation is

$$
S=\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M,\qquad
P_{ij}=\frac{\exp(S_{ij}-m_i)}{\sum_j\exp(S_{ij}-m_i)},\qquad O=PV.
$$

Here the transpose affects the final two axes, $m_i=\max_j S_{ij}$ is a row maximum, and $M$ contains zero for allowed positions and $-\infty$ for forbidden ones. Each query produces one distribution **over keys**, so summing the wrong axis changes the operation even when the output shape looks plausible.

For a tiny check, give a query access to exactly one key. Its output must equal that key's value, regardless of the score. Then change a forbidden future token: earlier causal outputs must remain unchanged. These checks expose mistakes that a random shape test misses.

Explain the limitation of the simple implementation. Explicitly materializing $P$ uses $O(T_qT_k)$ score storage per head. A reference implementation is useful for correctness; a tiled kernel can avoid that materialization while preserving the mathematical attention operation. Generation additionally needs correct target shifts, positions and cache state, not just a working matrix multiplication.

title: Design an API for Embedding and Classification Results
question:
Two models work as a pipeline: an embedding model turns a stored file into a vector, and a classifier turns that vector into a label. Clients want one API they can call with a file and get the classification back. Design that API and the service behind it so that it stays correct, responsive and affordable even when the models are slow or fail.

What you are given
1.
Stored file: the file is already in the system and has an identifier. Uploading files is out of scope.
2.
Stage 1, embedding model (black box): input is one file, output is an embedding for that file. You cannot change or inspect the model, so its exact input and output contract is part of the design.
3.
Stage 2, classification step: input is the embedding from stage 1, output is a classification result in JSON format.
4.
Client: a user calls your API to obtain the classification result for a file.
Requirements
1.
The API surface: endpoints, request and response JSON, status codes, and how the API is versioned.
2.
How a request flows through the embedding stage and then the classification stage, including what is passed between them.
3.
Whether the call is synchronous or asynchronous, and the exact behaviour of each choice, including idempotency and how a client retrieves a result.
4.
The data you store, and how embeddings are reused across requests.
5.
Failure handling: timeouts, retries, partial failure between the two stages, and invalid input.
6.
How you scale it and how you observe it.
Constraints and assumptions to state
The exact input type and size limits of the embedding model, the embedding dimension and dtype, and the label set of the classifier are not given. State your assumptions explicitly and show which parts of the design depend on them.
The model stages may be slow compared with an ordinary web request, and may fail independently.
Results must be consistent: the same file and the same model versions must give the same answer.

steps: Define versioned endpoints and schemas for token processing, embeddings and classification; specify input normalization, maximum sizes, supported batch shapes and error types.
Keep model/preprocessing versions in responses and cache keys. Batch compatible work under latency budgets, preserve request/output mapping and handle partial errors explicitly.
For streaming input, retain only the state the model needs and distinguish append-only token updates from corrections. Return normalized probabilities or scores under a documented label order.
Enforce tenant quotas, privacy and bounded queues; measure quality, p99 latency, token throughput and failure rates under representative lengths.
solution.example: A stored embedding produced by version A must not silently be compared with a query embedding from incompatible version B. A failed item cannot shift every later batch result by one index.
solution.trap: A supposedly generic API that hides model-version, dimension and normalization differences.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Separate service time, queueing and memory

A request's observed latency is not just the model kernel duration:

$$
T_{\rm request}=T_{\rm queue}+T_{\rm preprocess}+T_{\rm prefill}
+T_{\rm decode}+T_{\rm delivery}.
$$

Prefill processes the prompt; decode repeatedly adds tokens. Measure both time to first token and inter-token latency, because a configuration can improve aggregate throughput while worsening the user's experience. Batching amortizes work but may increase waiting.

Estimate the KV tensor budget independently of fixed weights. For equal-length requests,

$$
M_{\rm KV}=2BLT H_{\rm KV}d_h s,
$$

where $L$ is layer count, $T$ cached length and $s$ bytes per element. The factor two is keys plus values. With $L=32$, $T=4096$, $H_{\rm KV}=8$, $d_h=128$, $B=1$ and $s=2$, the raw cache is $512$ MiB, before allocator overhead.

Use measured capacity to set admission and live-token limits. If a worker serves batches of at most $b$ in $s_b$ seconds, $b/s_b$ is an optimistic service-rate ceiling, not a per-request guarantee. Sustained arrivals above that rate grow backlog; even lower averages can hide damaging bursts. Bound queues, define cancellation and partial-failure behavior, and compare latency on matched length/concurrency distributions rather than one isolated request.

title: Design Sora Video Generation Scheduling with Preemption
question:
Design the job scheduler behind a Sora-style text-to-video product. A user types a prompt and waits for a short generated clip; each clip occupies a multi-GPU node for minutes, and at the daily peak there are more requests than GPUs.

Users are on one of three plans: Pro (highest), Plus, and Free. When the fleet is full, work from a higher plan must be able to take a node from a lower-priority job that is already running, and that job must later continue rather than be lost. Your design decides who runs, who waits, and who gets interrupted.

Scale and requirements

All numbers are assumptions you may adjust if you say why.

1.
Fleet: 1,200 nodes of 8 GPUs each, all serving the same video model. A node runs one clip at a time.
2.
Job: a 10-second 1080p clip. Generation is 50 iterative denoising steps of about 5 seconds each on one node, followed by about 50 seconds of decoding and encoding. Weights stay loaded on every node; starting or resuming a job on a node still takes about 3 seconds (receiving the job's inputs or its saved state and preparing the pipeline).
3.
Demand: 2 clips per second for 20 hours of the day and 5 clips per second during a 4-hour peak, so 216,000 clips per day and 2.5 per second on average. Of all requests, 10% come from Pro, 30% from Plus and 60% from Free.
4.
Start-time targets: a job has started when its first denoising step begins on a node. A Pro job starts within 15 seconds of submission, Plus within 2 minutes, and Free has no hard target but must eventually run.
5.
Interrupted work: a preempted job resumes later from where it stopped, on any node, and the user sees one finished clip.
6.
Bursts: during the peak, the total Pro rate can jump from 0.5 to 8 clips per second for one minute (for example after a feature launch). Plus and Free traffic stay at their peak rates.
What to design
1.
The request path and job states, from submission to the delivered clip, including cancellation by the user.
2.
The queues and the priority each queued job gets.
3.
The preemption mechanism: how a running job is stopped, what is saved, and how it resumes.
4.
Capacity estimates: fleet throughput, backlog at peak, and the cost of a preemption in GPU-seconds.
Example scenarios
1.
The fleet is full of Free jobs and one Pro request arrives: it should start within its target, and the Free job it displaces finishes later without redoing its finished steps.
2.
Peak traffic runs for 4 hours: paid requests keep their targets, and the Free backlog that builds up is cleared after the peak.
Follow-ups
Follow-up 1: priority signals beyond the plan

Besides how much the account pays, what other factors should raise or lower a job's priority, and how do you combine them into one ordering?

Follow-up 2: the preemption contract

Define the rules a running job is preempted under: who may preempt whom, when the job is told, how long it has before it must yield, what it must save, and which jobs are protected.

Follow-up 3: starvation

How do you make sure Free jobs are not starved when paid demand stays high for hours?

Follow-up 4: observability

Which metrics and alerts would you build to monitor preemption and scheduling health?

steps: Design preemptible long-running generation jobs. Treat a generation request as durable state with progress and versioned intermediate artifacts.
Record job inputs, priority, resource needs, model/configuration versions and checkpoint capability.
Schedule compatible resources, checkpoint before preemption when supported and resume from verified state; otherwise state the recomputation cost.
Make final publication idempotent and track partial, failed, canceled and completed outcomes separately.
Design a fair GPU job scheduler. The scheduler must satisfy resource constraints while making progress and controlling queueing, rather than merely picking the shortest job.
Represent GPU count, memory, topology, priority, estimated duration and checkpoint support in each job request.
Use admission checks, quotas and a queue policy; reserve whole compatible allocations for distributed jobs to avoid partial-allocation deadlocks.
Support leases, heartbeats, retries and checkpoint-aware preemption. Monitor utilization, wait percentiles and starvation across tenants.
solution.example: Preempting a 30-minute job after 29 minutes without a usable checkpoint can waste nearly all of its compute.
solution.trap: Assuming every model's internal state can be checkpointed and resumed cheaply.

title: Online Token Processing, Embeddings, and Classification
question:
Apple ML Engineer phone screen (Round 2), shared editor. You are given a stream of labeled (text, label) records and must build an end-to-end online pipeline that:

1.
Processes tokens online — one record at a time, no pre-reading the whole corpus.
2.
Generates embeddings for each token/document.
3.
Trains a classifier on the stream and predicts for new records.

Keep it simple: hashed token ids, an embedding table you update online, mean-pool for the document vector, a linear softmax head, and SGD. It is not asking you to pretrain word2vec or a Transformer.

Before coding, clarify: single-pass online vs. replayable stream; binary vs. fixed multi-class C; vocabulary growth (feature hashing vs. lazy growth); embedding dim (32–64); optimizer; and metrics (progressive validation).

steps: Define versioned endpoints and schemas for token processing, embeddings and classification; specify input normalization, maximum sizes, supported batch shapes and error types.
Keep model/preprocessing versions in responses and cache keys. Batch compatible work under latency budgets, preserve request/output mapping and handle partial errors explicitly.
For streaming input, retain only the state the model needs and distinguish append-only token updates from corrections. Return normalized probabilities or scores under a documented label order.
Enforce tenant quotas, privacy and bounded queues; measure quality, p99 latency, token throughput and failure rates under representative lengths.
solution.example: A stored embedding produced by version A must not silently be compared with a query embedding from incompatible version B. A failed item cannot shift every later batch result by one index.
solution.trap: A supposedly generic API that hides model-version, dimension and normalization differences.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Separate service time, queueing and memory

A request's observed latency is not just the model kernel duration:

$$
T_{\rm request}=T_{\rm queue}+T_{\rm preprocess}+T_{\rm prefill}
+T_{\rm decode}+T_{\rm delivery}.
$$

Prefill processes the prompt; decode repeatedly adds tokens. Measure both time to first token and inter-token latency, because a configuration can improve aggregate throughput while worsening the user's experience. Batching amortizes work but may increase waiting.

Estimate the KV tensor budget independently of fixed weights. For equal-length requests,

$$
M_{\rm KV}=2BLT H_{\rm KV}d_h s,
$$

where $L$ is layer count, $T$ cached length and $s$ bytes per element. The factor two is keys plus values. With $L=32$, $T=4096$, $H_{\rm KV}=8$, $d_h=128$, $B=1$ and $s=2$, the raw cache is $512$ MiB, before allocator overhead.

Use measured capacity to set admission and live-token limits. If a worker serves batches of at most $b$ in $s_b$ seconds, $b/s_b$ is an optimistic service-rate ceiling, not a per-request guarantee. Sustained arrivals above that rate grow backlog; even lower averages can hide damaging bursts. Bound queues, define cancellation and partial-failure behavior, and compare latency on matched length/concurrency distributions rather than one isolated request.

title: Implement Dense Layer with Numpy
question:
Implement a simple Dense Layer using Numpy, where you need to implement the forward pass and backward pass, and derive the Sigmoid function.

Requirements:

Write a Python function dense_layer_forward that takes input data matrix X, weight matrix W, and bias vector b, and returns the output matrix Y.
Write a Python function dense_layer_backward that takes the output gradient dY, input data matrix X, weight matrix W, and bias vector b, and returns the input gradient dX, weight gradient dW, and bias gradient db.
Use Sigmoid as the activation function, and provide separate functions sigmoid and sigmoid_derivative.

Provide a complete implementation and several test cases including scenarios for both forward and backward passes. Assume input data are Numpy arrays with compatible dimensions.

Sample Test Case:

X: np.array([[0.5, 0.2]])
W: np.array([[0.3, 0.8], [0.5, 0.2]])
b: np.array([0.1, 0.4])
Output: Appropriate matrix result

Example

Input

X = np.array([[0.5, 0.2]])
W = np.array([[0.3, 0.8], [0.5, 0.2]])
b = np.array([0.1, 0.4])

steps: Derive a dense layer's input, weight and bias gradients. Each parameter receives the sum of contributions from every example that used it.
For Y=XW+b with X:(N,D), W:(D,C), let upstream G:(N,C).
Compute dX=G@Wᵀ, dW=Xᵀ@G and db=sum(G,axis=0).
Do not average again unless the scalar objective's reduction requires it; G may already include the mean factor.
solution.contract_notes: If the dense layer includes sigmoid, cache a=sigmoid(XW+b), compute dZ=dY*a*(1-a), then dX=dZ Wᵀ, dW=Xᵀ dZ and db=sum_rows(dZ). Use a stable branchwise sigmoid for large positive/negative logits. If the layer is affine-only, do not introduce this activation derivative; the prompt’s activation contract decides.
solution.example: For one example x=[2,3] and scalar upstream 4, the weight gradient is [8,12].
solution.trap: Summing the bias gradient over features instead of examples or silently transposing the weight convention.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Derive a local rule, then apply the chain rule

Treat a layer as a function with a declared input and output shape. Write the scalar loss and its reduction first: a sum, mean over rows and mean over all elements produce different gradient scales. For an affine layer $Y=XW+b$ with upstream gradient $G=\partial L/\partial Y$,

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X}=GW^\top,\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=X^\top G,\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=\sum_i G_{i,:}.
$$

The bias sum is over all leading positions where the same bias was reused. Do not average again if $G$ already contains the mean-loss factor. For example, with one row $x=[2,3]$ and scalar upstream derivative $4$, the weight derivative is $[8,12]$.

Cache the forward values needed by the derivative; compute all gradients before updating parameters. Updating $W$ midway would make the earlier-layer derivative use a different function from the one evaluated forward.

Check a scalar objective using central differences:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_j}\approx
\frac{L(\theta+h e_j)-L(\theta-h e_j)}{2h}.
$$

Use float64 and several sensible $h$ values. An arbitrarily tiny $h$ loses the difference to rounding, while a large one measures curvature rather than a local derivative. Avoid ReLU's kink at zero during this check, and test inputs, weights and biases separately.

title: ML Coding — BERT Span / Keyphrase Extraction
question:
ML Coding — BERT Span / Keyphrase Extraction

ML coding round in a notebook: extract the single most relevant span from a text (e.g. an IMDB review) by predicting start/end positions with BERT. Scaffolding is provided; you implement the model (init/forward), the loss, and the training pieces so the notebook trains to a reasonable accuracy. GPT-style models are explicitly disallowed.

Requirements

Given a passage (e.g. an IMDB movie review), output the key span — the start and end token positions of the most relevant fragment (not necessarily a full sentence). Implement a BERT-based extractor in a provided notebook:

Define the model: a BertModel encoder plus a linear head producing start and end logits over the sequence.
Implement forward (and a predict that turns logits into a span), and the loss (cross-entropy on start and end indices, averaged).
Fill in the training loop so the notebook runs end-to-end and trains to a reasonable metric (≈90%+ accuracy was expected in one case).
Follow-ups: how would you improve training, and how would you improve evaluation?
Examples
import torch
from torch import nn
from transformers import BertModel

class KeyphraseExtractor(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, bert_model_name='bert-base-uncased'):
super().__init__()
self.bert = BertModel.from_pretrained(bert_model_name)
self.linear = nn.Linear(self.bert.config.hidden_size, 2)  # start & end logits

def forward(self, input_ids, attention_mask):
outputs = self.bert(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask)
sequence_output = outputs.last_hidden_state        # (B, L, H)
logits = self.linear(sequence_output)              # (B, L, 2)
start_logits, end_logits = logits.split(1, dim=-1)
return start_logits.squeeze(-1), end_logits.squeeze(-1)

Training step: cross-entropy of start_logits vs start_idx and end_logits vs end_idx, averaged, then backward() / optimizer.step().

Notes
Despite Figma being an AI-forward team, the task is encoder-style span extraction (BERT), not generative GPT prompting — asking to use GPT is declined. Candidates who only prepped GPT-style work struggled; the key blocker was rusty BERT/fine-tuning fundamentals.
Conducted in a notebook with substantial boilerplate already written; you implement the model definition, loss, and the missing training pieces, and the whole notebook must actually run and train.
This is the recurring AI/ML-team coding screen, often paired the same day with a hiring-manager chat.

steps: Why is a next-token model trained with shifted targets? At position t, the model sees tokens through t and predicts token t+1. The target shift makes the training task match autoregressive generation.
Given tokens [x0,x1,x2,x3], use inputs [x0,x1,x2] and targets [x1,x2,x3], unless the library performs this shift internally.
Apply a causal mask to prevent access to later input positions. Use cross-entropy over vocabulary logits without an extra softmax first.
For instruction tuning, mask unwanted target positions after aligning the shift. Divide by the count of supervised targets, not padded sequence length.
Fit a baseline on messy tabular data without leakage. Build a trustworthy split and simple baseline before sophisticated feature engineering.
Define the target, prediction time and unit of independence, then split by time or group if required.
Fit imputation, scaling and category encodings on training folds only. Start with a dummy baseline and a regularized linear or small tree model.
Evaluate slices, missingness patterns and calibration; document features unavailable at decision time and remove them.
solution.contract_notes: For span/keyphrase extraction, tokenize with offset mappings, align annotated character spans to token labels, and mask special/padding tokens. Choose token BIO classification or start/end heads explicitly; train the matching loss and decode only valid spans. Score exact and overlap-based span F1 separately. A word-level label copied to every subword without a stated rule changes the task.
solution.example: If a prompt ends at input position 3 and the first answer is token 4, the prediction at position 3 is the first supervised answer target.
solution.trap: Shifting twice because both a data collator and the model's loss already shift labels, or supervising the wrong prompt boundary.

Treat a layer as a function with a declared input and output shape. Write the scalar loss and its reduction first: a sum, mean over rows and mean over all elements produce different gradient scales. For an affine layer $Y=XW+b$ with upstream gradient $G=\partial L/\partial Y$,

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial X}=GW^\top,\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=X^\top G,\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=\sum_i G_{i,:}.
$$

The bias sum is over all leading positions where the same bias was reused. Do not average again if $G$ already contains the mean-loss factor. For example, with one row $x=[2,3]$ and scalar upstream derivative $4$, the weight derivative is $[8,12]$.

Cache the forward values needed by the derivative; compute all gradients before updating parameters. Updating $W$ midway would make the earlier-layer derivative use a different function from the one evaluated forward.

Check a scalar objective using central differences:

$$

\frac{L(\theta+h e_j)-L(\theta-h e_j)}{2h}.
$$

title: Transformer Block with a Manual Backward Pass
question:
Implement one post-LayerNorm Transformer block: multi-head self-attention, a two-layer ReLU feed-forward network, two residual connections and two LayerNorms. Then write its backward pass by hand. It returns the gradient of the loss with respect to the input and to every parameter, without any automatic differentiation.

Setting

Matrices are plain Python lists of row lists, and one sequence is processed at a time (no batch axis). The editor provides helpers you may use unchanged: zeros, matmul, transpose, add, add_into, cols, set_cols, linear, linear_grad, softmax_rows and layernorm. A linear layer follows the nn.Linear convention y = x @ Wᵀ + b, so a map from D to F features is stored as an F x D matrix. layernorm(x, gamma, beta, eps) uses the biased variance (divide by D) and returns (y, xhat, inv_std).

Forward pass

For an input x of shape S x D, H heads of width hd = D / H:

Q, K, V = linear(x, W_Q), linear(x, W_K), linear(x, W_V)          S x D
for each head h (columns h*hd .. (h+1)*hd - 1 of Q, K, V):
P_h   = softmax_rows(Q_h K_hᵀ / sqrt(hd))                      S x S
ctx_h = P_h V_h                                                S x hd
ctx  = the heads' ctx_h concatenated column-wise                   S x D
attn = linear(ctx, W_O)
n1   = LayerNorm1(x + attn)
y    = LayerNorm2(n1 + linear(relu(linear(n1, ffn1_w, ffn1_b)), ffn2_w, ffn2_b))
Requirements
1.
softmax_rows_grad(P, g): given P = softmax_rows(z) and the upstream gradient g = dL/dP (both S x S), return dL/dz.
2.
layernorm_grad(g, xhat, inv, gamma): given the upstream gradient g = dL/dy and the xhat, inv_std returned by layernorm, return the tuple (dL/dx, dL/dgamma, dL/dbeta). The parameter gradients are summed over the rows.
3.
ManualTransformerBlock(embed_dim, num_heads, ff_hidden_dim, params, eps=1e-5), where params is a dict with keys W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O (D x D), ffn1_w (F x D), ffn1_b (length F), ffn2_w (D x F), ffn2_b (length D), and norm1_gamma, norm1_beta, norm2_gamma, norm2_beta (length D):
forward(x) returns y (S x D) and caches whatever the backward pass needs.
backward(grad_output) takes dL/dy (S x D) for the most recent forward call and returns (dL/dx, grads), where grads has exactly the keys of params and each gradient has the shape of its parameter.
4.
backward must not call anything that differentiates for you; every gradient is derived by hand from the forward formulas.
Input
x: a list of S rows, each a list of D floats.
params: the weights described above; D is divisible by H.
grad_output: a list of S rows of D floats.
Output
forward: the block output, S x D.
backward: (dL/dx, grads) as described in requirement 3.
Examples

Example 1: the softmax backward on one row.

softmax_rows_grad([[0.5, 0.5]], [[1.0, 0.0]])  ->  [[0.25, -0.25]]

Here P = softmax_rows([[0.0, 0.0]]) = [[0.5, 0.5]] and rowsum(g ⊙ P) = 0.5, so the entries are 0.5 · (1 − 0.5) = 0.25 and 0.5 · (0 − 0.5) = −0.25.

Example 2: a constant upstream gradient.

softmax_rows_grad([[0.5, 0.5]], [[1.0, 1.0]])  ->  [[0.0, 0.0]]

A constant upstream gradient yields zero, because every row of P sums to 1.

Example 3: one forward pass. Take D = 2, H = 1, F = 2, every weight matrix the 2×2 identity, every bias and beta zero, every gamma one, and x = [[1.0, 3.0]].

forward([[1.0, 3.0]])  ->  [[-0.9999978, 0.9999978]]   (rounded to 7 places)

With one token, P = [[1.0]], so attn = x and x + attn = [[2, 6]]. LayerNorm of a 2-vector [a, b] with a < b gives about [-1, 1], so n1 ≈ [[-1, 1]]. The ReLU keeps [0, 1], the second residual gives about [[-1, 2]], and the second LayerNorm maps that back to about [-1, 1]. The values sit just inside ±1 because of eps.

Constraints
1 <= S <= 16, 1 <= H <= D <= 64, 1 <= F <= 128.
Every returned gradient must agree with a central finite difference of the loss to within 1e-6.
Discussion
1.
Why is the attention score divided by sqrt(hd)?
2.
What happens to the gradients when the attention weights saturate and one key position dominates a row?
3.
How would you verify a manual backward pass against an automatic-differentiation framework?
4.
How would you extend the block to masked or causal attention?
5.
What would you optimise first for GPU performance?

steps: Derive a manual attention backward pass. Backpropagate through value mixing, rowwise softmax and the scaled score product.
For O=P@V and upstream G, compute dV=Pᵀ@G and dP=G@Vᵀ.
For each softmax row, dS=P*(dP-sum(dP*P)); zero forbidden-score gradients.
For S=QKᵀ/sqrt(d), use dQ=dS@K/sqrt(d) and dK=dSᵀ@Q/sqrt(d), then chain through projections.
Implement LayerNorm forward and backward. Each row is centered and rescaled independently across its features; the backward pass must include the effects of both statistics.
Compute mean, centered values, population variance and inv_std=1/sqrt(var+eps). Set xhat=centered*inv_std and out=gamma*xhat+beta.
For g=dout*gamma, use dx=inv_std*(g-mean(g)-xhat*mean(g*xhat)), with means over features.
Sum dout*xhat and dout over the batch for dgamma and dbeta. Verify with central finite differences in float64.
Derive a dense layer's input, weight and bias gradients. Each parameter receives the sum of contributions from every example that used it.
For Y=XW+b with X:(N,D), W:(D,C), let upstream G:(N,C).
Compute dX=G@Wᵀ, dW=Xᵀ@G and db=sum(G,axis=0).
Do not average again unless the scalar objective's reduction requires it; G may already include the mean factor.
solution.contract_notes: Complete the block by chaining residual addition, normalization and FFN derivatives in reverse forward order. At every residual join, add the direct upstream gradient to the sublayer gradient. Validate every projection, bias, normalization scale and input gradient independently; attention-only gradients are not a full Transformer-block backward pass.
solution.example: Every row of dS sums approximately to zero because softmax is invariant to adding a row constant.
solution.trap: Materializing an enormous softmax Jacobian or forgetting the scale in both Q and K gradients.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Derive the normalization and its gradient

For row $x_i\in\mathbb R^D$, compute population statistics across **features**, independently of the other rows:

$$
\mu_i=\frac1D\sum_jx_{ij},\quad
v_i=\frac1D\sum_j(x_{ij}-\mu_i)^2,\quad
s_i=(v_i+\epsilon)^{-1/2},\quad
\hat x_{ij}=(x_{ij}-\mu_i)s_i.
$$

Then $y_{ij}=\gamma_j\hat x_{ij}+\beta_j$. The epsilon goes inside the square root. Compute variance from centered deviations, not $E[x^2]-E[x]^2$: the latter subtracts two huge nearly equal numbers when inputs share a large offset.

Let $G_{ij}=\partial L/\partial y_{ij}$ and $U_{ij}=G_{ij}\gamma_j$. The chain rule has three paths: a direct input path, the row mean path and the row variance path. Combining them gives

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_{ij}}=
 s_i\left(U_{ij}-\overline U_i-
 \hat x_{ij}\,\overline{U_i\hat x_i}\right),
$$

where each overline averages across the $D$ features of that row. The parameter gradients sum over rows:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\gamma_j}=\sum_iG_{ij}\hat x_{ij},\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\beta_j}=\sum_iG_{ij}.
$$

For $[1,2,3,4]$, the mean is $2.5$ and variance $1.25$. With unit scale and zero bias, the result is approximately $[-1.3416,-0.4472,0.4472,1.3416]$. A constant row normalizes to zero, so its output equals the bias. Its input derivative is not universally zero: it depends on the upstream pattern and epsilon.

The forward cache stores normalized inputs, inverse standard deviations and scale. Do not mutate these before backward. Validate $x$, $\gamma$ and $\beta$ derivatives independently with float64 central differences; checking only output shape cannot catch omitted statistic paths. Both passes cost $O(ND)$.

title: CI/CD Job Scheduler Design using Kubernetes and Docker
question:
Design a CI/CD job scheduler: a multi-tenant service that runs build, test and deploy pipelines described in YAML, each stage in its own container on Kubernetes. Users push code, the service starts the pipeline, streams logs to a dashboard, passes build outputs from one stage to the next, and recovers when a stage or a scheduler node fails.

Requirements
1.
Functional: accept declarative pipeline definitions (YAML); run each stage in an isolated container; schedule, queue and limit concurrency; pass artifacts between stages; stream and store logs; report status per pipeline run, stage and attempt.
2.
Retry policy: a failed stage is retried on its own (completed stages are not rerun), at most 3 attempts per stage with exponential backoff; the run fails when a stage exhausts its attempts, and later stages are skipped.
3.
Multi-tenancy: tenants must not read each other's code, secrets, logs or artifacts, and one tenant must not starve the others.
4.
Scale to design for: 50,000 pipeline runs per day with a peak of 2,000 concurrent stage executions, about 500 tenants, 5 stages per run on average, and 10 MB of logs and 200 MB of artifacts per run.
5.
Targets: a stage starts within 30 seconds of becoming runnable when capacity exists (10 seconds with a warm image); logs appear in the dashboard within 5 seconds; logs are kept 30 days and artifacts 14 days; the scheduler survives the loss of any single node without losing or double-running a stage.
Example

A code push triggers this pipeline:

YAML
pipeline:
stages:
- name: build
image: node:18
script:
- npm install
- npm run build
- name: test
image: node:18
script:
- npm test
- name: deploy
image: gcr.io/deploy-tool:latest
script:
- deploy-to-prod

Stages run in the listed order unless a stage has an optional needs: list naming the stages it waits for (for example needs: [build] on both a lint and a test stage lets them run in parallel after build). Here no stage has needs:, so each waits for the one before it.

Expected behavior: the scheduler starts a pod for build; when it succeeds, its output is stored as an artifact and the test pod starts and receives that artifact; when test succeeds, the deploy pod starts. Logs of every pod stream to the dashboard. If test fails, only test is retried (up to 3 attempts, with backoff); if all attempts fail, the run is marked failed and deploy never starts.

What to cover
1.
Scale estimates: runs per second, concurrent pods, log and artifact storage per day.
2.
API: submit a pipeline, get run status, stream logs, cancel a run.
3.
Data model: pipeline, run, stage, attempt, and the states of each.
4.
Scheduler design: the state machine of a stage, how runnable stages are found, and how needs: dependencies (stages that may run in parallel) are handled.
5.
Deep dive A: the job queue and fair scheduling across tenants (quotas, priorities, preventing starvation).
6.
Deep dive B: failure recovery of the scheduler itself (leader election, persisted state, idempotent pod creation, orphaned pods).
7.
Deep dive C: artifact passing between stages and log collection.
8.
Security, autoscaling, and trade-offs.

steps: Represent CPU, GPU memory/count, topology, image, deadline and checkpoint needs as explicit resource requests. Keep the DAG or workflow definition separate from execution attempts.
Admit only jobs with feasible complete allocations. Use quotas plus a fair priority queue; gang-schedule coupled GPU workers so partial allocations cannot deadlock the job.
Agents launch isolated workloads, report heartbeats and release resources on completion. A controller reconciles desired and observed state rather than trusting one RPC response.
Checkpoint before supported preemption, retry with fenced ownership and audit resource usage. Report utilization together with wait-time percentiles; do not starve large jobs to inflate utilization.
solution.example: A two-stage CPU preprocessing job can feed a four-GPU training job only after its output is committed; scheduling four unrelated single-GPU fragments is insufficient when the training topology requires one fast interconnect group.
solution.trap: Treating a Kubernetes pod state or process launch as proof that the application completed its work.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Follow tensor ownership and the resource bottleneck

For every major tensor, state who owns it before and after each collective. Data parallelism divides examples; tensor parallelism divides operations/weights; pipeline parallelism divides layers. Their communication and memory effects differ, so a diagram saying “use more GPUs” is incomplete.

For $C=AB$, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times k}$ and $B\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}$, a row partition gives

$$
C_r=A_rB,\qquad C=\operatorname{ConcatRows}(C_0,\ldots,C_{p-1}).
$$

Concatenating output shards is different from summing partial products. Backward communication depends on which variables were replicated and where multiple contributions to the same derivative must be added.

Estimate the bottleneck with a roofline bound:

$$
\text{attainable FLOP/s}\leq
\min\!\left(F_{\rm peak},\;\text{bandwidth}\times\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}}\right).
$$

Then add synchronization, imbalance, launch and checkpoint overhead rather than treating the ideal bound as achieved speed.

For a platform/scheduler, distinguish desired state, observed state and durable job completion. Launching a container or receiving a provider response does not prove the computation succeeded. Checkpoint application state, fence stale owners, publish only complete artifacts and monitor both utilization and tenant wait time. A design that maximizes utilization by starving a large job violates a different important service objective.

title: Cloud IDE
question:
Problem Description
Design a Cloud IDE

Design a cloud-based IDE where users can write code, manage files, and run terminal commands entirely in the browser. The core challenges are VM lifecycle management, real-time terminal output streaming, and strong per-user isolation at scale.

Functional Requirements
1.
Users can create, read, update, and delete files and directories.
2.
Users can run commands and receive stdout and stderr interactively.
3.
Users can send terminal input, resize the terminal, and stop running processes.
4.
Users can install packages during an active session.
5.
Users can share a workspace using owner, viewer, and editor permissions.
6.
Source files and workspace metadata survive sandbox termination.
7.
Real-time collaborative text editing is out of scope.
Non-Functional Requirements
Requirement	Target
Concurrent users	100,000
Sandbox allocation	2 vCPU and 4 GB RAM
Startup latency	Under 5 seconds
Terminal-output latency	Under 100 ms
Availability	99.9%
Maximum interactive session	12 hours
Security	Strong tenant isolation

Use these numbers for capacity estimates.

Clarifying Questions

Ask these questions before drawing the architecture:

1.
Should source files survive sandbox termination?
2.
Should installed packages survive between sessions?
3.
Are users allowed to access the public internet from a sandbox?
4.
Do we need containers, microVMs, dedicated VMs, or dedicated hosts?
5.
Are long-running background jobs in scope?
6.
What terminal replay behavior is expected after reconnecting?
7.
Is workspace sharing read-only, editable, or collaborative in real time?
Follow-up: SSH access to development hosts

Change the access path: users connect to a provisioned development host over SSH instead of using the browser, and a task scheduler runs background tasks across the host fleet. What changes in allocation, access control and scheduling, and what stays the same?

steps: Separate the control plane (users, projects, permissions, quotas and desired jobs/environments) from isolated execution agents. Expose stable provider adapters instead of embedding one vendor’s API throughout the service.

For experiments, store immutable configurations, code/data/model versions, runs, metrics and artifacts; instrument repeatable reset/seed behavior for simulators or embodied tasks.
Collect logs and heartbeats, reap abandoned resources safely and account for cost. Define session recovery and artifact durability independently from VM/container lifetime.
solution.example: Stopping a notebook VM must not delete its only copy of a completed experiment artifact. A provider API timeout leaves provisioning status to reconcile, not proof that no VM was created.
solution.trap: Running untrusted user code in the web server process or assuming an ephemeral VM disk is durable experiment storage.

title: Compute Resource Scheduling for ML Jobs
question:
Design a scheduler that allocates CPU / GPU resources across multiple clusters for user-submitted ML jobs while keeping utilization high.

Requirements:

Users submit ML jobs with CPU, GPU, memory, runtime, image, and priority requirements.
Multiple clusters, each with different CPU/GPU inventory.
Start jobs when resources are available; keep utilization high.
Track job status: queued, running, succeeded, failed, canceled.
Handle retries, preemption, quota, and noisy-neighbor isolation.
Provide APIs for submission, status, cancellation, and logs.

title: Design a Hosted ML Notebook Platform
question:
Design a cloud platform where data scientists create isolated workspaces, edit notebooks, execute code interactively, persist files, suspend idle compute, and resume later. Workspaces may use CPU or GPU kernels and versioned custom environments.

Workload assumptions
500,000 users may be connected concurrently through the web application.
Up to 50,000 workspaces execute code concurrently; the remainder are editing, viewing output, or idle.
A typical active runtime requests 2 vCPU and 8 GB RAM. Up to 5% of active runtimes request one GPU.
Typical suspended workspaces must become interactive within 5 seconds at p95. Large custom images and very large dependency environments may use a separately reported cold-resume service level.
Notebook files and committed artifacts must survive suspend, runtime loss, and regional service restarts.
Requirements
1.
Support idempotent create, delete, suspend, and resume operations with visible lifecycle status.
2.
Stream execution requests, output, errors, interrupts, and heartbeats over reconnectable bidirectional sessions.
3.
Isolate untrusted code, enforce CPU, memory, GPU, network, storage, and time quotas, and prevent access to host or cloud metadata credentials.
4.
Persist notebooks separately from disposable compute. Define which in-memory kernel state, if any, survives suspension.
5.
Support standard kernels, signed custom images, dependency metadata, and GPU-backed environments.
6.
Minimize idle cost while meeting the normal p95 resume target. Cover warm pools, image distribution, storage mounts, snapshots, admission control, and capacity reservations.
7.
Handle duplicate commands, runtime and node failure, control-plane retry, orphan cleanup, storage outage, capacity exhaustion, and regional disaster recovery.
8.
Provide audit logs, tenant quotas, abuse detection, observability, and cost attribution.
Scenarios
A resume request is retried after the client times out. Exactly one runtime becomes active, and both requests return the same operation state.
A runtime node dies during cell execution. Durable files remain intact, the user sees the execution failure, and the workspace can start on another node.
A popular 12 GB custom image is requested by thousands of users at the start of a class. Explain how the system avoids a registry and network stampede.
Follow-ups
1.
Add collaborative editing while keeping kernel execution ordered and access-controlled.
2.
Add enterprise workspaces attached to customer networks with stronger tenant isolation.
3.
Describe a multi-region layout and estimate capacity and major cost drivers.
Deliverable

Present estimates, APIs, metadata and state models, architecture, lifecycle flows, the fast-resume path, scheduling and isolation choices, failure recovery, security, observability, and trade-offs.

title: Design a Lab-Wide Experiment Platform for Embodied AI
question:
Design a lab-wide experiment management platform for an embodied AI (robotics) team. Researchers improve robot policies by running experiments that combine real robot logs, simulation scenarios, model training, evaluation jobs and comparison with earlier baseline policies. The platform must make each experiment trackable, comparable and reproducible.

A concrete motivating case: a manipulation policy often fails to pick up transparent objects, especially in poor lighting. A researcher wants to turn that observed failure into a measured improvement.

What the platform must support
1.
Select the relevant real-world failure logs.
2.
Generate targeted simulation scenarios around the failure.
3.
Train or fine-tune candidate policies from a baseline checkpoint.
4.
Run evaluation jobs on both a targeted suite and a broad regression suite.
5.
Compare candidate policies against the baseline policy.
6.
Track all artifacts, configs, metrics, logs and failures.
7.
Reproduce any experiment later from a single run ID.

1.
Core objects and APIs. The central object of the system, what is stored for each experiment run, and how configs, data versions, model versions and evaluation suites are represented.
2.

3.
Evaluation system. How evaluation jobs run, how the environment, the model server and the scoring (judging) logic interact, and which metrics you compute for the transparent-object case.
4.
Reproducibility. What another researcher does with a run ID to reproduce the experiment, and which versions and artifacts must be pinned.
5.
Failure handling. Common failures in training and evaluation jobs, and how the platform detects, reports, retries and recovers from them.
6.
Scale and extensibility. How the platform serves many researchers, experiments and policies, and how new robot tasks, simulators, evaluation suites or metrics are added later.

A high-level design answer: components and their responsibilities, the data model, the workflow and the evaluation infrastructure, with the key trade-offs. No production code is required.

title: Design a Multistage CPU and GPU Job Scheduler
question:
Description

Design a durable job scheduling system for workflows made of multiple dependent stages. Each stage declares CPU, memory, and optional GPU needs; the scheduler must place CPU-heavy stages on a CPU cluster and GPU-heavy stages on a GPU cluster. Use a database to preserve workflow state and a queue to make runnable work available without losing dependency or retry information.

What to implement

Present the APIs, data model, components, scheduling loop, and state transitions for the system.

POST /v1/jobs: accept a client-generated idempotency key and a directed acyclic graph of stages. Each stage includes an identifier, dependency identifiers, a resource request, and a retry-safe execution payload.
GET /v1/jobs/{job_id}: return the job state and the state, attempt count, and output reference of every stage.
POST /v1/jobs/{job_id}:cancel: prevent undispatched stages from starting and request cancellation of running stages.
Input

A job contains at most 20 stages. The dependency graph must be acyclic. A stage requests 1–32 CPU cores, 1–256 GiB of memory, and either 0 GPUs for CPU work or 1–8 GPUs for GPU work. Stage payloads and results live in object storage; API and queue messages carry references rather than large blobs.

Output

The submission API returns a stable job_id. Status reads expose one terminal job state—SUCCEEDED, FAILED, or CANCELED—only after all relevant stage transitions have been durably recorded. The design response should include capacity estimates, API behavior, database records and indexes, queue message fields, CPU/GPU routing, dependency release, retries, cancellation, reconciliation, and observability.

Rules
1.
A stage becomes READY only after every dependency is SUCCEEDED. Independent ready stages may execute concurrently; no ordering is required beyond dependency edges.
2.
The database is the source of truth for job, stage, dependency, attempt, and lease state. Queue delivery is at least once, so workers and completion handling must be idempotent.
3.
Plan for 50,000 submitted jobs per day, an average of 8 stages per job, bursts of 200 job submissions per second, and up to 200,000 active jobs. Of all stages, 20% require GPUs.
4.
Target p95 submission latency below 200 ms, p95 dispatch of a resource-feasible READY stage below 5 seconds, and 99.9% monthly control-plane availability.
5.
Workers heartbeat every 30 seconds and hold renewable 2-minute leases. With a lease granted at t = 0, renewals are scheduled at t = 30, 60, and 90 seconds; a renewal at the t = 120 expiry boundary is too late. A stage receives at most 3 total attempts.
6.
After a stage exhausts its third attempt, the job enters nonterminal FAILING. The system must fence and request cancellation of every other live attempt, durably mark all remaining nonterminal stages so they cannot run, and expose FAILED only after every stage transition and lease revocation is durable. Completion is accepted only while the job is active, so work from a FAILING or terminal job cannot release dependencies or overwrite state.
7.
Duplicate submissions with the same client idempotency key return the same job. Duplicate queue deliveries, late completions, and completion after cancellation must not corrupt terminal state or release a dependent stage twice.
8.
A CPU- or GPU-cluster outage must not lose accepted work. Work for the healthy cluster should continue, while resource-feasible work for the unavailable cluster remains pending and is dispatched after recovery.
Examples
Example 1: Mixed preprocessing and training

decode(CPU) -> {augment(CPU), train(GPU)} -> evaluate(CPU)

After decode succeeds, augment is offered to the CPU cluster and train to the GPU cluster concurrently. evaluate remains blocked until both predecessors succeed, illustrating dependency ordering without imposing a total job order.

Example 2: Worker loss and duplicate delivery

A GPU worker starts train attempt 1, stops heartbeating, and its lease expires. The scheduler makes attempt 2 eligible; later, the queue redelivers the attempt-1 message and the original worker reports success.

The stale delivery and late completion must be rejected using the recorded attempt and lease token. Only the current attempt may commit a terminal transition, so downstream stages are released at most once.

Constraints
The design must use a queue and a transactional database, and must route work to distinct CPU and GPU execution clusters.
Scheduler and API instances may fail and restart at any point.
Queue delivery can be duplicated, delayed, or reordered.
GPU capacity is scarcer than CPU capacity; avoid head-of-line blocking between resource classes.
Prefer standard managed primitives, but explain consistency boundaries and recovery rather than relying on product names.
Follow-up 1: Survive a resource-cluster outage

Explain state transitions, backpressure, alerts, and recovery when the GPU cluster is unavailable for 30 minutes while CPU work continues.

Follow-up 2: Add fair scheduling

Extend the design so a single tenant with a large backlog cannot monopolize GPU capacity, while retaining the dispatch-latency target for other tenants.

title: GPU Cloud VM Manager - Provider-Agnostic CLI and Fleet Manager
question:
Problem: GPU Cloud VM Manager

Build a provider-agnostic command-line tool, vm, that manages GPU virtual machines across three cloud providers whose APIs differ in protocol, scoping and synchronicity, and then grow it into a small fleet manager.

Providers

You are given a repository with three mock servers, one per provider:

Provider	Protocol	Scoping	Operations	Reservations
Crusoe Cloud	REST	project-scoped	asynchronous; supports reboot / reset / restart	reservations
Lambda Cloud	REST, flat and simple	none	synchronous	reserved instances
Nebius AI Cloud	gRPC	parent-scoped	asynchronous	reservation policies
Layer 1: Unified CLI (about 30–40 minutes)

Implement these commands so that the caller never sees a provider-specific difference:

# 1. List all instances across all providers, or filter by provider
vm list [--provider <provider>]

# 2. Create a new instance
vm create --provider <provider> --gpu <gpu_type> --count <count> [--name <name>] [--region <region>]

# 3. Get instance details
vm get --provider <provider> <instance_id>

# 4. Stop an instance
vm stop --provider <provider> <instance_id>

Requirements:

1.
One provider-neutral instance model (id, provider, name, GPU type, count, region, state) and one normalized state set, whatever each provider returns.
2.
Asynchronous providers must look synchronous to the CLI: create and stop return once the operation has finished or a timeout is reached.
3.
vm list without --provider aggregates all providers; a failing provider is reported, not fatal.
4.
Invalid arguments and provider errors produce clear messages (for example not found, quota exceeded, provider unavailable).
Later layers: Fleet manager
5.
Reservations — one reserve / release interface that maps onto each provider's reservation model.
6.
Fleet operations — aggregate GPU usage per provider and GPU type, create N instances within each provider's capacity, and reconcile the running fleet against a desired specification.
Deliverable

Working code against the mock servers for Layer 1, a design that extends to the later layers without changing the CLI, and a short explanation of the trade-offs you made (for example, a synchronous facade over asynchronous APIs, partial results versus failing fast).

title: HPC Host Control Plane and Job Coordination
question:
HPC Host Control Plane and Job Coordination

Design a central service that tracks many hosts, knows their current state, and coordinates job assignment. The prompt explicitly focuses on communication between hosts and the central service, database choice and schema, high-concurrency handling, and a roughly 1,000-host scale target; detailed job-scheduling policy is out of scope.

Requirements

Design a central control-plane service for an HPC software environment.

Functional requirements:

Maintain current state for many hosts under the central service.
Let hosts communicate health, availability, and resource state to the central service.
Support job assignment coordination, while leaving detailed scheduling algorithms mostly out of scope.
Store host and job-related state in a database with a clear schema.
Handle high concurrency when many hosts update state at once.

Scale / constraints:

Reason about approximately 1,000 hosts.
Host state should refresh frequently enough for job assignment decisions.
The central service should avoid becoming a single point of failure.
Notes

The expected discussion is a narrow control-plane design, not a broad cloud platform.

Heartbeats are a natural host-to-service communication model; clarify heartbeat interval, timeout, retry behavior, and stale-host handling.
In-memory stores such as Redis can make fast host-state updates easy, but the answer still needs persistence / recovery and clear ownership of authoritative state.
Atomic updates matter under concurrency. Lua scripts or transactions can be used to update related host fields consistently in Redis-style designs.
The schema should distinguish host identity, resource capacity, current allocation, health state, last heartbeat, and job assignment state.
High availability needs leader election or active / standby service instances, plus a plan for failover without double-assigning work.

For experiments, store immutable configurations, code/data/model versions, runs, metrics and artifacts; instrument repeatable reset/seed behavior for simulators or embodied tasks.
Collect logs and heartbeats, reap abandoned resources safely and account for cost. Define session recovery and artifact durability independently from VM/container lifetime.
solution.example: Stopping a notebook VM must not delete its only copy of a completed experiment artifact. A provider API timeout leaves provisioning status to reconcile, not proof that no VM was created.
solution.trap: Running untrusted user code in the web server process or assuming an ephemeral VM disk is durable experiment storage.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Follow tensor ownership and the resource bottleneck

For every major tensor, state who owns it before and after each collective. Data parallelism divides examples; tensor parallelism divides operations/weights; pipeline parallelism divides layers. Their communication and memory effects differ, so a diagram saying “use more GPUs” is incomplete.

For $C=AB$, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times k}$ and $B\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}$, a row partition gives

$$
C_r=A_rB,\qquad C=\operatorname{ConcatRows}(C_0,\ldots,C_{p-1}).
$$

Concatenating output shards is different from summing partial products. Backward communication depends on which variables were replicated and where multiple contributions to the same derivative must be added.

Estimate the bottleneck with a roofline bound:

$$
\text{attainable FLOP/s}\leq
\min\!\left(F_{\rm peak},\;\text{bandwidth}\times\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}}\right).
$$

Then add synchronization, imbalance, launch and checkpoint overhead rather than treating the ideal bound as achieved speed.

For a platform/scheduler, distinguish desired state, observed state and durable job completion. Launching a container or receiving a provider response does not prove the computation succeeded. Checkpoint application state, fence stale owners, publish only complete artifacts and monitor both utilization and tenant wait time. A design that maximizes utilization by starving a large job violates a different important service objective.

title: Sample from a Gaussian Distribution Using Only Uniform Sampling
question:
Some simulators and embedded systems only offer a uniform random number generator that returns floats in [0, 1). Many models still need noise from a standard normal distribution, with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Build a sampler that turns uniform draws into one standard normal sample, without any library sampler.

What to implement
uniform() -> float: provided. It returns a float drawn uniformly from [0, 1). It can return exactly 0.0.
sample_gaussian() -> float: return one sample from the standard normal distribution, built only from calls to uniform().
Rules
1.
Use the Box-Muller transform and return its cosine output.
2.
Each call to sample_gaussian() calls uniform() exactly twice. The first value is u1 and the second is u2.
3.
u1 sets the radius and u2 sets the angle.
4.
Use 1 - u1 wherever the transform takes the logarithm of u1. Since 1 - u1 lies in (0, 1], a draw of 0.0 never causes a math domain error.
5.
Do not use numpy.random, random.gauss, random.normalvariate or any other ready-made normal sampler. Only math and uniform() are allowed.
6.
Return a plain Python float. Do not cache the unused sine output between calls.
Examples

Each example fixes the two values that uniform() returns, in order.

Example 1: draws 0.5, 0.0. Output: 1.1774100225154747.

Explanation: 1 - u1 = 0.5 gives radius sqrt(2 ln 2) ≈ 1.17741, and the angle is 0, so the cosine is 1.

Example 2: draws 0.5, 0.5. Output: -1.1774100225154747.

Explanation: the radius is the same as in Example 1, and the angle is half a turn, so the cosine is -1.

Example 3: draws 0.0, 0.3. Output: 0.0.

Explanation: 1 - u1 = 1 and ln 1 = 0, so the radius is 0. The draw of 0.0 is safe because of rule 4.

Example 4: draws 0.75, 0.0. Output: 1.6651092223153954.

Explanation: 1 - u1 = 0.25 gives radius sqrt(2 ln 4) ≈ 1.66511, and the cosine of angle 0 is 1. Taking the logarithm of u1 itself would give 0.75853 instead.

Constraints
Results are compared with a tolerance of 1e-9.
Over many calls with a real uniform(), the samples must have mean close to 0, variance close to 1, and about 68.3% of them inside (-1, 1).
One call must run in O(1) time and space.

steps: Generate Gaussian noise using only uniform random numbers. The Box–Muller transformation converts two independent uniforms into two independent standard Gaussian draws.
Draw U1 in (0,1) and U2 in [0,1), avoiding log(0).
Set R=sqrt(-2*log(U1)) and theta=2*pi*U2; return R*cos(theta) and R*sin(theta).
For mean mu and standard deviation sigma, transform each z to mu+sigma*z. Test sample moments and distribution shape rather than exact draws.
solution.example: With U1=exp(-0.5) and U2=0, the pair is (1,0).
solution.trap: Using the same uniform twice or treating good sample moments alone as proof of independence.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Name the random experiment and condition on the right event

Write the sample space and independence assumptions before counting. Bayes' rule reverses conditioning:

$$
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)},\qquad P(B)>0.
$$

A $90\%$ detection rate is not a $90\%$ probability that an alert is genuine. Prevalence and false-positive rate determine the latter. Work expected counts in a hypothetical population when the formula feels abstract.

For waiting-time and random-walk exercises, first-step analysis often gives a solvable recurrence:

$$
h(s)=1+\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s)h(s'),\qquad h(s)=0\text{ at absorbing states}.
$$

Specify what counts as one step: two particles moving once each may cost two coin flips but only one elapsed second. At a forced horizon, all surviving probability mass must be assigned to the final stopping time.

For expected counts, indicator variables and linearity do not require independent indicators. For uncertainty or variance, dependence does matter. Check normalization, limiting cases and a small enumeration. Simulation is useful validation but not a replacement for a requested exact derivation; conversely, a neat-looking fraction should not be asserted merely because a numerical estimate is close to it.

title: Statistics Derivations: Correlation, Order Statistics, Regression Bias, Random Graphs
question:
Work through the following four derivations in probability and statistics. For each, state your assumptions, write the distributions, constraints and formulas first, and give an exact closed form (not a simulation or approximation).

Requirements
1.
Correlation feasibility. Three random variables x, y, z have all pairwise correlations equal to p. Find the range of p for which such variables exist, using the positive semi-definite condition on the correlation matrix (eigenvalues, determinant, or the cosine-of-angle picture). Then extend the result to n variables with a common pairwise correlation.
2.
Order statistics. For n i.i.d. Uniform(0, 1) variables, compute the covariance of the maximum and the minimum, using Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] and their joint density.
3.
Omitted-variable bias. In the model y = b1*x1 + b2*x2 + e, x2 is left out of the regression. Derive the limit of the estimated coefficient on x1, say when the bias is nonzero and what sign it has, and prove the result in matrix form.
4.
Random graph. In a complete graph on n vertices with i.i.d. continuous random edge weights, a pair (a, b) is *good* if each endpoint is the other's maximum-weight neighbor. Compute the expected number of good pairs.
Notes
Indicator variables and linearity of expectation are the natural tools for any "expected number of" question.
Check each closed form on a small case (for example n = 2 or n = 3).

steps: Equicorrelation: R=(1-p)I+p*11ᵀ has eigenvalues 1-p (multiplicity n-1) and 1+(n-1)p. Positive semidefiniteness gives -1/(n-1)<=p<=1; for three variables the range is [-1/2,1].

For min U and max V of n iid uniforms, the joint density is n(n-1)(v-u)^(n-2) on 0<u<v<1. Integration gives E[U]=1/(n+1), E[V]=n/(n+1), E[UV]=1/(n+2), hence Cov(U,V)=1/((n+1)²*(n+2)); handle n=1 directly as Var(U)=1/12.

Omitted-variable bias with intercept/centering and E[x1*e]=0 is b2*Cov(x1,x2)/Var(x1). In matrix form beta_hat1=beta1+(X1ᵀX1)^-1 X1ᵀX2 beta2+(X1ᵀX1)^-1 X1ᵀe; take probability limits under valid moment/rank assumptions.

A pair is mutually maximum exactly when its shared edge is the largest among the 2n-3 edges incident to either endpoint. IID continuous weights make each edge equally likely: probability 1/(2n-3), and expected good pairs n(n-1)/(2*(2n-3)).
solution.example: At n=2 the order-statistics covariance is 1/36 and the graph has exactly one good pair in expectation, matching the formulas.
solution.trap: Assuming the two endpoint-max events are independent; they share an edge and overlapping comparisons.

title: Content Moderation System Design
question:
Design a content-moderation system for a high-volume short-video / live / e-commerce platform.

Requirements
Functional: ingest UGC (video, image, text); pre-publish moderation; flag violations into a human review queue; expose the outcome to publishing.
ML infra: per-modality model serving (vision, ASR transcript, OCR, text classifier); feature pipeline; offline retraining loop.
Scale: 100M+ uploads/day; sub-second decision SLA for short videos; full re-scan within minutes.
Reliability: at-least-once delivery; replay past content on rule changes; audit log.
Follow-up: a job scheduler for high-frequency re-moderation (priority queue + worker pool + at-least-once).
Notes

Three planes: ingestion / decision / review. Hourglass model serving — cheap rule filters -> vision/ASR/OCR -> expensive multimodal LLM for ambiguous cases only. Idempotent processing keyed on content_id + rule_version.

steps: Design multi-modal harmful-content detection. Use a calibrated triage system that combines automated decisions with human review capacity.
Define harm categories, policy versions and separate precision/recall targets per action and category.
Run cheap per-modality filters, then stronger joint models on uncertain cases; reserve pre-publication and asynchronous paths with separate latency budgets.
Prioritize a bounded review queue, audit decisions and retrain from reviewed labels with sampling-bias checks.
solution.example: A high-confidence severe violation can be blocked, while ambiguous content may receive limited distribution and human review under the specified policy.
solution.trap: Optimizing one aggregate accuracy metric while hiding catastrophic errors on a rare category.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Design the decision, not only the predictor

State which user action follows the model output, when the prediction occurs and which errors are costly. Then define labels and features using information available at that time. A feature recorded after the outcome is not made legitimate by being stored in the same table.

For a retrieval/ranking product, use a cascade: generate a broad eligible set, score a bounded candidate set, then apply policy and presentation rules. Evaluate retrieval recall separately because a ranker cannot rescue an item excluded upstream. Availability, permissions and budgets are hard constraints, not merely features a model may learn to respect.

Expected action utility can be written as

$$
a^*(x)=\arg\max_a\sum_y P(y\mid x)\,U(a,y).
$$

This makes clear why a probability metric and a product objective are different. The same calibrated probability may produce different actions when error costs change.

Describe a baseline, time/entity-aware validation, exposure logging and one controlled rollout. For a recommender, unexposed items are not automatically observed negatives. For moderation or fraud, mature labels and human-review capacity matter. Finish with a failure walkthrough: what happens when features are stale, the model is unavailable or the distribution changes? A simpler fallback with explicit monitoring is often more defensible than an elaborate system without an operational plan.

title: Design a Game Recommendation System
question:
Design the recommendation system of a large online game platform, with millions of users and hundreds of thousands of user-created games. For each user the system returns a ranked list of games they are likely to enjoy and keep playing. The design should cover the whole pipeline end to end, with breadth across the parts rather than depth on one component.

What to cover
1.
Problem framing: the objective the system optimizes (engagement, retention, monetization), the metric that stands for long-term value, and how new users and new games (cold start) are handled.
2.
Data and features: user, game and context signals, including social signals, and how they are computed offline and online.
3.
Candidate generation: how the catalog is narrowed from the full set of games to a few hundred candidates per request.
4.
Ranking: the model that scores the candidates, its inputs and outputs, and the re-ranking rules for diversity and freshness.
5.
Evaluation: offline metrics for retrieval and ranking, and why they are not enough.
6.
Online experimentation: how the system is A/B tested, and the pitfalls to guard against (feedback loops, popularity bias, label bias, non-stationarity).
Constraints
Serving latency of a recommendation request is on the order of 100 ms.
The catalog changes continuously: new games appear and old ones decay every day.

steps: Design a recommendation system from candidate generation to ranking. A cascade reduces a huge catalog to a small set worth scoring with expensive models.
Generate candidates using complementary signals such as collaborative, content and popularity retrieval.
Rank with user, item and context features, ensuring training features were available at event time.
Apply policy and diversity constraints, log exposures and outcomes, and evaluate retrieval recall, ranking utility and online guardrails separately.
Choose metrics for ranking and recommendation. The right metric should reflect the ordered choices users see and the value of a good recommendation.
For retrieval, inspect recall@K to ensure relevant items survive candidate generation.
For ranking, use an order-sensitive measure such as NDCG@K or a task-specific utility measure, and define relevance labels and position discounts.
Validate online impact with guardrails for latency, diversity, safety and long-term outcomes; correct or acknowledge exposure and selection bias.
solution.contract_notes: Game recommendations should use genre/content and age/platform compatibility for cold starts; split by user/time and inspect popularity/exposure bias.
solution.example: Retrieve 1000 candidates from a million items, rerank 100, then display 10; each stage trades compute for selectivity.
solution.trap: Training only on clicked items and treating unexposed items as observed negatives.

question:
Design a recommendation system for a brand-new product that launches with little to no interaction data — the cold-start problem — for both new users and new items.

In your design, address:

the multi-stage recommender funnel — cheap candidate retrieval (millions of items → hundreds) then an expensive ranker,
feature and representation design (content / metadata embeddings) when there is no collaborative signal,

question:

title: Design a Restaurant Recommendation and Ranking System for a Food Delivery App
question:
Design an end-to-end machine learning system that recommends and ranks restaurants for each user in a food-delivery app. Cover the feature pipeline, model training, online serving, evaluation and the experimentation framework, and say how the same design carries over to related marketplace prediction problems such as feed ranking and delivery-time (ETA) prediction.

Requirements
1.
Prediction target: define what the model predicts and why (click-through rate, order conversion, ETA error, matching success) and which business metric it serves.
2.
Feature pipeline: design the offline batch features, the online real-time features and the entity joins (user, restaurant, location, time), including how training features match serving features.
3.
Model family: choose and justify one (gradient-boosted trees, wide-and-deep, two-tower retrieval, Transformer ranker), and describe the candidate-generation and ranking stages.

title: Design an Online Fraud Detection Pipeline
question: Design an online fraud detection pipeline that scores user actions in near real time and escalates suspicious activity.

title: Design Harmful-Content Detection (Weapon Sales) at Scale

Design an integrity ML system that detects harmful content (e.g., weapon sales, harmful ads) at scale with precision high enough to take action while minimizing false positives against legitimate creators.

steps: Design multi-modal harmful-content detection. Use a calibrated triage system that combines automated decisions with human review capacity.

title: ML System Design: Bad / Unsafe Content Detection
question:
Design a content-understanding pipeline that flags unsafe / bad pins (or bad images) at upload time and at re-evaluation time. Used by Trust & Safety / Content Signal teams; the framing changes between teams but the underlying ML system is recognizably one design.

Requirements

Design an end-to-end content-safety pipeline for Pinterest pins. Address:

How content (image + text + metadata) is represented as features.
Multi-modal embedding choice — image + caption + board context.
Labeling strategy: human review queue, weak labels from report signals, gold-set evaluation.
Model architecture and training (multi-label classification, threshold calibration per policy).
Inference pipeline: synchronous (block upload) vs asynchronous (post-publish takedown).
How the system handles model updates and re-scoring of historical content.
How human reviewers feed back into training.
Notes
Multi-modal embedding is the central design choice. The expected answer covers image embeddings (CNN / ViT) + text embeddings (transformer) + a fusion layer; many candidates underspecify the fusion and lose signal.
Calibration matters more than accuracy in this domain — policy thresholds are set per category, and miscalibrated probabilities translate to wrong policy enforcement. Mention temperature scaling or isotonic regression as the calibration step.
Asynchronous re-scoring of historical content is a common follow-up. The accepted answer: a Kafka-backed event log of all pins, a worker pool that consumes the log against the current model version, sharded by content-id to limit duplicate work.
Bias-and-fairness analysis is sometimes pushed — subgroup metric breakdowns and counterfactual evaluation.
One reported variant is bank/transaction fraud detection used as a generic real-time scoring system; the architecture overlaps (feature pipeline -> scoring -> threshold -> action).

steps: Design multi-modal harmful-content detection. Use a calibrated triage system that combines automated decisions with human review capacity.
Define harm categories, policy versions and separate precision/recall targets per action and category.

Prioritize a bounded review queue, audit decisions and retrain from reviewed labels with sampling-bias checks.
solution.example: A high-confidence severe violation can be blocked, while ambiguous content may receive limited distribution and human review under the specified policy.
solution.trap: Optimizing one aggregate accuracy metric while hiding catastrophic errors on a rare category.
