title: Design a Settings Store with User and Team Sync
question:
Design a service that stores the settings of a code editor and keeps every copy of the editor up to date. A person has personal settings, and a team has shared settings that its administrators can push to every member. The editor must start with the right settings, keep working offline, and converge when it comes back online.

What to design

A settings store and sync system with two entities, User and Team. A user belongs to exactly one team at a time, and each user runs the editor on several devices. Give the data model, the API, the sync protocol between server and device, and the failure behaviour.

Rules
1.
A setting is a key (for example editor.fontSize) with a JSON value. A User has personal settings. A Team has team settings.
2.
The settings a device uses are the team settings overlaid with the user's personal settings. Define what happens when both define the same key, and whether a team can mark a key as enforced.
3.
When a team setting changes, every device of every member must receive it. A new member receives the team settings on joining, and a member who leaves stops receiving them.
4.
A user's own change on one device must reach that user's other devices.
5.
A device may be offline for hours or days, and may edit personal settings while offline.
Examples
A team administrator changes editor.tabSize from 2 to 4. Every online device shows 4 within seconds. A laptop that was closed over the weekend shows 4 within seconds of reconnecting.
A user changes the theme on a desktop while the laptop is offline. When the laptop reconnects it receives the new theme, and a font change made on the laptop in the meantime is not lost.
Constraints (assumptions to state and use in your estimates)
2,000,000 users, 50,000 teams, and 3 devices per user on average.
At any moment 30% of devices hold an open connection to the service.
Settings for one scope are about 20 KB. The largest team has 20,000 members.
500,000 setting changes per day across all scopes. An average change is 200 bytes.
After a service outage, all connected devices reconnect within a 60-second window.
A newly changed setting should reach online devices within 5 seconds at the 95th percentile.
Follow-up 1: versioning of a setting

How is the version of a setting, or of a whole settings document, defined? What happens when two writers change the same scope at the same time, and how does a stale write get handled? Describe how a version update travels to a device, and how old versions are kept or discarded.

Follow-up 2: a device drops offline and reconnects

Show how a device ends up with the right settings after a disconnect without losing an update, applying one twice, or hitting a version conflict. Cover updates the device missed, updates delivered twice or out of order, edits made offline, and a reconnect storm.

title: Understanding Cross-Origin Issues and Their Solutions
question:
Understanding Cross-Origin Issues and Their Solutions

palo-alto-networks

Please explain what is cross-origin and describe several solutions to cross-origin issues. What are the main aspects involved in cross-origin?

steps: An origin is scheme+host+port. The browser’s same-origin policy restricts scripts reading responses from other origins; CORS is the server’s mechanism for allowing selected browser reads.
For non-simple requests, respond to the preflight with the permitted origin, methods and headers. Return the actual CORS headers on the real response too.

Credentialed access needs an explicitly allowed origin and suitable cookie/token policies; do not combine wildcard origins with credentialed sharing. Server-side authentication and authorization remain necessary.

title: Book Seller External Fan-Out Broker Service
question:
Design a broker service that helps customers buy books at the cheapest price. The service does not sell books directly; it fans out to many partner bookstores to find the best deal.

Flow

1.
A customer sends a request with: Book ID (ISBN), the maximum price they'll pay (Max Price), and payment details (credit card).
2.
The service asks 50-200 partner seller APIs for their prices, finds the lowest, and:
If Low Price ≤ Max Price: it orders the book and charges the customer.
If the lowest price exceeds Max Price: it returns the lowest quote it found as a suggestion.

Scale & constraints

1-2 million unique books; 50-200 seller APIs.
End-to-end latency SLA: 10-20 seconds. Requests are asynchronous (return a job id, notify when done).
Must avoid overwhelming partner APIs.

Discuss: parallel quoting without exceeding per-seller rate limits, circuit breakers / backoff, handling sold-out inventory (try cheapest-to-most-expensive), when to charge the customer, quote expiry, and scaling to 10,000 sellers.

steps: Normalize the request into a typed query with required vendors, deadline and a stable request id. Call independent seller adapters concurrently under per-vendor quotas and timeouts.

Convert responses into a common schema, deduplicate equivalent editions/offers and preserve currency, shipping and availability timestamps. Return partial results with explicit missing/error status if the contract allows it.
Use request cancellation, circuit breakers, bounded retries and short freshness-aware caches; one slow vendor must not hold every request forever.
Keep purchasing separate from price lookup and revalidate final terms before any transaction. Evaluate tail latency and result completeness under vendor outages.
solution.example: If four sellers respond within the deadline and one times out, the API can return four offers plus a timeout marker rather than fabricate the fifth offer or wait without bound.
solution.trap: Retrying all vendors on any single failure or comparing prices without shipping/currency normalization.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Bound parallelism and make partial completion visible

A frontier or fan-out broker manages many pieces of independent work, but it still needs identity, deadlines and resource limits. Normalize/deduplicate work under a documented equivalence rule; two URLs that look similar are not automatically the same resource.

Claim work durably or through a suitable scoped in-flight record, then perform bounded external I/O. Track attempts, next retry time and terminal/permanent failures separately. A per-host/provider quota prevents concurrency from becoming overload, and retry budgets stop outages from multiplying traffic.

For crawlers, handle redirects, link scope, content-size limits and cycles. For external search/offer aggregation, normalize units, currency and availability timestamps before comparing results. Return partial data with explicit missing providers only if the API contract permits it.

Walk through worker death after a fetch and before checkpointing: replay must not double-count the content or derived aggregate. Define the durability of fetched bytes and metadata independently. Measure completion coverage, queue age, freshness and tail latency; a high request rate that silently drops difficult sources is not a successful complete pipeline.

title: Design a Distributed Web Crawler
question:
Design a distributed web crawler at scale (sometimes framed as a Google Flight price aggregator, where 'URLs' become route queries and dedup is on price snapshots).

Functional: crawl billions of URLs, extract content and links, deduplicate, and store for indexing. Scale ~1B URLs/day, ~10 KB avg page (~10 TB/day new content), per-domain rate limits. Cover the URL frontier, scheduling, dedup, storage, politeness, and failure handling. Expect a follow-up: 'now crawl JavaScript-rendered pages.'

steps: Maintain a durable URL frontier, normalized visited keys, per-host politeness/rate budgets and retry state. Fetch with time/size limits and record response status, content hash and discovered links.
Parse and canonicalize links under an explicit equivalence rule; perform atomic claim/check-and-insert so concurrent workers do not duplicate the same work.
Partition by host or URL key, use leases for recovery and respect the allowed crawl scope and relevant access restrictions. Prioritize under a bounded queue rather than launching unbounded requests.
Store versioned content/metadata, deduplicate repeated pages and quarantine permanent failures. Test redirect loops, enormous pages, dynamic URLs, duplicate discovery and worker crashes.
solution.example: Two pages linking to the same normalized URL should create one active frontier claim. A redirect loop must terminate at a configured hop budget.
solution.trap: Assuming a thread-safe local set prevents duplicate fetches across an entire distributed fleet.

Seed the crawler with a starter URL set.
Fetch each URL, persist HTML, extract embedded links, enqueue new URLs.
Honor robots.txt per-domain and respect crawl-delay directives.
Deduplicate at the URL level and (optionally) the content level.

Crawl ~10B pages over ~5 days.
Per-domain politeness of ~1 req/sec.
Survive worker / DNS failures without restarting from scratch.

title: Wikipedia Internet Archive / Web Crawler
question:
Design a crawler/archive system that starts from a primary VM and roughly 1000 small bot VMs, creates an initial copy of Wikipedia-like content, and keeps the archive updated over time.

Requirements
Start from a primary VM and around 1000 small bot VMs.
Create an initial copy of Wikipedia-like web content.
Keep the copied content updated over time.
Fetch web pages at large scale; one prompt note mentions roughly 100m pages.
Bots must parse fetched pages and discover new URLs.
Handle scheduling, deduplication, frontier management, retry, and politeness/rate control.
Store page content and metadata so updates can be detected.
Notes
Split the design into frontier service, crawler workers, parser/extractor, content store, metadata/index store, and scheduler.
A clean data flow is: pop URL from frontier, resolve/fetch, parse content, store page/blob plus metadata, extract links, normalize/dedup links, enqueue new or recrawl candidates.
The strongest design decision is how to partition URLs across 1000 bots while avoiding duplicate fetches. Consistent hashing or URL-host partitioning are natural options.
Per-host politeness belongs near scheduling, not inside ad hoc worker sleeps. Use host-level rate limits and queues so one large domain cannot starve the rest of the crawl.
Update handling can use periodic recrawl, content hashes, ETag/Last-Modified when available, and priority queues for frequently changing pages.
Candidate failures tend to come from shallow follow-up handling: bottleneck ownership, worker failure, duplicate URL explosions, and how to recover progress after a bot dies.

title: Design a Read-Once Password Sharing Service
question:
Design a service that lets a signed-in user hand a password to another person through a link that works only once. The user creates the secret, receives a URL, and sends the URL to someone else. The first time the recipient opens it they see the password; every later attempt must fail.

Requirements
1.
Create: a signed-in user submits a secret (a short text of up to 4,096 bytes) and gets back a URL. The user can add a label such as the recipient's name.
2.
Read once: the URL reveals the secret to exactly one successful reader. Two people opening it at the same moment must not both succeed. After a successful read the stored secret is gone.
3.
Many users: any number of users can create secrets independently. A user sees only their own secrets and their status.
4.
Same password, many creators: two users may share the same password text. Their secrets must stay separate, and nothing in storage may reveal that the two texts are equal.
5.
Same password, many recipients: one user may share the same password with several people. Each recipient has their own URL, reading one URL does not use up the others, and the user can see which recipient has read it.
6.
Confirm the read: the creator can ask whether a URL has been read, and when. Say precisely what the system can and cannot confirm.
7.
Expiry and revoke: a secret expires after a time the creator picks, at most 7 days. The creator can revoke an unread secret early. An expired, revoked or already read URL gives the same answer as an unknown one.
8.
Recipients are anonymous: a recipient does not need an account.
Scale
2,000,000 secrets are created per day, spread over the day, with a peak of 10 times the average.
On average each URL receives 3 page loads, because chat tools and mail scanners fetch links to preview them, and 90% of URLs are eventually read by a person.
Metadata (not the secret) is kept for 90 days for audit.
Deliverables
1.
The API: endpoints, request and response fields, and status codes.
2.
The data model and what is stored in plain, hashed and encrypted form.
3.
The URL: what it contains and why it cannot be guessed.
4.
How the read-once rule holds when two requests race, when the server crashes mid-request, and when a link-preview bot opens the URL first.
5.
Capacity estimates for request rates and storage.
6.
The corner cases from requirements 4 to 7, each with the behavior you choose.
Examples
Alice creates one secret and sends the URL to Bob. Bob opens it and sees the text. Bob opens it again and gets the same "not found" answer a random URL would give. Alice sees the status change from pending to read, with the time.
Alice and Carol both choose the password hunter2. Alice shares it with Bob and Dave using two URLs. Bob reads his; Dave's URL still works; Carol's secret is unaffected, and the stored data for the three secrets looks unrelated.

steps: Design a read-once secret-sharing service. The key correctness property is atomic consumption under concurrent requests, not just hiding a URL.
Create a high-entropy token and store encrypted payload, expiry and access metadata under a minimal retention policy.
Atomically transition unused to consumed while retrieving or deleting the payload; define failures between consumption and delivery.
Avoid logging secrets, use secure transport and explicit expiration, and explain the tradeoff between strict one-attempt access and retryability.
solution.example: Two concurrent readers must not both observe an unused record and both receive the secret.
solution.trap: Promising perfect one-successful-read semantics across arbitrary client/network failures without defining what counts as consumption.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### State what an acknowledgment guarantees

Distinguish accepted in memory, appended to a local file, flushed durably, replicated and committed. A client-visible success must correspond to the promised boundary; otherwise recovery can lose operations the client believes are complete.

A retry is not necessarily a new logical operation. Use a stable operation id, bind it to request parameters, and atomically record its state and result with the business change where possible. If a worker finishes an effect and crashes before acknowledgment, the repeated id lets a recipient recognize it.

Timeouts mean lack of observed response, not proof that no action happened. Leases and heartbeats detect suspected failure; fencing tokens prevent an expired owner from committing after a successor took over. In a partition, stronger consistency may require rejecting some requests rather than allowing conflicting leaders.

Walk through one failure between each pair of durable transitions. For tree aggregation, record one contribution per child and request id; duplicate messages must not increase the count. For an external effect, reconcile uncertain outcomes rather than silently retrying under a new identity. Explain liveness assumptions separately: permanent loss of access to required state can make guaranteed completion impossible even when the protocol preserves safety.

title: Design a Notification / Alert Fan-Out System
question:
Design a notification system that receives alerts from upstream services and fans out to all subscribers across multiple channels — email, SMS, push, in-app.

Functional

Upstream services publish alerts (order ready, dasher arrived, promo, system incident).
Subscriber model: per user, per alert type, per channel.
Alerts fan out to all matching subscribers via their preferred channels.
Users can mute / opt out per alert type and per channel.
Throttle: a user never receives more than N notifications/minute regardless of upstream volume.

Non-functional

High fan-out: one system-incident alert can target millions of subscribers.
Per-channel SLAs differ: push near-real-time; email/SMS tolerate 1-2 min; in-app eventually consistent.
Email/SMS have hard provider rate limits; backpressure must propagate, not drop.
At-least-once delivery; dedupe by (user_id, alert_id, channel).

steps: Store durable notification intents with event id, recipient, channel, preference version and delivery status. Expand recipients through a partitioned fan-out pipeline rather than blocking the initiating request.
Check current opt-outs and quiet hours at the appropriate sending boundary. Deduplicate per event/recipient/channel and use bounded retries with provider-specific throttles.
Separate immediate alerts from digests; batch by recipient and time window while preserving the meaning of urgent events. Treat delivery, receipt and read status as different observations.
Support preference changes, stale-device tokens, replay and partial provider outages. Report end-to-end lag and user-visible duplicates, not only successful API calls.
solution.example: An event that fans out to one million followers becomes many idempotent delivery tasks; replaying the event must not create a second notification per recipient.
solution.trap: Sending directly to every follower inside the posting request or treating provider acceptance as proof the user read the message.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Separate authoritative events from their many derived deliveries

A post, like or notification intent should have one logical identity even if it produces many feed entries or channel deliveries. Store the event/state transition durably, then use idempotent fan-out tasks keyed by event, recipient and destination.

Fan-out-on-write makes common reads cheaper but can be expensive for very large follower counts. Fan-out-on-read avoids those writes but adds read-time merging. A hybrid can materialize ordinary publishers and merge high-follower publishers later; explain pagination and consistent deletion/privacy behavior in both paths.

A notification also needs preferences, channel budgets, quiet hours and a distinction between provider acceptance, device receipt and user read. A social count may be a current-state view rather than a blind event sum: repeated “like” is not two active likes, and “unlike” should not make a count negative.

Walk through replay, a membership change and one unavailable delivery provider. Permissions must remain effective at serving time under the declared revocation policy, even if a feed was cached earlier. Measure end-to-end freshness, missing/duplicate delivery and user outcome, not only worker throughput. A fast queue that quietly omits hard-to-reach recipients does not satisfy an all-recipient delivery contract.

title: Notification System — Push to Followers on New Post
question:
Notification System — Push to Followers on New Post

Onsite SD round. Design a push-notification service: when a user creates a new post, every follower receives a notification. The interviewer treats it as a product-flavored design (not pure infra), so weighting is on data model + fanout strategy + delivery guarantees rather than on cluster topology.

Requirements

Functional:

A user creates a post → every follower of that user gets a notification.
Notifications must be deliverable to multiple device types (mobile push via APNs / FCM, web push, in-app inbox).
Support read / unread state, mark-as-read, and delete from inbox.
Tolerate offline followers — notifications queue until the device reconnects.

Scale (rough working numbers for the discussion):

100M users, average 300 followers, peak post rate ~10K/s.
Latency target: p50 < 5s, p99 < 30s for normal authors (first-batch delivery should feel real-time); availability 99.9%+; durability is the hard requirement — a lost post event is unrecoverable.

Decision points the interviewer probes:

Fanout-on-write vs fanout-on-read — when does each break down (celebrity users with millions of followers)?
Hybrid fanout: write for normal users, read for celebrities. Where do you draw the line?
Idempotency and deduplication when a worker retries.
Backpressure when a downstream provider (APNs) throttles.
Notes
The round is in-person on a laptop — type your reasoning into the shared doc rather than relying on a whiteboard photo.
The product-design angle matters: define the notification payload schema, the inbox API, and how it interacts with feed ranking.
Cover the celebrity problem explicitly. Pure fanout-on-write with a 50M-follower account writes 50M rows per post; degrade to fanout-on-read for that segment and merge at fetch time.
Discuss exactly-once vs at-least-once delivery — push providers are at-least-once; the inbox layer must dedupe by (post_id, user_id).
Mention metrics: delivery latency p50/p99, fanout queue depth, provider throttle rate.
The standard hybrid threshold in production designs is on the order of ~10K followers: under it, fan-out-on-write into a per-user precomputed-feed table (≤200 recent × ~2KB per row); over it, store the post once and merge at read time. Celebrities are flagged in the Follow table so the post-create worker can skip their write-fanout.
Two *different* thresholds are in play: the fan-out-on-write-vs-read line (~10K) above, and a separate *paced-campaign* trigger for true hot authors — below ~100K opted-in followers enqueue all shards at high priority; above it, create a campaign that splits followers into ~50K-follower shards and *paces* shard dispatch so provider quotas are respected and progress is checkpointed (never scan all of a celebrity's followers in one query).
Use a pub/sub bus (Kafka / Redis pub-sub) keyed on user_id for the delivery side: each post-create publishes a fanout job, sharded workers consume and route to the per-device WebSocket or push provider. This is the same shape WhatsApp-style designs use to scale a single chat-server farm — any worker can serve any user because routing is decoupled from connection ownership.
Track delivery per (user_id, client_id) not per user_id — a user with phone + tablet + web has three rows in the Inbox table and three independent ack states.
Behind the fanout bus, a bounded queue is doing two jobs that often get conflated: (1) decoupling post-create latency from delivery latency, and (2) backpressure when APNs/FCM throttle — the queue absorbs the slowdown without spilling 429s back to the author. Surface both in the design.
Cache hot-key reads (viral post inbox entries) in a non-sharded Redis replica set to avoid a single shard's CPU melting.
Provider failures & token hygiene: retry *temporary* provider errors with exponential backoff + jitter; on a *permanent* error mark the device token invalid and stop sending, emitting an invalid-token event back to the Device service for cleanup. Cap retry age so a stale "new post" push is never delivered hours late, and batch sends by provider + platform. Provider acceptance ≠ user-visible delivery — an APNs/FCM success only means the message was accepted, not seen.
Multi-region: run stateless API / orchestration / dispatch workers in several regions with region-local, mirrored-failover queues; the follower graph and notification store tolerate eventual consistency across regions — only the initial post write needs strong consistency, so keep it off the cross-region synchronous path.
Canonical data model & write-path details
Transactional outbox between POST /posts and the post_created event: write the post row and an outbox row in the *same* transaction, then a relay publishes to the bus. Publishing separately is the classic lost-notification bug — the post commits but the trigger is dropped if the process crashes.
Model the follower edge as (author_id, shard_id, follower_id) so a celebrity never collapses to one partition; carry per-edge notify_on_post / muted / blocked on the edge, but keep user-global quiet_hours + timezone in a separate preference so a timezone change does not rewrite every follow edge.
Split the record in two: a follower-level Notification (canonical, with a UNIQUE dedupe_key on (post_id, follower_id, channel)) and per-device NotificationReceipt rows. The parent status aggregates from children — dispatched = ≥1 device accepted, opened = any device opened, exhausted = all devices permanently failed or retry budget spent. The full Notification.status lifecycle is scheduled → queued → dispatched → opened, with terminal suppressed (filtered out before send), expired, and exhausted.
Quiet hours = defer, not drop. Create the notification, compute the next valid send time in the user's timezone, set scheduled_for, and release it from a delayed queue later.
Filter as late as possible (during shard expansion / just before dispatch), not at event-creation time — otherwise a user who mutes or unfollows seconds after the post still gets pushed.
Working capacity numbers for the estimate: ~30M DAU, ~15M posts/day, ~200 opted-in followers/post → ~3B candidate notifications/day (~35K/s avg, 350K/s peak), celebrity fanout up to ~20M recipients per post; store ~250 bytes of compact metadata per recipient (template id, actor, post id, state) and render the provider payload at dispatch time. At ~250 bytes × ~3B/day that is ~750 GB/day of hot notification state, ~5.25 TB at 7-day retention before replication.

steps: Store durable notification intents with event id, recipient, channel, preference version and delivery status. Expand recipients through a partitioned fan-out pipeline rather than blocking the initiating request.
Check current opt-outs and quiet hours at the appropriate sending boundary. Deduplicate per event/recipient/channel and use bounded retries with provider-specific throttles.
Separate immediate alerts from digests; batch by recipient and time window while preserving the meaning of urgent events. Treat delivery, receipt and read status as different observations.
Support preference changes, stale-device tokens, replay and partial provider outages. Report end-to-end lag and user-visible duplicates, not only successful API calls.
solution.example: An event that fans out to one million followers becomes many idempotent delivery tasks; replaying the event must not create a second notification per recipient.
solution.trap: Sending directly to every follower inside the posting request or treating provider acceptance as proof the user read the message.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Separate authoritative events from their many derived deliveries

A post, like or notification intent should have one logical identity even if it produces many feed entries or channel deliveries. Store the event/state transition durably, then use idempotent fan-out tasks keyed by event, recipient and destination.

Fan-out-on-write makes common reads cheaper but can be expensive for very large follower counts. Fan-out-on-read avoids those writes but adds read-time merging. A hybrid can materialize ordinary publishers and merge high-follower publishers later; explain pagination and consistent deletion/privacy behavior in both paths.

A notification also needs preferences, channel budgets, quiet hours and a distinction between provider acceptance, device receipt and user read. A social count may be a current-state view rather than a blind event sum: repeated “like” is not two active likes, and “unlike” should not make a count negative.

Walk through replay, a membership change and one unavailable delivery provider. Permissions must remain effective at serving time under the declared revocation policy, even if a feed was cached earlier. Measure end-to-end freshness, missing/duplicate delivery and user outcome, not only worker throughput. A fast queue that quietly omits hard-to-reach recipients does not satisfy an all-recipient delivery contract.

title: Daily Puzzle Submission and Leaderboard System
question:
Design a daily-puzzle product where users submit one answer per day, see their score, and view a leaderboard; the system also schedules puzzles.

Functional: schedule one puzzle per day per locale; accept a single submission per user per puzzle, score it server-side, return the score and current rank; serve a leaderboard (per locale/day and all-time).

Scale: 10M+ users, ~1M DAU; heavy leaderboard reads; submission burst at midnight local time; single-region or active-active. Design decisions: where to score, idempotent submission, leaderboard storage (Redis sorted-set vs columnar batch).

steps: Define score semantics, tie-breaking, update frequency and leaderboard scope/time window. Keep an authoritative submission/score log with idempotency and anti-abuse checks.

Use an ordered score index for top-K and rank queries; materialize per-day or per-game views from durable accepted events. A daily puzzle needs a trusted answer checker and server-side time/attempt rules.
Handle score corrections and season rollover through versioned events; support pagination with stable rank/tie keys rather than assuming offsets remain fixed.
Test duplicate submissions, equal scores, late updates, cheating and recovery. Explain whether exact global rank is required or an approximate/partitioned view suffices.
solution.example: If two users have equal score, the displayed order may use earliest valid completion then user id; that policy must be the same in rank queries and page cursors.
solution.trap: Updating a cache score before persisting the accepted submission and then losing it during a crash.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Make state transitions deterministic before adding networking

Define a state, legal actions and a pure transition rule. An action should be validated against an authoritative version: two clients cannot both independently advance the same turn just because each displayed the previous state.

Keep game rules separate from transport, matchmaking and persistence. A stable event id supports deduplicating retries; a snapshot plus ordered event cursor supports reconnect/replay. Clocks require an authoritative time basis and explicit charge-at-action/timeout behavior rather than trusting arbitrary client timestamps.

For leaderboards, define whether the score is additive, replacing or a maximum, and choose a deterministic tie rule. Ranking queries and page cursors must use the same rule. Anti-abuse checks and authoritative answer validation are necessary when accepting submissions affects rewards or standings.

Work a short event sequence by hand, then replay it through the implementation and compare the final state. Include one invalid action, duplicate event and time-boundary race. If the rules are missing, declare an illustrative rule set instead of calling invented outcomes the answer to an unspecified simulation. The reasoning quality is in the invariant and recovery behavior, not the number of classes.

title: Game Leaderboard System Design
question:
Design a real-time global game leaderboard supporting score updates and top-K queries for millions of players. Starts single-server (top-K reads, 1 write/sec, no friends) and incrementally adds friend leaderboards, time windows, and replication toward 100K writes/sec and 1M reads/sec.

Requirements
Functional: submit a score; read top-K (K configurable, default 100); read personal best / rank; read neighborhood (top-K around a player); client learns whether a submission updated personal-best, rank, or neither.
Core framing: NOT store-every-score-forever; persist only a new personal best or a top-K break; filter the rest before durable storage.

Redis Sorted Set (ZADD / ZREVRANGE / ZREVRANK, O(log N)); shard by player-id with scatter-gather top-K; friend leaderboard = per-user ZSCORE + client sort; rolling sorted set per time window; durable log + leaderboard processor with idempotency; deterministic tiebreak (score DESC, achieved_at ASC, submission_id ASC); hot-game hierarchical top-K.

title: Design a Pickup Area Driver Queue
question:
Design an internal pickup-area driver queue service that maintains, in real time, an ordered queue of eligible drivers for each geofenced pickup zone (such as an airport staging lot).

The core challenges are real-time geofence membership and ordered state management:

Deciding when a driver is inside an area.
Keeping queue order stable under continuous movement and noisy location events.
Serving fast queue reads (position, next-up).

Discuss ingestion, geofence detection, ordering/state machine, storage, idempotency, and how you keep the queue correct despite GPS noise and out-of-order events.

steps: Represent locations with timestamps, uncertainty and a spatial index; define serviceability, travel-time and safety constraints before optimizing distance.

Generate nearby feasible candidates using cells/R-trees, then score travel time or the stated objective. For queues, preserve eligibility and policy order; for routing, distinguish shortest path from multi-stop vehicle-routing complexity.
Assign through a versioned atomic claim so a rider/order/vehicle is not concurrently committed twice. Use reservations, timeout/reconciliation and periodic position refresh.
Evaluate wait time, completion, fairness and stale-location failures. For perishables include expiry/temperature history and traceability, not only the current coordinate.
solution.example: The closest driver by straight-line distance may be across a river and farther by road. A late GPS report must not overwrite a newer location.
solution.trap: Calling a heuristic globally optimal or using a location update as proof that a physical delivery occurred.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Time and coordinate uncertainty matter as much as location

Specify coordinate reference frame, units, timestamp and accuracy. A latitude/longitude in degrees cannot be subtracted directly from a local Cartesian meter offset. A stale location can be numerically precise and operationally wrong.

Use a spatial index to generate candidates, then apply the exact serviceability or distance/travel-time predicate. A cell cover of a circle generally includes points outside the circle, and straight-line proximity does not encode bridges, road direction or access restrictions.

Assignment also needs concurrency control. Reserve a driver, inventory unit or pickup slot through an authoritative versioned transition, with timeout and reconciliation. Several simultaneous requests must not independently commit the same exclusive resource.

For prediction, define the forecast horizon and split by time/session or location to prevent nearby observations leaking across the evaluation boundary. For control, distinguish a delivered command from measured physical effect and account for telemetry delay. Test late updates, disconnected devices, uncertain measurements and empty candidate sets. Be honest about heuristic optimization: a practical local routing or clustering solution need not be a proven global optimum.

title: Design Multi-Carrier Package Delivery Routing System
question:
Design a system that ships customer packages through multiple delivery partners (UPS, USPS, FedEx, last-mile contractors), choosing a partner per package based on cost, capacity, and SLA, and tracking the package through each partner's API.

Functional: accept a package creation request (origin, destination, weight, dimensions, service-level requested); select a carrier; book the shipment with that carrier; track status updates from the carrier and surface them to the customer; handle exceptions (carrier rejects pickup, package lost, address invalid).

title: ML System Design: Choose Passenger Drop-off Location
question:
L6 ML design round: when a Waymo passenger arrives at the destination, decide where exactly to pull over. Walk through model features, ranking objective, safety constraints, and how human / regulatory rules interact with the ML score.

Requirements
At trip end, choose a curbside parking spot for the AV to stop and drop off the passenger.
Inputs: ego state + sensor view of the immediate area, map data (lane markings, parking regulations, building entrances), passenger preferences (door choice, accessibility needs), historical drop-off data at the same location.
Output: a ranked list of candidate stop poses with scores; the planner consumes the top feasible candidate.
Constraints: legality (no-stopping zones, fire hydrants), safety (clear lane visibility, distance from intersections), passenger experience (proximity to the destination door, lighting), and operational considerations (re-merge cost into traffic).
Notes
Candidate generation. Sample candidate stop poses along the destination block face, e.g. every 0.5 m. Filter for legality from map annotations. Filter for safety from real-time perception (no obstacles in the proposed spot).
Scoring. Use a learned ranker that combines (a) walking distance from the stop pose to the destination door, (b) historical success rate at the same micro-location, (c) lane congestion / disruption cost, (d) passenger preference signals. Calibrate the score so the top-K candidates form a usable shortlist for the planner.
Hard constraints vs soft scoring. Legality and safety are hard filters — never let the model override them. The learned ranker only orders the remaining feasible set.
Long-tail and human override. Rare failure modes (unusual side request, construction zones, special events) require either a high-confidence override path or a graceful fallback to a rule-based default. Capture these in training data via labeling pipelines on overridden rides.
Evaluation. Offline: walking distance, override rate, ranker-vs-rule agreement. Online: passenger satisfaction (1–5), planner abort rate, time spent searching for a new spot, second-pull-over rate. Run a multi-armed bandit at deployment to balance exploitation of the learned ranker with exploration of new candidate generation strategies.
Personalization. Per-rider preferences (curb side, walking budget, accessibility) are stored as features but kept narrow to avoid privacy / fairness issues.

title: Perishable-Goods Tracking & Location System
question:
Phone-screen system design (part of a combined ~55-min round). Design a service that tracks and locates perishable products across multiple stores: when an item expires it moves to a storage area, and the system must locate any product by ID, persist a ledger, and answer 'which store has which expired items, and where in storage they are now.'

Requirements
Track perishable products across multiple stores. When a product expires it is moved to a storage area; many stores, many products, many storage areas.
Functional: locate any product by ID; persist a durable ledger of product state and movements; answer at query time which store holds which expired products and where in the storage area each currently is.
This is a high-level design round (API + data model + scaling), not a low-level schema-DDL exercise.
Notes
API: REST web tier, GET /products/{id}/location. Datastore probe: relational (RDS/Postgres/MySQL) vs NoSQL (DynamoDB) - consistency is NOT the only justification; bring query flexibility (store x expiry x location joins favor relational) and key-based scale/throughput (favor DynamoDB). Expiry-scan probe: do not re-scan the full table; index on expiry time and pull only items expiring in the next window into a time-bucketed queue. Read-heavy: cache layer for hot location lookups, load balancing + horizontal autoscaling.

title: Query System — Time + Geo Filtered User Activity
question:
Design a query system that lets internal users look up an end-user's searches and bookings, filtered by time window and geographic region. Read-heavy, batch-tolerant freshness, large catalog.

Requirements
Functional
Query API: (user_id, start_ts, end_ts, geo_bbox) → list of search + booking events.
Aggregations by region and time bucket (count, sum amount).
Non-functional
Tens of TB of historical data.
Query latency < 1s for the typical (single user, week-window, country-sized region) query; multi-second acceptable for analytics-style sweeps.
Eventual consistency on ingest is fine — staleness up to ~5 minutes.

steps: Store event id, user/entity id, event time, ingest time and normalized coordinates. Define the interval boundaries and whether spatial queries mean a box, radius or polygon.

Partition primarily by time for retention/pruning and use a spatial index or cell-covering secondary path. Cover the requested region with candidate cells, then apply the exact distance/polygon predicate to remove false positives.
Keep pagination tied to a stable sort/version, deduplicate late/replayed events and specify how corrected locations are represented.

Benchmark narrow-time/wide-area and wide-time/narrow-area queries separately, with tenant permissions applied in every access path. Preaggregate only at a grain that can answer the requested exactness contract.
solution.example: A cell covering a circle includes corner points outside the radius; the final exact filter is required even if the cell index is fast.
solution.trap: Using a cell prefix as exact geographic membership or filtering unauthorized results only after a top-K cutoff.

title: Ride-Hailing System Design (Uber)
question:
Design an Uber-style ride-hailing service. The interviewer drives on high-frequency driver GPS writes (dedup/throttle), geospatial indexing (Quadtree vs H3), and Redis GEO caching.

Requirements
Design a ride-hailing service (Uber/Lyft-style): riders request rides and the system matches them to nearby drivers.
Ingest high-frequency driver GPS updates and keep a fresh driver-location index.
Match a rider to nearby available drivers via a geospatial query.
Serve location reads with low latency under heavy write load.
Notes

title: Airbnb Booking System Design
question:
Design the core booking pipeline: search availability, hold a listing for a date range, complete payment, confirm reservation. Race conditions over the same listing-date pair are the central deep-dive.

Requirements
Functional
Search listings by date range, location, guest count.
Tentatively hold a listing on a date range for ~10 minutes during checkout.
Confirm the booking once payment succeeds; release the hold otherwise.
Cancel / refund.
Non-functional
Concurrent booking attempts on the same listing-date pair must produce exactly one confirmation.
Search is read-heavy and cache-tolerant; booking is write-heavy and consistency-critical.
Geographically distributed users; place reads near the user.

steps: Separate browsing/search availability from authoritative inventory. A listing may be cached, but a hold or purchase must validate the resource and version on the write path.
Represent a hold with resource ids, owner, price version and expiry. Acquire it atomically through a conditional update or lock; enforce one active owner per exclusive seat or room-night.
Confirm with an idempotent order state machine and durable payment reconciliation. Expired/canceled holds release inventory; failed payment cannot leave an undocumented permanent hold.
Protect flash-sale traffic with admission control, short queues and bounded retries. Test simultaneous buyers, expiry/payment races, partial external inventory updates and replayed confirmations.
solution.example: Two clients can both see seat A1 as available, but only one conditional hold may succeed. A timed-out confirmation must be queried before a new payment is submitted.
solution.trap: Treating a cache decrement as the final inventory authority or promising atomic transactions across an unrelated external hotel provider.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### The browsing view is not the booking authority

Several clients may see the same resource as available. Correctness comes from an atomic hold or purchase transition against authoritative inventory, not from hiding the buy button or decrementing a local cache.

Represent resource id, owner, hold expiry, price/version and lifecycle state. A conditional update such as “available at version $v$ becomes held by request $r$” allows only one winner under the declared exclusivity rule. A hotel night, event seat and fungible stock quantity need different invariants, even when the surrounding API looks similar.

Separate hold, payment, confirmation, cancellation and refund. External systems do not join an ordinary local database transaction; keep pending/unknown states and reconcile. An expired hold racing with payment completion needs a deterministic policy, not two handlers that can independently claim success.

Use idempotency keys and stable order ids so retries do not reserve or charge twice. Queue/admit traffic during a flash sale rather than permitting unlimited contention. Test no inventory, simultaneous buyers, last-millisecond expiry, partial external-provider failure and an acknowledgment lost after a successful confirmation. The failure trace is the core of the design, not an appendix.

title: Airline Booking System: Search, Seat Hold, Purchase and Cancel
question:
Design and implement a simplified airline booking system that lets a traveller find a flight, reserve a specific seat for a short time, pay for it, and cancel it later.

Requirements
1.
Search: find flights by departure city, arrival city, or a departure-time range. Any combination of these filters may be given.
2.
Seat map: for one flight, list which seats are available.
3.
Hold: temporarily reserve one seat for one user so that the user can finish payment. If payment does not complete in time, the seat must become available again without any manual step.
4.
Purchase: turn a hold into a purchase. The payment provider may be a stub in your implementation.
5.
Cancel: cancel a purchased seat so that it can be sold again, and leave a record of the refund.
Assumptions
Every aircraft has the same fixed layout, for example 24 rows with 6 seats per row.
The flight list may be hardcoded.
The system must be callable and testable, for example through a small command-line tool or a set of functions with tests.
Deliverables
1.
The data model: how a seat is represented, which states it can be in, and which transitions are allowed.
2.
The schema of the tables, including the time columns and the indexes that serve the search in requirement 1.
3.
The reference logic for hold, purchase, cancel and expiry, and how it behaves when two users ask for the same seat at the same moment.
4.
The transaction and locking plan: when a lock is taken, when it is released, and what happens when a client disconnects in the middle of a flow.
5.
The payment plan: how a retried request never charges twice, and what is written when a purchase is cancelled.
6.
A short note on how the design changes if a new column, such as a seat class, must be added later.
Constraints
A seat must never be held or sold to two users at once.
A transaction must not stay open while waiting for the user or for the payment provider.
State the capacity assumptions you use and compute them.

title: Design a Shopping Cart Service With Inventory Consistency
question:
Shoppers put items in a cart long before they pay, and during a sale many of them want the last few units of the same product. Design the cart service of a large online retailer: it stores carts, turns a cart into an order at checkout, and never confirms more orders than there are units in stock. The hard part is deciding how carts and inventory interact without making every cart action slow.

Requirements
1.
Cart operations: a shopper can add an item, remove an item, change a quantity and view the cart. Reads are far more frequent than writes, and every operation must feel instant.
2.
Guest and signed-in carts: a guest keeps a cart without an account. When the guest signs in, the guest cart merges with the cart already saved on the account, and nothing the shopper added is silently lost.
3.
Checkout: the cart turns into an order. Prices, availability and promotions are re-validated at that moment, and one click must never create two orders.
4.
Availability: the cart must keep working when part of the system fails; a shopper should not lose a cart because one server restarted.
Inventory consistency rules
1.
Stock is limited and several shoppers may want the last units at the same time. The system must never confirm more orders than there are units.
2.
Decide what, if anything, is reserved when an item is added to the cart, and what is reserved or decremented at checkout. Justify the choice both for ordinary items and for a very popular item during a sale.
3.
Abandoned carts must not hold stock forever.
Deliverables
1.
The architecture: services, data stores and the path of a request for each cart operation.
2.
The data model and the partitioning key for the cart store.
3.
Back-of-envelope sizing for carts, request rate and storage, with every assumption stated.
4.
The inventory strategy, including the order of operations at checkout, the handling of retries and the handling of a hot item.
5.
Failure behaviour and what you would monitor.
Follow-ups
Follow-up 1: two checkouts race for the last unit

What happens when two checkouts try to buy the last unit at the same moment?

Follow-up 2: reserving stock at add-to-cart

Why not reserve stock at add-to-cart for every item?

Follow-up 3: merging carts that hold the same item

How do you merge a guest cart and an account cart when both contain the same item?

Follow-up 4: stale price and stock in an old cart

How do you keep the displayed price and stock from going stale in a cart that has sat for a week?

title: Design an Event Ticket Marketplace: Seat Holds and On-Sale Traffic
question:
Design an online marketplace that sells tickets to live events (concerts, sports, theatre), in the style of Ticketmaster. Fans find an event, pick seats on a seat map, and pay for them.

Scale and assumptions
1.
Catalog: tens of thousands of upcoming events across many venues. A large venue has about 50,000 assigned seats.
2.
Orders: a typical order is 4 seats.
3.
On-sale spikes: a popular event goes on sale at a published time. About 2 million users arrive within the first 10 minutes, far more than there are seats.
4.
Normal traffic: outside on-sales, traffic is mostly browsing and search, with steady low purchase volume.
5.
Payments: an external payment provider authorizes and captures card payments. Calls to it can time out.
Functional requirements
1.
Browse and search events by name, performer, city and date.
2.
View an event's seat map with live availability and prices.
3.
Select seats and place a temporary hold on them. A hold expires after a fixed time (for example 10 minutes) if the purchase is not completed.
4.
Complete the purchase: pay, confirm the order and issue tickets.
5.
A seat is never sold to two buyers, and a buyer is never charged twice for one order.
Parts to address
1.
API and data model for events, venues, seats, holds, orders and tickets.
2.
Seat holds: how a hold is placed atomically for several seats, how expiry works, and what happens when two users try to take the same seat at the same moment.
3.
Purchase flow: the steps from hold to issued ticket, including payment timeouts, retries and a hold that expires during payment.
4.
On-sale traffic: how the system survives millions of users arriving at once, including a virtual waiting room (queue), how users are admitted, and how the seat map stays fast.
5.
Scaling and storage: which data needs strong consistency and which can be cached or eventually consistent, and how the inventory store is partitioned.
Deliverables
1.
The architecture, naming the services on the browse, hold and purchase paths.
2.
Capacity estimates for a large on-sale: arrival rate, seat-map read rate, admission rate and hold write rate.
3.
The failure behaviour for a payment timeout, a crashed service holding seats, a cache that shows a sold seat as free, and bots.
Constraints
General system design; no machine-learning components are required.
State any assumption you add beyond the numbers above.

title: Design an Expedia-Style Hotel Reservation System
question:
Design a hotel reservation system similar to Expedia — an aggregator that resells rooms sourced from many hotel groups' own systems/APIs (e.g. Marriott), rather than a single chain's first-party system.

Users search and book hotel rooms across many providers.
Hard requirement: room-availability latency must be very low.
Availability must stay correct: a room shown as available must (as much as possible) still be bookable when the user commits.
Notes

The central tension is cache vs consistency. Pre-fetching/caching each hotel group's availability gives low read latency, but a provider may sell a room out-of-band right after you cached it — so a confirm step against the provider can fail or be slow; calling the provider live on every read keeps inventory fresh but blows the latency budget. One workable direction: aggregators pre-negotiate and lock a block of rooms from each hotel group, so reads serve from your own cache/DB quickly; when the locked block is exhausted, fall back to the provider API. Distinguish a fast, possibly-stale availability read from an authoritative confirm-at-booking step. A single design round — reason about inventory caching, staleness windows (TTLs, write-through/invalidation), and graceful fallback when a cached room is gone at confirm time.

title: Ticketmaster-Style Seat Booking Design

title: Waitlist System Design
question:
Design a waitlist subsystem: users join a waitlist for a listing; when capacity opens, the system notifies subscribers in priority order. Booking integration is assumed to exist; the design focus is API + schema + notification fan-out.

Functional
join_waitlist(user_id, listing_id, criteria) — add a user with date/price criteria.
leave_waitlist(user_id, listing_id).
When matching availability appears, notify all subscribers whose criteria match.
Idempotent join (duplicate calls do not create multiple entries).
Non-functional
Tens of millions of waitlist rows across the catalog.

title: Core Dump Collection System Design
question:
Design a core-dump collection system. Agents on many hosts upload crash artifacts; the backend stores large binaries durably and extracts searchable metadata; engineers query, group, and download dumps for debugging; and the platform enforces retention, access control, and scale limits.

Functional requirements:

Collect core dumps / crash artifacts from many hosts or services.
Store large binary dumps durably while extracting searchable metadata (service, host, version, timestamp, signal, stack signature).
Let engineers search, group, and download relevant dumps.
Enforce access control, retention, and deletion (dumps may contain sensitive memory).

Constraints to clarify: dumps are large; crash spikes after a bad deploy cause bursty ingestion; retention cost matters.

steps: Collect immutable events/artifacts with stable ids, timestamps, actor or process identity, schema version and integrity metadata. Buffer and transport with bounded resource use so collection does not crash the primary workload.
For core dumps, encrypt and restrict access because memory can contain credentials and personal data; deduplicate by content/signature and separate metadata search from large-object storage.

For audit logs, use append-only authorized writes, ordered sequence/checkpoint verification and retention/legal-hold policies as applicable. Avoid claiming cryptographic immutability without defining the trust and key model.

Support retry/replay, ingestion lag monitoring and controlled deletion/expiry. Query by indexed metadata and provide evidence of missing/gapped records rather than silently presenting an incomplete audit as complete.
solution.example: A log line acknowledging a transfer is not a replacement for the ledger transaction; a core dump should never be placed in a public diagnostic bucket.
solution.trap: Logging raw secrets or confusing ordinary writable application logs with an audited append-only trail.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Preserve enough information to aggregate correctly

Logs describe events; counters, gauges and histograms summarize different measurements. A counter increment is not interchangeable with the current number of live objects, and a gauge may decrease for legitimate reasons.

For latency, percentiles are not mergeable by averaging them. Combine raw observations or compatible histogram/sketch state, then compute the requested quantile. An average is mergeable through sum and count, but carries different information from a tail measure.

Keep client queues bounded and state whether an emit call means accepted in RAM, written or durably flushed. Batch/fsync group commit can amortize I/O, but acknowledging before the required flush weakens durability. Backpressure/drop policy must protect the application rather than cause an outage while observing it.

Use event and ingest timestamps for late data, and avoid unbounded labels such as a unique request id in every metric series. Alert on sustained actionable conditions with deduplication and recovery state. Test collector failure, disk-full conditions, malformed records and counter resets. Security also matters: core dumps and diagnostic payloads may contain credentials, so indexing convenience must not imply broad access.

title: Cross-Platform Client Logging Library
question:
Design a logging library that runs on both web (browser SPA) and mobile (iOS/Android) clients and ships logs to a backend collector without degrading client-side performance.

Logs are emitted by application code and must reach a backend collector.
Hard constraint: emitting a log must never block the calling thread or noticeably degrade UX.
The backend has a single ingest API; throughput from any client is variable and can spike.
Drive hard on backpressure: what happens when call volume grows and the in-flight batch gets too large to send.

steps: Expose a small stable logging API with levels, structured fields and runtime-configurable sinks. Resolve environment-specific configuration at startup or through a controlled refresh path.
Buffer immutable records in a bounded queue; one writer batches output. Separate formatting, transport and storage so callers do not depend on the environment.
Define whether success means buffered, written or fsynced. Group commit lets several callers share one fsync, but each durable acknowledgment must occur after that flush succeeds.
Flush on shutdown under a deadline, handle disk-full conditions explicitly and redact sensitive fields. Test concurrent writes, rotation, interrupted flushes and configuration changes.

steps: Expose a small stable logging API with levels, structured fields and runtime-configurable sinks. Resolve environment-specific configuration at startup or through a controlled refresh path.
Buffer immutable records in a bounded queue; one writer batches output. Separate formatting, transport and storage so callers do not depend on the environment.
Define whether success means buffered, written or fsynced. Group commit lets several callers share one fsync, but each durable acknowledgment must occur after that flush succeeds.

solution.example: If ten records are acknowledged after one successful fsync, all ten can share its cost. Acknowledging them when merely placed in RAM provides a weaker durability contract.
solution.trap: Calling write() equivalent to durable fsync, or letting a logging failure recurse into the same broken logger.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Preserve enough information to aggregate correctly

Logs describe events; counters, gauges and histograms summarize different measurements. A counter increment is not interchangeable with the current number of live objects, and a gauge may decrease for legitimate reasons.

For latency, percentiles are not mergeable by averaging them. Combine raw observations or compatible histogram/sketch state, then compute the requested quantile. An average is mergeable through sum and count, but carries different information from a tail measure.

Keep client queues bounded and state whether an emit call means accepted in RAM, written or durably flushed. Batch/fsync group commit can amortize I/O, but acknowledging before the required flush weakens durability. Backpressure/drop policy must protect the application rather than cause an outage while observing it.

Use event and ingest timestamps for late data, and avoid unbounded labels such as a unique request id in every metric series. Alert on sustained actionable conditions with deduplication and recovery state. Test collector failure, disk-full conditions, malformed records and counter resets. Security also matters: core dumps and diagnostic payloads may contain credentials, so indexing convenience must not imply broad access.

title: HFT Onsite Round 3 — Sort Complexity + Linux Fundamentals + tail(n) Design
question:
A fully verbal / whiteboard Citsec HFT (Singapore) onsite round — no live coding submission, a wide-ranging interrogation across three areas:

1.
Sort-algorithm complexity, especially quicksort worst case: average vs worst, pivot-selection strategies, when quicksort beats/loses to heapsort and mergesort.
2.
Linux fundamentals: shared memory (shm, mmap), interrupt handling, context switching, system calls.
3.
Design tail -n on a very large file: backward seeking, chunked reads, mmap, and what to do when n is itself large.

Reported as a high-pressure round with rapid cross-examination — treat that as calibration, not a personal signal.

steps: State sorting bounds precisely: comparison sorting needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, while bounded-key non-comparison methods have different assumptions. Explain expected/worst behavior for the chosen algorithm.

For tail(n) on a seekable file, scan fixed-size byte blocks backward, count newlines and retain only enough suffix data to locate the last n lines; define terminal-newline behavior and decode bytes carefully.
For a non-seekable stream, keep a deque of at most n lines. This uses O(size of retained lines) memory; a single line can itself be arbitrarily large.

Explain file descriptors, buffering, page cache and process/thread scheduling only as they affect the requested path. Benchmark filesystem and I/O behavior rather than attributing all latency to CPU complexity.
solution.example: For a billion-line file and n=10, backward scanning avoids reading the entire file when the tail lines are short; a pipe cannot seek and must be consumed.
solution.trap: Claiming a line-count-limited deque has constant byte memory regardless of line length.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Explain the assumptions behind a familiar formula

A definition, implementation and asymptotic guarantee are related but different. A linked list can insert in constant time **given the needed node/predecessor**, but locating that node may take linear time. Randomized quicksort has expected $O(n\log n)$ comparisons, not a universal worst-case guarantee.

For numerical mathematics, write the function and the local approximation. Newton's method comes from setting the tangent-line estimate to zero:

$$
0\approx f(x_k)+f'(x_k)(x_{k+1}-x_k),\qquad
x_{k+1}=x_k-\frac{f(x_k)}{f'(x_k)}.
$$

A simple root and a sufficiently good starting point can give quadratic local convergence; small derivatives or a poor start can cause failure. A memorized update alone does not explain that behavior.

For probability limits, state moment and independence/dependence assumptions. The CLT concerns a normalized sample mean, not a claim that all raw data become normally distributed. For information quantities, state support and log base. A useful interview answer gives the definition, one small example, the computational or statistical consequence and one case where the usual shortcut is invalid.

title: Build a Discord-like TCP Chat Server with Slash Commands, Rooms, Reconnection, and Persistence
question:
Build a runnable multi-client TCP chat server with slash commands, chat rooms, per-room history, reconnection, and persistence across restarts.

Requirements
1.
Multi-client TCP server: listen on a configurable port, serve many clients at once, and read line-based input terminated by
. Each line is either a command (starts with /) or a chat message.
2.
Slash commands, at least:
/help: list the available commands.
/nick <name>: set or change this user's nickname.
/users: list the users currently online.
/quit: disconnect gracefully.
3.
Rooms: create a room (for example /create <room>), join a room (/join <room>), and list rooms (/rooms). A message sent to a room is broadcast to every user in it. A plain message from a user who is in no room gets a helpful error.
4.
History: when a user joins a room, show that room's last 10 messages.
5.
Reconnection: define a user identity (for example user id plus token). A user who disconnects can reconnect later, restore their identity, and rejoin the rooms they were in.
6.
Persistence: users and nicknames, rooms, memberships and room history (at least a retained window) survive a server restart. Any storage is fine (SQLite, files, a key-value store); describe your data model.
7.
Scalability: the server need not be distributed, but explain how the design would scale: the concurrency model for many connections, the storage bottleneck, broadcasting across several server instances, and slow clients.
Input
A port number on the command line.
Lines typed by clients connected with telnet, nc, or PuTTY.
Output / deliverable
A runnable server, a short description of the protocol and data model, and a manual test script showing two clients chatting in a room, history on join, and state restored after a server restart.
Example
client A: /nick alice        -> id=<id> token=<token> nick=alice
client A: /create general
client A: /join general
client B: /nick bob
client B: /join general
client A: hello              -> client B sees "[general] alice: hello"
(restart the server)
client A: /login <id> <token> -> welcome back alice, rooms and last 10 messages restored

steps: Authenticate connections and authorize room membership for every relevant operation. Assign stable message ids and per-conversation ordering metadata, then persist before the promised acknowledgment.

Fan out through a durable broker or partition owner; online connections receive pushes while offline users read from stored conversation history. Use client acknowledgments/cursors to resume after disconnects.
Treat presence as an expiring approximation rather than durable membership. Define edit/delete/tombstone visibility, retention, media upload and multi-device synchronization.
Deduplicate client retries, bound per-client buffers and apply backpressure. Cross-region design must choose an ordering/consistency contract rather than claiming every message is globally instant.
solution.example: On reconnect a client resumes after message sequence 41; replayed message 41 is ignored and messages 42 onward are delivered without inventing a gap-free guarantee the storage layer cannot provide.
solution.trap: Writing only to a socket without durable history, or assuming arrival order across independent servers is a total conversation order.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Define order, persistence and conflict resolution independently

A connection carries messages but is not the durable conversation. Give each operation a stable id and a per-conversation/document version or sequence. After reconnect, a client needs a snapshot/cursor and a way to ignore duplicate replay.

A server can promise order within one partition or conversation without promising a universal global order. Explain which component assigns that order and what happens during failover. Presence is usually an expiring approximation, distinct from durable membership and access rights.

For collaborative text or cells, specify the operation model and conflict rule. Operational transformation and CRDTs need compatible operations and transformation/merge semantics; merely selecting the acronym does not define convergence. A spreadsheet also needs formula dependency tracking and cycle behavior.

Walk through two concurrent changes, one disconnect and a duplicate delivery. Every replica should reach the declared result under the chosen rule, while old snapshots retain their stated version. Deletion and media authorization need consistent serving rules; an offline cache must not silently defeat revocation. Bounded queues and slow-subscriber policy prevent one client from stalling the entire broadcast path.

title: Design a 1:1 Chat System (Pub/Sub, Partitioning, Multi-Region)
question:
Design a one-on-one (1:1) chat system: two users exchange text messages in real time from phones, laptops and browsers, and each user may be logged in on several devices at once.

Scale and assumptions
1.
Users: 100 million daily active users. Each sends about 50 messages per day. Peak traffic is 3 times the average.
2.
Message: a sender, a recipient, a client-generated message id, a timestamp and a text body of up to 4 KB. The average encoded size is 300 bytes.
3.
Presence: at peak, about 20% of daily active users hold an open connection.
4.
Regions: users are spread over three geographic regions (for example US, EU and Asia-Pacific). Two users in a conversation may live in different regions.
5.
History: messages are kept indefinitely, and a user can scroll back through any conversation.
Functional requirements
1.
Send a message to one other user. When the recipient is online, every one of their connected devices receives it within about 500 ms in the same region.
2.
When the recipient is offline, the message is stored and delivered when a device reconnects. Nothing is lost and nothing is shown twice, even when a client retries a send.
3.
Messages within one conversation appear in the same order on every device of both users.
4.
Delivery and read receipts are sent back to the sender.
5.
Load the most recent page of a conversation's history, and page backwards.
Parts to address
1.
Pub/sub and fan-out: how a message travels from the sender's connection to each of the recipient's live connections. Cover which component holds connections, how the system knows where a user is connected, and what happens when a device is offline or reconnects.
2.
Partition key: how messages are partitioned in the message store and in any queue or topic. State the key, why it serves the read and write paths, and what alternatives you rejected.
3.
Cross-region: what happens when sender and recipient are in different regions. Cover where the conversation's data lives, the latency a cross-region message pays, and what happens when a region fails.
4.
Database scaling: how the message store grows to years of history, including sharding, replication, hot conversations and the split between recent and old data.
Deliverables
1.
An architecture diagram (in words is fine) naming each component on the send and receive paths.
2.
The data model for messages and conversations.
3.
Capacity estimates: write rate, storage per day and per year, number of connection gateways, and number of storage shards.
4.
The failure behaviour for a lost acknowledgement, a dropped connection, a gateway crash and a region outage.
Constraints
Group chats, media attachments and end-to-end encryption are out of scope, but the design should not prevent adding them.
State every assumption you add beyond the numbers above.

steps: Define the editable object, operation set, offline behavior and consistency visible to collaborators. Assign document versions and unique operation ids.

Design the feature where a user clicks anywhere on a Figma/FigJam canvas to start a comment thread, and comments update in real time for everyone viewing the file. Often framed as 'design the data model first, then the server architecture' — explicitly not 'design Google Docs'.

Design in-canvas commenting:

A user can click any point on the page to anchor a new comment thread; others can reply, forming threads.
Comments (new threads and replies) propagate to all current viewers of the file in real time.
Interviewers often structure it as: (1) design the data model, then (2) design the server architecture — so deliver a concrete schema before the distributed picture.
Notes
This is not "design Google Docs." Several candidates over-prepared a full collaborative-document/OT design and found it useless — the scope is comment threads anchored to canvas coordinates, nothing more. Go try the feature in FigJam before the interview.
Real scale is modest, so resist over-engineering. Nail the data model (thread anchored to a position, ordered replies, resolved state, author/timestamps) and a sane real-time path (WebSocket/SSE fan-out to file subscribers) before reaching for heavy distributed machinery.

title: Credit Card Service with Points Earning and Redemption System
question:
Design a credit card service that offers points as the customer spends on the card. The customer can redeem their points at any time, with 1 point equating to USD 0.01 in value. Please provide your design.

Example

Input

customer1
100

steps: Use an append-only double-entry ledger in integer minor currency units; for each transfer, debits and credits balance within the currency. Distinguish ledger balance, available balance, holds and external settlement.
Create a durable operation state machine keyed by an idempotency key bound to request parameters. Atomically validate funds and commit ledger entries; serialize conflicting updates for an account.

External providers and subscriptions need pending/retry/reconciliation states, event deduplication and an outbox/inbox pattern. Store effective time, posting time and versioned pricing/points rules rather than rewriting history.
Handle reversals with compensating entries, audit every transition and test concurrent withdrawals, duplicate webhooks and failures between external and local commits.
solution.example: Two simultaneous withdrawals of 80 from an available balance of 100 cannot both succeed. A retry of one successful transfer must return the same operation, not post new ledger entries.
solution.trap: Using floating-point balances or assuming one database transaction can atomically include an arbitrary external payment network.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
#### Model immutable money movements and uncertain external outcomes

Use integer minor units or a controlled decimal representation, with currency and rounding rules explicit. For a balanced transfer within one currency,

$$
\sum_k \operatorname{debit}_k=\sum_k \operatorname{credit}_k.
$$

A ledger balance, an available balance after holds and an external settled balance can differ legitimately. Explain which one the API returns and when each changes.

Bind an idempotency key to a request fingerprint. Within a local transaction, validate the authoritative funds/version, append balanced entries and record the operation result. On a repeated matching key, return that result or its in-progress status; reject a conflicting request that reuses the key.

A payment-provider timeout leaves an unknown outcome. Reconcile using the stable provider operation id and authenticated events rather than sending a fresh charge blindly. Record refunds/reversals as new compensating entries so history remains auditable.

Test concurrent withdrawals, partial settlement, duplicate webhooks, period rollover and rule-version changes. A monthly subscription is not just a timer: proration, retries and effective plan changes need state. These mechanisms are educational system-design patterns, not statements of current financial rules or a recommendation to transact.

title: Design a Highly Reliable Account Balance System
question:
Design the backend that tells a bank customer their current account balance and records every change to it. Customers must never see money lost or counted twice, even when a whole cloud region fails. The ledger of transactions is the authoritative record, and the balance shown to customers must stay consistent with it.

Requirements

Functional:

1.
Read the current balance of an account.
2.
Apply a balance update (credit or debit) with a client-supplied idempotency key. A retried request with the same key must take effect once.
3.
Reconcile displayed balances against the authoritative ledger and surface any account where they differ (drift).

Non-functional, with the targets to design for:

Scale: 50 million accounts, up to 20,000 balance updates per second and 100,000 balance reads per second at peak.
Latency: 99th-percentile read at most 100 ms; 99th-percentile write at most 500 ms.
Consistency: writes are strongly consistent. A customer who has just made an update sees it in the next read (read-your-writes); other readers may see a balance at most 5 seconds old.
Durability and availability: after a single-region outage, RPO is 0 (no acknowledged update is lost or duplicated) and RTO is at most 5 minutes.
Reconciliation: drift for any account is detected within 24 hours, and within 1 hour for the 1% of accounts with the highest balances.
What to deliver
1.
The API, covering the read, the idempotent update and the reconciliation report.
2.
The data model for the ledger and the balance, and which one is the source of truth.
3.
A high-level design with the write path, the read path and the replication between regions.
4.
Failover: what happens to in-flight updates when the primary region fails, and what balance a customer sees afterwards.
5.
The reconciliation design: how drift is found, how often, and what happens when it is found.
6.
Capacity estimates for storage and throughput, using the scale above.
7.
Trade-offs and failure modes you accepted, for example the cost of RPO 0 on write latency.
